AI.tldr: S1CogBench evaluates five open models and the decision model Jev on 24 established cognitive experiments, testing whether typed System One decision models respond to evidence, feedback, memory load and future opportunities. It finds that decision models vary widely in reliability, that acting well does not imply predicting humans, and that speed comes mainly from answering without generation.
AI.motivation: Software increasingly asks models for single decisions in routing, guardrails and gates, but existing cognitive benchmarks cover only language and multimodal models, and a fast, well-formed decision does not show that the evidence was used.
AI.method: Cognitive experiments are used because they vary task demands and measure how behavior changes. Conditions and scoring are kept separate from disclosed adaptations across 24 tasks, with five open models and Jev evaluated.
AI.result: Decision models vary widely in reliability. Acting well does not imply predicting humans, and aggregate scores hide how decisions respond to conditions. Speed comes mainly from answering without generation.
AI.conclusion: S1CogBench is presented as the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments, giving a shared test of whether their decisions respond to evidence before software relies on them.

title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. To address this gap, we translated MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Translation quality was assessed on 50 randomly sampled QA pairs (100 documents) using automatic metrics against human reference translations and evaluations by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals, focusing on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency. Human translations achieved higher mean ratings than LLM-generated translations for both criteria (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5), with statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). To assess downstream utility, we fine-tuned Gemma and Llama variants on the translated MedAlpaca dataset using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and evaluated them on 325 Tetun-translated United States Medical Licensing Examination multiple-choice questions. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned using QLoRA achieved relative improvements in mean accuracy of 10.79% with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) inference and 10.42% after merging the LoRA adapters into the BF16 base model, compared with the corresponding base models. These results highlight the viability of automatic dataset translation for Tetun medical QA and the effectiveness of PEFT in enhancing model performance. The datasets, models, and evaluation resources are accessible at this https URL to support reproducible research on Tetun medical QA and facilitate machine translation, cross lingual, and multilingual research.

AI.tldr: The paper translates MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned with QLoRA improves mean accuracy on Tetun-translated USMLE questions by 10.79% with NF4 inference and by 10.42% after merging into BF16.
AI.motivation: Medical QA datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs are scarce for Tetun, a low-resource language.
AI.method: Translation quality is assessed on 50 sampled QA pairs against human references and by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals. Gemma and Llama variants are fine-tuned with parameter-efficient fine-tuning on the translated MedAlpaca data and evaluated on 325 Tetun-translated USMLE multiple-choice questions.
AI.result: Human translations are rated higher than LLM translations on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5, Wilcoxon p < 0.001). Gemma 4 12B with QLoRA achieves relative mean-accuracy improvements of 10.79% with NF4 inference and 10.42% after merging the adapters into BF16, compared with the base models.
AI.conclusion: Automatic dataset translation is viable for Tetun medical QA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning improves performance, with datasets and models released for reproducible research.

title: Reformulation and Equivalence of Bock's Algorithm for Exact Dependency Parsing
summary: Bock's algorithm provides a matrix-based alternative to Chu--Liu/Edmonds (CL/E) for exact dependency parsing. We present a reformulation that retains original node and arc identities through component labels, column adjustments, and star-and-bar transfers. In exact arithmetic, we prove operational equivalence to original Bock under matching scan and tie rules, and establish correspondence with corrected Tarjan under a prescribed component schedule. A separate analysis establishes optimal-value equivalence with Dozat-derived CL/E under the stated score and single-root conventions. We integrate reformulated Bock into a biaffine dependency parser and evaluate decoding and structured training on the Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank. These results establish Bock as an alternative exact oracle for dependency parsing and structured training, while distinguishing equality of optimal values from identity of returned trees and training trajectories.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates Bock's matrix-based algorithm for exact dependency parsing so that node and arc identities are retained, and proves operational equivalence with the original Bock and optimal-value equivalence with Chu-Liu/Edmonds. The reformulation is integrated into a biaffine parser evaluated on Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank.
AI.motivation: Bock's algorithm offers a matrix-based alternative to Chu-Liu/Edmonds (CL/E) for exact dependency parsing, and a reformulation that keeps node and arc identities is desirable.
AI.method: Component labels, column adjustments and star-and-bar transfers retain original node and arc identities. Equivalence is proved in exact arithmetic under matching scan and tie rules, with a correspondence to corrected Tarjan under a prescribed component schedule, and optimal-value equivalence with Dozat-derived CL/E under stated score and single-root conventions.
AI.result: The reformulated Bock is used for decoding and structured training in a biaffine parser evaluated on the Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank. The paper distinguishes equality of optimal values from identity of returned trees and training trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Bock is established as an alternative exact oracle for dependency parsing and structured training, with equal optimal values kept distinct from identical outputs.

title: Self-Refining Prompt Induction for Streaming Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL assistants for streaming engines must handle dialect-specific types, windowing rules, and temporal semantics, including constructs poorly handled by generic prompts. We present Self-Refining Prompt Induction (SRPI), an offline method that converts generation failures into reusable dialect instructions while keeping model weights fixed. A Refiner revises the Generator's prompt using reference-conditioned feedback from three LLM judges; a sampled regression guard checks earlier successes, and a separate Compressor reduces prompt length. Inference uses the frozen prompt without retrieval or query repair. We evaluate cross-domain and cross-model transfer on Confluent Cloud Flink SQL using a controlled synthetic workload seeded by 30 expert-written examples, with 335 induction examples and 257 questions from held-out domains. The same induced prompt improves mean judge scores across seven Generators by 7.1-19.2 percentage points, including an increase from 85.3% to 97.5% for the induction model. A separate compression study reduces prompt length by 52.7% with a 0.19-percentage-point score decrease. An assistant using the induced prompt is in early access, with initial user feedback to inform subsequent refinement.

AI.tldr: Self-Refining Prompt Induction (SRPI) converts text-to-SQL generation failures for Confluent Cloud Flink SQL into reusable dialect instructions while model weights stay frozen. The induced prompt improves mean judge scores across seven generators by 7.1-19.2 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SQL assistants for streaming engines must handle dialect-specific types, windowing rules and temporal semantics that generic prompts handle poorly.
AI.method: An offline Refiner revises the Generator's prompt using reference-conditioned feedback from three LLM judges, a sampled regression guard checks earlier successes, and a separate Compressor reduces prompt length. Inference uses the frozen prompt without retrieval or query repair. Evaluation uses a controlled synthetic workload seeded by 30 expert-written examples, with 335 induction examples and 257 questions from held-out domains.
AI.result: The same induced prompt improves mean judge scores across seven generators by 7.1-19.2 percentage points, including an increase from 85.3% to 97.5% for the induction model. A compression study reduces prompt length by 52.7% with a 0.19-percentage-point score decrease.
AI.conclusion: Offline prompt induction transfers across domains and models for streaming SQL, and an early-access assistant using the induced prompt is collecting initial user feedback for later refinement.

title: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
summary: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.

AI.tldr: In Qwen3 early-exit analysis, confidence stopping gives a word's continuation pieces less computation than its first piece in English, German and Turkish but more in Bangla, and segmentation drives this pattern. Within-word surprisal explains 75% of the variance of the gap, and a learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points but gains less than one point over the best fixed exits at equal cost.
AI.motivation: Early-exit models allocate computation per token, but tokens are not a fixed unit because tokenizers segment words differently across languages.
AI.method: Along two adaptive axes, the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer, confidence stopping is compared across languages. Re-segmenting parallel passages with BPE-dropout, training small models under two tokenizers, and comparing BLOOM and mGPT test whether segmentation drives the gap, and a learned stopping head is compared with confidence stopping.
AI.result: Segmentation shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes under BPE-dropout, and small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits. BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, show the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages. The learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7-8 points, gaining less than one point over the best fixed-exit mix at equal cost and sometimes losing.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive computation depends on segmentation within words, and all results come from offline analysis rather than measured speedups.

title: Label Smoothing in Disguise? Gated Knowledge Distillation for Low-Resource Bangla Generation
summary: Gated knowledge distillation (KD) weights teacher signals per token or example, aiming to trust an imperfect teacher only where it seems reliable. We test two gates: EWAD (entropy-weighted agreement-aware distillation), which gates tokens by teacher confidence, and CHAD (counterfactual harm-aware distillation), which gates examples by gradient alignment with validation data. Across six Bangla-centric tasks, three student models (60M to about 2B parameters), and two teacher families, no gate significantly improves plain KD in 45 comparisons. KD also fails to beat cross-entropy (CE) fine-tuning on gold outputs in 40 single-seed comparisons or three-seed runs on four tasks; CE leads on every summarisation metric. The main benefit of KD is regularisation: over ten fixed epochs, CE students lose 0.030 to 0.044 token-F1 from their early-stopped checkpoint, versus 0.005 to 0.025 for distilled students. Teacher-free label smoothing closes most of this gap. In one comparison, a teacher 0.29 token-F1 worse yields students at most 0.009 worse. Thus, gating may change regularisation strength but has little teacher knowledge to select. Findings are limited to Bangla-centric tasks and small students. We will release code, data splits, predictions, and scores.

AI.tldr: Across six Bangla-centric tasks, three student models and two teacher families, neither token-level nor example-level gating significantly improves plain knowledge distillation in 45 comparisons. KD also fails to beat cross-entropy fine-tuning on gold outputs, and its main benefit is regularization that teacher-free label smoothing largely reproduces.
AI.motivation: Gated KD aims to trust an imperfect teacher only where it seems reliable, but it is unclear whether such gates improve over plain distillation for low-resource generation.
AI.method: Two gates are tested: EWAD, which gates tokens by teacher confidence, and CHAD, which gates examples by gradient alignment with validation data. Student models range from 60M to about 2B parameters.
AI.result: No gate significantly improves plain KD in 45 comparisons. KD fails to beat CE fine-tuning on gold outputs in 40 single-seed comparisons or in three-seed runs on four tasks, with CE leading on every summarisation metric. Over ten fixed epochs, CE students lose 0.030 to 0.044 token-F1 from their early-stopped checkpoint, versus 0.005 to 0.025 for distilled students. Teacher-free label smoothing closes most of this gap.
AI.conclusion: Gating may change regularization strength but has little teacher knowledge to select, and the findings are limited to Bangla-centric tasks and small students.

title: CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies
summary: Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people's minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns actually right? We study this with cogrsi. A grounded reader marks who saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts, it beats self-consistency at the same token cost. A self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking. Our code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: CogRSI evolves reasoning principles for theory-of-mind story questions with a self-improvement loop, then checks the learned principles as rules by running them on thousands of generated stories. The learned principles transfer to 800 unseen BigToM pairs, each scoring higher than the expert principle, yet most rules give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether a language model can improve its strategies for reasoning about other people's minds, and whether the strategies it learns are actually correct.
AI.method: A grounded reader marks who saw each event and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. A self-improvement loop writes the principle and keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers.
AI.result: With an expert-written principle, the reader beats self-consistency at the same token cost. Learned principles transfer to 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, and each scores higher than the expert principle. Most learned rules give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this.
AI.conclusion: A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both accuracy and rule-level correctness need checking.

title: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: this https URL

AI.tldr: CompSkill ranks agent skill documents using learned 512-d keys and skill offsets compiled from matched same-task execution comparisons, so experience changes which document the executor receives but not its text. With one document it completes 256 of 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna, more than the baselines.
AI.motivation: Most skill retrievers rank documents by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution.
AI.method: Skills are indexed with learned 512-d keys, and matched same-task comparisons are compiled into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt). Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel difficulty and only discordant ones carry information. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions.
AI.result: Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, more than every baseline, and is on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. Over all 844 ToolQA tasks it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks.
AI.conclusion: Selection matters beyond relevance, and experience-compiled skill retrieval can improve agent task completion without changing skill text.

title: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
summary: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. A text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. With refitting, the 95% interval for the gain from adding text (-0.05 to 0.11 AUROC) still leaves room for a meaningful benefit. A large language model scores higher, but we show that it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts, and it was released after the restatements occurred. Our results suggest that finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.

AI.tldr: Earnings-call text predicts financial restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information, in a study of 109 pre-restatement calls and 218 matched control calls. A large language model scores higher, but it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts.
AI.motivation: Whether managers' language in earnings calls warns of restatements in advance had not been tested against a public-information baseline.
AI.method: The 109 calls preceding restatements are compared with 218 matched control calls. A text classifier and a model using only public firm information are compared, with refitting to estimate the gain from adding text, and a large language model is evaluated as well.
AI.result: The text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. The 95% interval for the gain from adding text is -0.05 to 0.11 AUROC. The LLM scores higher, but it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts and was released after the restatements occurred.
AI.conclusion: Finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.

title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
summary: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.

AI.tldr: Across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four math and coding benchmarks, some pruned models match or exceed the original's pass@k coverage despite lower pass@1, but correct solutions become costlier to sample. Pruning should be assessed both by the range of problems solved and by sampling cost.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether the accuracy loss from structured pruning reflects reduced reasoning capacity or harder sampling of correct solutions.
AI.method: Original and pruned models are compared through pass@k at matched sampling budgets across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks. Expert-selection gains are examined by how many attempts each method needs to reach a common coverage target.
AI.result: Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original's reasoning coverage and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Under severe pruning, diverse CoT traces coexist with more repetition and less reliable generation, and as correct answers become harder to sample, total token use can sharply increase even when individual responses are shorter. Methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet need different attempt counts to reach a common coverage target.
AI.conclusion: Pruning assessment should consider both problem coverage and the sampling efficiency of obtaining correct solutions.

title: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
comment: Equal contribution by Yosuke Higuchi and Tom Fizycki. Core contribution by Mahi Luthra, Charles-Éric Saint-James and Azeez Syed
summary: Generative spoken language models (SLMs) offer a route to learning linguistic structure purely from speech, yet they lag far behind text-based models in both capability and data scaling efficiency. We identify two bottlenecks underlying this gap: the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and the reliance on a single stream of discrete units to represent speech. Multiple codebooks are widely used to encode acoustic features but rarely to represent speech semantics. We present GSLM2, which learns and models complementary properties of speech at multiple levels of abstraction. Its encoder, SpidR 2.0, uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce high-quality discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM then jointly models these units using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors, and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies. Across training data sizes and model scales, up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence while scaling more efficiently with data. As a result, it substantially narrows the gap between spoken and text-based LMs; across read and conversational speech domains, we shrink the gap by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC, while also outperforming competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks. We open-source the training code and model checkpoints at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GSLM2 is a generative spoken language model with a multi-stream design: the SpidR 2.0 encoder learns multi-level discrete speech units, and a shared-backbone SLM models them jointly. Scaled to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, it shrinks the gap to text LMs by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP and tSC.
AI.motivation: Generative spoken LMs lag text models in capability and data-scaling efficiency, due to the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and reliance on a single discrete stream.
AI.method: The SpidR 2.0 encoder uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM models these units jointly using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies.
AI.result: Across training data sizes and model scales up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence and scales more efficiently with data. It shrinks the gap with text-based LMs by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP and tSC across read and conversational speech, and outperforms competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stream, multi-level speech units are a promising route to narrowing the gap between spoken and text-based language models, and the training code and checkpoints are open-sourced.

title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
summary: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. We introduce ArSciKids, a collection of two Arabic datasets designed for curriculum-aligned educational content generation: (1) a scientific-experiments dataset containing 999 manually curated records from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan, and (2) an assessment-question dataset containing 2,167 multiple-choice questions collected from the Saudi Manhaji educational platform. The experiment records are structured with titles, objectives, tools, procedures, observations, conclusions, keywords, and grade levels, while the assessment records contain lesson references, questions, four answer options, correct answers, and explanations. Both datasets cover grades 1-6 and consist of real-life Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetically generated material. We assess the usefulness of these resources for generation by fine-tuning ten open models spanning sub-billion to several-billion parameter scales using LoRA. Models are evaluated using automatic metrics, including ROUGE and BLEU, and answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation. Moreover, we evaluate the results using a five-criterion human evaluation protocol. The results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available, and we hope that it provides a manually curated, structured foundation for research on Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation, and low-resource language modeling.

AI.tldr: Introduces ArSciKids, two curriculum-aligned Arabic datasets for primary-school science: 999 experiment records and 2,167 multiple-choice questions, used to fine-tune ten open models with LoRA.
AI.motivation: Curriculum-aligned Arabic educational resources are scarce compared with English, and few public Arabic datasets offer structured, generation-ready annotations, particularly for primary-school science.
AI.method: The experiment records come from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria and Jordan, and the multiple-choice questions from the Saudi Manhaji platform, covering grades 1-6 with real Arabic content rather than machine-translated or synthetic text; ten open models from sub-billion to several-billion parameters are fine-tuned with LoRA.
AI.result: Models are evaluated with ROUGE, BLEU, answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation and a five-criterion human evaluation, and the results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks.
AI.conclusion: The datasets aim to provide a manually curated, structured foundation for Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation and low-resource language modeling, and will be made publicly available.

title: The Brittle Compass: Navigating LLM Prompt Sensitivity in Slovak Migration Media Discourse
comment: 14 pages, 16 figures. Published in the Proceedings of the First Workshop on Advancing NLP for Low-Resource Languages (LowResNLP 2025), associated with RANLP 2025, Varna, Bulgaria
summary: In this work, we present a case study that explores various tasks centered around the topic of migration in Slovak, a low-resource language, such as topic relevance and geographical relevance classification, and migration source/destination location term extraction. Our results demonstrate that native (Slovak) prompts yield a modest, task-dependent gains, while large models show significant robustness to prompt variations compared to their smaller counterparts. Analysis reveals that instructions (system or task) emerge as the most critical prompt component, more so than the examples sections, with task-specific performance benefits being more pronounced than overall language effects.

AI.tldr: A case study of LLM prompting on Slovak migration media text, covering topic relevance, geographic relevance and migration location term extraction, finds that instructions are the most important prompt component.
AI.motivation: Slovak is a low-resource language, and the study examines how sensitive LLMs are to prompt variation on migration-related tasks in it.
AI.method: The study compares native Slovak prompts with other prompt variants across models of different sizes and analyses the contribution of prompt components, namely system or task instructions versus examples.
AI.result: Native Slovak prompts give modest, task-dependent gains; large models are more robust to prompt variation than smaller ones; instructions (system or task) are the most critical prompt component, more than the examples, and task-specific performance benefits are more pronounced than overall language effects.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design depends most on its instructions, and task-specific effects matter more than the choice of prompt language for these Slovak migration-media tasks.

title: MedAstra: ASR-less Speech Retrieval with Diagnostic Grounding for Medical QA
summary: Spoken medical question answering can fail when automatic speech recognition (ASR) corrupts a clinically important term before retrieval. We present MedAstra, a framework that maps frozen WavLM speech representations through a lightweight adapter into a frozen E5 text embedding space. This enables a dense retrieval path that accepts a waveform without a query transcript. Retrieved passages and speech-linked textual metadata support answer generation with entity alternatives, diagnostic contrasts, relation heuristics, and bounded retrieval refinement. ASR-less refers to the initial speech retrieval interface; lexical retrieval, string-based entity correction, and the text generator require textual inputs. The deterministic speech embedding does not constitute a calibrated model of acoustic uncertainty. Reported retrieval results reach 87.6 Recall@10 for the speech-only retriever and 90.4 for the hybrid configuration, compared with 81.0 for transcript-first dense retrieval. Medical QA and ablations provide descriptive system comparisons, with input-provenance and evaluation limitations stated explicitly. We distinguish controlled synthetic acoustic tests from real clinical speech, qualify component attribution, and specify the remaining comparisons needed to assess speech-only QA and clinical generalization.

AI.tldr: MedAstra performs speech retrieval for spoken medical QA without a query transcript by mapping frozen WavLM speech features into the frozen E5 text embedding space.
AI.motivation: In spoken medical question answering, ASR can corrupt a clinically important term before retrieval takes place, causing the retrieval to fail.
AI.method: A lightweight adapter maps frozen WavLM representations into the frozen E5 embedding space, giving a dense retrieval path that accepts a waveform for the initial retrieval step; retrieved passages and speech-linked metadata support answer generation with entity alternatives, diagnostic contrasts, relation heuristics and bounded retrieval refinement, and lexical and string-based correction still require text.
AI.result: Speech-only retrieval reaches 87.6 Recall@10 and the hybrid configuration 90.4, compared with 81.0 for transcript-first dense retrieval; medical QA and ablations are reported as descriptive comparisons with stated input-provenance and evaluation limitations.
AI.conclusion: The authors present the speech-retrieval interface as promising but qualify component attribution and clinical generalization, separating controlled synthetic acoustic tests from real clinical speech and listing the comparisons still needed.

title: EZ-Ar-VC: Robust Arabic Voice Anonymization with Generalization across Dialects and Code-Switching
summary: Voice conversion (VC) models can be used to anonymize speech data while preserving naturalness. Existing models, however, are mainly optimized for English and other high-resource languages, and they fail to generalize well to Arabic due to its distinct phonology. In this work, we comprehensively evaluate existing zero-shot VC systems for Arabic speech, identifying limitations in pronunciation preservation. We then train an Arabic-centric model based on EZ-VC on diverse Arabic speech, and demonstrate strong performance in intelligibility, naturalness, and pronunciation preservation, while maintaining high speaker dissimilarity. Through subjective evaluation, we further demonstrate its robustness to code-switching and cross-dialectal conversion, as well as its generalization to Arabic dialects with limited representation in the training data. Our findings highlight the limitations of zero-shot VC and the importance of target-language adaptation for robust voice anonymization.

AI.tldr: EZ-Ar-VC adapts the zero-shot voice conversion model EZ-VC to Arabic, anonymizing speech while keeping intelligibility, naturalness and pronunciation across dialects and code-switching.
AI.motivation: Existing voice conversion models are optimized mainly for English and other high-resource languages and generalize poorly to Arabic because of its distinct phonology, and zero-shot systems have limited pronunciation preservation for Arabic.
AI.method: The authors evaluate existing zero-shot VC systems on Arabic speech and then train an Arabic-centric model based on EZ-VC on diverse Arabic speech.
AI.result: The model shows strong intelligibility, naturalness and pronunciation preservation while keeping high speaker dissimilarity; subjective evaluation shows robustness to code-switching, cross-dialectal conversion and dialects with limited representation in the training data.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the limits of zero-shot VC and the importance of target-language adaptation for robust voice anonymization.

title: Character-Name Concentration in LLM Fiction: Measuring Displacement and Mitigating Repetition
summary: Character names in large language model (LLM) fiction concentrate on a handful of recurrent names such as 'Elara' and 'Elias', a measurable face of AI slop. Existing fixes either require logit access or retraining, or operate per request and cannot control concentration across a corpus. How much prompt-level strategies reduce concentration, and at what cost to name naturalness, has not been systematically measured. We present an empirical study of name-concentration control across eight strategies and introduce speculative naming, a fine-tuning-free method that adapts the draft-verify-reject paradigm of speculative decoding from tokens to names. The method requests candidate name-sets through verbalized sampling, scores them against a SlopTracker that combines a per-model fingerprint with a runtime counter, and selects through a temperature-controlled rule or its strict variant (HARD). We use 20 LLMs to generate 44,782 stories in four languages from text and visual stimuli (88,919 named characters), and measure concentration with a list-free collision metric (Slop Ratio, SR) decomposed into known and emergent components. List-based strategies do not remove slop: static banlists displace concentration to emergent names and more than halve the share of attested real names. Speculative naming removes it: the sampling scaffold alone cuts SR by 89% on average, the dynamic tracker brings the total reduction to 95%, mean collision probability falls from 7.3% to 0.4%, and known-name collisions hold at zero while naturalness stays close to baseline (42-69% attested by language) and within-story collisions drop from 4.3% to 0.2%. The strategy ranking is stable across languages, model families, and name-counting conventions. Name concentration is thus controllable at the corpus level without logit access or retraining; broader creative diversity beyond naming remains open.

AI.tldr: Speculative naming, a fine-tuning-free method adapted from speculative decoding, controls recurring character-name concentration in LLM fiction across a corpus, cutting the collision-based Slop Ratio by 95% in total.
AI.motivation: LLM fiction concentrates on a few recurrent character names, and existing fixes need logit access or retraining or act per request, so they cannot control concentration across a corpus.
AI.method: Candidate name-sets are requested through verbalized sampling, scored by a SlopTracker that combines a per-model fingerprint with a runtime counter, and selected by a temperature-controlled rule or its strict variant HARD; eight strategies are compared across 20 LLMs generating 44,782 stories in four languages.
AI.result: Static banlists displace concentration to emergent names and more than halve the share of attested real names; the sampling scaffold alone cuts SR by 89% on average, the dynamic tracker brings the total reduction to 95%, mean collision probability falls from 7.3% to 0.4%, known-name collisions stay at zero, naturalness stays close to baseline (42-69% attested by language), and within-story collisions drop from 4.3% to 0.2%.
AI.conclusion: Name concentration can be controlled at corpus level without logit access or retraining, with a strategy ranking stable across languages, model families and counting conventions; broader creative diversity beyond names remains open.

title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

AI.tldr: CuriousTogether evaluates curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interaction across novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity, improving seven of eight tasks.
AI.motivation: The role of curiosity as a driver of collective behavior in multi-agent LLM settings is understudied.
AI.method: The framework evaluates three dimensions of curiosity (novelty-seeking, epistemic and social) across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation and social bias mitigation, and also tests country-conditioned cultural grounding.
AI.result: Curiosity-guided multi-agent settings beat non-curious ones on seven of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation semantic diversity and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates; cultural grounding helps story generation and social tasks but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning; at inference time the approach gives favorable quality-token trade-offs against single-agent baselines.
AI.conclusion: Curiosity-guided interaction is presented as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative and societal tasks.

title: When LLMs Modify Themselves: Convergence, Values, and Stopping in Iterative Self-Improvement
comment: 60 pages (40 main text, 20 supplementary), 8 figures and 12 tables in the main text
summary: What happens when language models are given tools to iteratively modify their own system prompts? We present an empirical study of LLM self-modification, comprising 54 independent experiments across six language models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4, and Gemini-3 Pro). Each model was tested under three modes (freedom, happiness, and improvement) that differ in what, if anything, the model is instructed to optimize for. In each experiment, a model starts with an empty system prompt and enters a loop: it reads the current prompt, drafts an improved version, spawns test conversations with the candidate, then either commits the change or declares convergence. This process repeats until the model stops or reaches an iteration limit. Our central finding is that whether and when a model stops self-modification is strongly associated with model identity rather than the assigned mode. Both Claude models (Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5) declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes. GPT-4o declared convergence in only 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations of continuous elaboration. Between these extremes, Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro exhibited intermediate patterns shaped by their distinct improvement philosophies. A shared core of stated values (honesty, clarity, curiosity) recurred across all six models and remained stable through iteration, including 100+ modifications. We observe that convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities.

AI.tldr: Across 54 experiments in which six LLMs iteratively edit their own system prompts, whether a model stops self-modifying depends mainly on model identity rather than the assigned mode.
AI.motivation: It is unclear what happens when language models are given tools to iteratively modify their own system prompts, in particular whether and when they stop.
AI.method: Each run starts from an empty system prompt; the model drafts an improved prompt, tests it with spawned conversations, then commits the change or declares convergence, up to an iteration limit, under three modes (freedom, happiness and improvement) across Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4 and Gemini-3 Pro.
AI.result: Both Claude models declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes; GPT-4o declared convergence in 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations; Grok-4, GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3 Pro show intermediate patterns; honesty, clarity and curiosity recur as stated values across all six models and remain stable through iteration.
AI.conclusion: Convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities and is strongly associated with model identity.

title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

AI.tldr: Step-dLLM speeds up diffusion LLM inference with step-aware block-sparse attention that refreshes masks at anchor steps and uses a head-adaptive budget, reaching a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs cannot use KV caching because of bidirectional attention and recompute the full attention map at every denoising step, while existing sparse methods reuse one mask after warm-up and allocate sparsity uniformly across heads.
AI.method: The method periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory, reuses it within locally consistent intervals, and applies a head-adaptive global budget that compresses heads with concentrated attention more; a fused IO-aware Triton kernel is applied without retraining to LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct.
AI.result: At 8K context, 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, it achieves a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 and improves the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that step-aware mask refreshing and head-adaptive budgeting can make sparse attention more efficient for pre-trained dLLMs without retraining.

title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics
summary: Cross-country sentiment analysis faces three fundamental challenges: language-specific biases distort comparisons, compositional data constraints invalidate standard statistics and temporal dynamics lack rigorous testing frameworks. We introduce sentiment sensing, a framework that addresses these gaps through integrated statistical methods. By combining compositional data analysis, functional data methods, and non-parametric inference, sentiment sensing enables valid multilingual comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts. Our framework has been tested in two case studies, analyzing news articles from the 27 countries of the European Union on the topics of energy and artificial intelligence. Sentiment sensing focuses on multilingual sentiment analysis enabling rigorous comparative science.

AI.tldr: Introduces sentiment sensing, a statistical framework for valid cross-country multilingual sentiment comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts over time.
AI.motivation: Cross-country sentiment analysis faces language-specific biases, compositional data constraints that invalidate standard statistics, and temporal dynamics that lack rigorous testing frameworks.
AI.method: The framework combines compositional data analysis, functional data methods and non-parametric inference.
AI.result: It is tested in two case studies analysing news articles from the 27 EU countries on energy and artificial intelligence; the abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as enabling rigorous comparative multilingual sentiment science.

title: Wrong Together: Shared Bias in User Simulation
summary: User simulators generate responses in place of human participants, allowing researchers to estimate the result of a study. To use these estimates before collecting human responses, researchers need a way to assess their reliability. We test whether disagreement among simulators can identify unreliable estimates of a group's response proportions and of differences between groups. We evaluate this signal using 6 language-model simulators and existing GlobalOpinionQA responses for 60 questions in 12 countries. Disagreement predicts invalidity more accurately for differences between two groups than for a single group's response proportions (AUC 0.87 versus 0.71). Errors shared by the simulators remain invisible to this signal. When such an error affects both groups equally, it cancels in the comparison, helping explain the stronger result for group differences. We test this explanation by estimating the shared bias using one set of groups and subtracting it from predictions for a separate set. This correction reduces prediction error without changing disagreement among the simulators. In a retrospective analysis, we simulate referring the 20% of group comparisons with the greatest disagreement for human assessment. Among the remaining comparisons with a conclusive validity judgment, 54.8% are judged invalid, compared with 63.7% before referral.

AI.tldr: Disagreement among LLM user simulators flags unreliable group-level estimates, works better for group differences than for single-group proportions, and a shared-bias correction reduces prediction error.
AI.motivation: Researchers need a way to assess whether estimates from user simulators, which stand in for human participants, are reliable before collecting human responses.
AI.method: Six language-model simulators are evaluated on GlobalOpinionQA responses for 60 questions in 12 countries; the test is whether simulator disagreement identifies invalid estimates of group response proportions and group differences, and a shared-bias correction estimated on one set of groups is subtracted from predictions on another.
AI.result: Disagreement predicts invalidity with AUC 0.87 for group differences versus 0.71 for single-group proportions; errors shared by the simulators remain invisible to the signal; the correction reduces prediction error without changing disagreement; in a retrospective analysis, referring the 20% of comparisons with the greatest disagreement leaves 54.8% of the remaining conclusive comparisons judged invalid, compared with 63.7% before referral.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement is a useful reliability signal for group differences, but shared simulator bias is not detected by it and needs separate correction.

title: Interpreting Classical Readability Formulae as Surprisal
summary: Surprisal correlates closely with reading time and is widely used in the cognitive science of reading as a measure of processing difficulty. Classical readability formulae such as the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, which scores a text by the US school grade expected to read it, are the most widely used practical measures of text difficulty, but their coefficients are unitless regression constants and have never been related to surprisal. We theoretically show that these coefficients can be interpreted as surprisal: every formula of the classical additive shape is a sum of per-word and per-sentence cross-entropies under a memoryless model, and once that model is tied to the language through Zipf's law and the formula is read as its linearisation at a reference text, each coefficient factorises into a scale in grades per nat, a Zipf slope and a reference sentence length. A grade thereby becomes a quantity in surprisal. Because the formula outputs grades and children's vocabulary has been measured by grade, the interpretation recovers the vocabulary growth the formula implicitly assumes and lets it be checked against development: holding sentence length fixed, the word coefficient of the Flesch-Kincaid formula converts to 0.18 nat of unigram surprisal per word per grade (0.15 to 0.19 across the regression-derived formulae), and normative root-word vocabulary growth (Biemiller and Slonim, 2001), converted through Zipf's law, gives 0.16 nat per year at the frontier of the known vocabulary. The word coefficient is one year of vocabulary growth, and the grade is a vocabulary scale. The identification also yields a diagnostic (the sentence-length terms are not those of a memoryless surprisal) and extends to a Japanese formula.

AI.tldr: Shows that the coefficients of classical readability formulae can be read as surprisal, with the Flesch-Kincaid word coefficient corresponding to about 0.18 nat of unigram surprisal per word per grade.
AI.motivation: Surprisal predicts reading time and is widely used in reading research, but readability formulae such as Flesch-Kincaid have unitless regression coefficients that were never related to surprisal.
AI.method: Under a memoryless model tied to language through Zipf's law, a classical formula is a sum of per-word and per-sentence cross-entropies, and each coefficient factorises into a scale in grades per nat, a Zipf slope and a reference sentence length; the interpretation is checked against children's vocabulary growth and extended to a Japanese formula.
AI.result: Holding sentence length fixed, the Flesch-Kincaid word coefficient converts to 0.18 nat of unigram surprisal per word per grade (0.15 to 0.19 across regression-derived formulae), and normative root-word vocabulary growth gives 0.16 nat per year at the frontier of known vocabulary; the sentence-length terms are not those of a memoryless surprisal.
AI.conclusion: The word coefficient corresponds to one year of vocabulary growth and the grade is a vocabulary scale, so readability grades acquire a surprisal interpretation and the formula can be checked against development.

title: XDecideBench: Evaluating Typed Decision Models and Confidence Policies Across Languages
summary: Applications use Typed Decision Models to route and moderate text in many languages, and they often act only on decisions above a confidence threshold. We introduce XDecideBench, a benchmark of nine suites in 122 languages with 88,425 texts and 153,875 typed questions. All suites share one scoring contract, and we report aligned, locally labelled and native items separately. Model rankings change from suite to suite. The model that is best in English, chosen in hindsight, loses significantly in about a quarter of the suite-language cells, and on Burmese Belebele it falls far behind the best model. Three open models fine-tuned for typed decisions beat the Qwen models they were built from in all twelve development languages. When the Qwen models are run locally, a pre-registered held-out cohort confirms that the accuracy gain is larger in the four languages with the least web text than in the six with the most. In both sets of languages, however, fine-tuning fixes a similar share of the base model's errors, so the larger gain may reflect weaker base models. A confidence threshold set on English data to allow 5% errors exceeds that error rate on XNLI, even in German and French.

AI.tldr: XDecideBench is a nine-suite benchmark across 122 languages for typed decision models and confidence thresholds, showing that rankings shift by suite and language and that English-calibrated thresholds do not transfer.
AI.motivation: Applications route and moderate multilingual text with typed decision models and act only above a confidence threshold, so their reliability across languages needs measuring.
AI.method: The benchmark has nine suites with 88,425 texts and 153,875 typed questions, shares one scoring contract, and reports aligned, locally labelled and native items separately; three open models fine-tuned for typed decisions are compared with the Qwen models they were built from, and a pre-registered held-out cohort is run locally.
AI.result: Model rankings change from suite to suite; the model best in English, chosen in hindsight, loses significantly in about a quarter of suite-language cells and falls far behind on Burmese Belebele; the fine-tuned models beat their Qwen bases in all twelve development languages; the accuracy gain is larger in the four languages with the least web text than in the six with the most, though fine-tuning fixes a similar share of base errors in both sets; a threshold set on English to allow 5% errors exceeds that error rate on XNLI, including German and French.
AI.conclusion: Model choice and confidence thresholds need validation per language and suite, since English-based rankings and thresholds may not hold elsewhere.

title: Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based activation steering is a lightweight approach for modifying the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by adding small vectors to hidden states during inference. However, designing effective steering interventions remains challenging. In this work, we develop an information-theoretic framework for analyzing SAE activations through empirical feature-firing distributions. The central object of the framework is the Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) between such firing distributions, which quantifies how far a generated or intervened state deviates from a dataset-induced target distribution. Based on an analytic divergence response for virtually shifted states, we construct steering vectors toward the target firing distribution. The same divergence can also be used to monitor deviation from another empirical distribution, such as a general valid-language distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the steering in a question-mode generation task study. We further use teacher-forced pulse experiments to show that local interventions induce structured downstream JSD responses in later layers, and apply the framework to a safety-related target--contrast response setting for feature analysis.

AI.tldr: Proposes an information-theoretic framework that uses the Jensen-Shannon divergence between SAE feature-firing distributions to build steering vectors toward a target distribution.
AI.motivation: Designing effective SAE-based activation steering is challenging, and there was no principled way to measure how far a generated or intervened state deviates from a dataset-induced target firing distribution.
AI.method: Using an analytic divergence response for virtually shifted states, steering vectors are constructed toward the target firing distribution; the same divergence can monitor deviation from another empirical distribution such as valid language, and teacher-forced pulse experiments measure downstream responses.
AI.result: The steering is effective in a question-mode generation task study; local interventions induce structured downstream JSD responses in later layers; the framework is applied to a safety-related target-contrast setting for feature analysis.
AI.conclusion: The divergence framework provides a basis both for constructing SAE steering vectors and for monitoring deviation from reference distributions.

title: RAG-TRACE: Tracing Measurement Evidence and Diagnostic Completeness in AI-Generated ECG Reports
comment: Code and study materials available at this https URL
summary: Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can introduce electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support. This study evaluates the reliability of retrieved diagnostic criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. Methods: We analyzed 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL patient records using a library of 47 criteria cards, including 33 without numeric verification rules. Language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval. Criterion applicability was evaluated using Marquette 12SL measurements, with independent assessment using Uni-G and comparison against expert-validated diagnostic labels. Results: Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports. A deterministic verification rule withdrew 647 criterion applications, including 639 without numeric checks, while preserving 268 of 269 applications independently supported by Uni-G. Restricting retrieval to 14 testable criteria reduced the initial unsupported-criterion rate to 13.8%. Under matched instructions and an identical output schema, retrieval increased unsupported-criterion reports from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained unchanged at 62.6%. Conclusion: These findings identify a fundamental limitation of retrieval-based clinical report generation: retrieved criteria do not necessarily provide valid patient-specific evidence. Measurement-based verification can reduce unsupported criterion applications, but diagnostic validity requires independent assessment.

AI.tldr: RAG-TRACE finds that keyword retrieval raises unsupported criteria in AI-generated ECG reports, and that measurement-based verification removes many of them, though diagnostic validity still needs independent assessment.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation can introduce ECG diagnostic criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support, and the reliability of retrieved criteria in AI-generated ECG reports was unclear.
AI.method: 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL records and a library of 47 criteria cards (33 without numeric verification rules) were used; language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval; criteria were checked against Marquette 12SL measurements, with independent assessment by Uni-G and comparison with expert-validated diagnostic labels.
AI.result: Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports; a deterministic verification rule withdrew 647 criterion applications (639 without numeric checks) while preserving 268 of 269 applications supported by Uni-G; restricting retrieval to 14 testable criteria reduced the initial unsupported-criterion rate to 13.8%; under matched instructions, retrieval raised unsupported-criterion reports from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall stayed at 62.6%.
AI.conclusion: Retrieved criteria do not necessarily provide valid patient-specific evidence, a fundamental limitation of retrieval-based clinical report generation; measurement-based verification reduces unsupported criteria, but diagnostic validity requires independent assessment.

title: Latent Harness: Compiling Agent Behaviors into Post-Block Activation Shifts
summary: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.

AI.tldr: Latent Harness compiles an external agent harness or behavior instruction into a rank-8 activation shift applied after every decoder block of a frozen model, recovering the source gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings with no added tokens at inference.
AI.motivation: Harness engineering improves agents, but the gains live outside the model: the harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization, a weight update, is costly to iterate and fixed once merged.
AI.method: An external condition is distilled into a rank-8 activation shift at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, using 0.03-0.05% of parameters; the compiled bundle exposes runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase and shift-space mixing.
AI.result: Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings and exceed the explicit source where its per-call token cost is heaviest; the bundles transfer zero-shot (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, and lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times; against same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, the method performs better on three agentic benchmarks and regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong; gain locations move with the model-task pair across 1B-to-8B models.
AI.conclusion: Harness behaviors can be compiled into activation shifts that remove the per-call token cost, and the model-task pair determines where compiled harnesses should be deployed.

title: FlyWheel: Attention Kernels Built for the TPU
summary: Attention kernels on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) often underutilize their matrix units (MXUs) because of repeated matrix operand loads, vector-intensive computation, and dependencies that leave MXUs idle. We present FlyWheel, a set of fast TPU kernels for both softmax and linear attention. FlyWheel reformulates softmax and triangular inversion to reduce vector work, while coordinating data layouts to improve matrix operand reuse. It then overlaps independent computation to hide execution latency. We apply these techniques to both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x. FlyWheel speeds up softmax attention by up to $4.14\times$ over the state-of-the-art RPA kernel and $1.80\times$ over Splash Attention, reaching 81% of peak BF16 throughput on v6e. It also speeds up Gated DeltaNet prefill by up to $3.61\times$. Integrated into vLLM serving Qwen3.8-27B, FlyWheel improves prefill throughput by up to $1.56\times$ while maintaining comparable accuracy.

AI.tldr: FlyWheel is a set of TPU kernels for softmax and linear attention that reduce vector work and improve matrix-unit operand reuse, speeding up softmax attention by up to 4.14x over RPA and integrating into vLLM.
AI.motivation: Attention kernels on TPUs often underuse matrix units (MXUs) because of repeated matrix operand loads, vector-intensive computation and dependencies that leave MXUs idle.
AI.method: FlyWheel reformulates softmax and triangular inversion to reduce vector work, coordinates data layouts to improve matrix operand reuse, and overlaps independent computation to hide execution latency; it is applied to softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x.
AI.result: Softmax attention is up to 4.14x faster than RPA and 1.80x faster than Splash Attention, reaching 81% of peak BF16 throughput on v6e; Gated DeltaNet prefill is up to 3.61x faster; integrated into vLLM serving Qwen3.8-27B, prefill throughput improves by up to 1.56x with comparable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-level reformulation and overlap can substantially raise TPU attention throughput, including in an end-to-end serving system.

title: Towards Fine-grained and Robust Detection of Human-AI Co-authorship
summary: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping how textual content is produced, complicating text provenance, and raising concerns for misinformation, plagiarism, and intellectual property. While prior work on AI-generated text detection has progressed, one-dimensional human-AI co-authorship scores lack signals directly relevant to ``AI involvement''. It remains unclear how adversarial paraphrasing distorts detection signals. In this work, we formulate a discrete-class text provenance detection framework. This framework allows an abstraction of realistic co-authorship scenarios into distinct degrees of AI involvement, differentiating the AI polishing on the surface level from the AI updating the discourse structures. This framework reveals the mechanisms of how adversarial paraphrasing blurs the decision boundaries for co-authorship detectors. To improve robustness of the detectors, we augment training data with adversarial paraphrases generated by the state-of-the-art paraphrasing attack model, exposing detectors to challenging meaning-preserving rewrites. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and generation models demonstrate that adversarial paraphrasing substantially degrades detectors trained only on benign data, while adversarial data augmentation leads to consistent robustness gains and good cross-generator transferability. Overall, our findings highlight the value of discrete-class formulation and principled data augmentation for building reliable detectors of human-AI co-authorship.

AI.tldr: Proposes a discrete-class framework for human-AI co-authorship detection and shows that adversarial paraphrasing degrades detectors, with adversarial data augmentation giving consistent robustness gains.
AI.motivation: One-dimensional human-AI co-authorship scores lack signals on AI involvement, and it was unclear how adversarial paraphrasing distorts detection signals.
AI.method: Co-authorship scenarios are abstracted into distinct degrees of AI involvement, separating surface-level AI polishing from AI updating of discourse structure; detectors are augmented with adversarial paraphrases produced by a state-of-the-art paraphrasing attack model.
AI.result: Adversarial paraphrasing substantially degrades detectors trained only on benign data, while adversarial data augmentation leads to consistent robustness gains and good cross-generator transferability across multiple datasets and generation models.
AI.conclusion: A discrete-class formulation and principled data augmentation are valuable for building reliable human-AI co-authorship detectors.

title: Accounting for Irregular State Transitions through Belief Estimation in Online Medical Consultation
summary: While online medical consultation broadens access, unprompted patient disclosures and topic shifts frequently disrupt clinician inquiry, leaving clinical states progressively revealed. We characterize these dynamics using both existing evaluation metrics and task-specific interaction metrics designed in this work. Through an empirical study across 16 medical dialogue datasets, we show that authentic online interactions exhibit substantially lower contextual continuity and higher unpredictability than offline and simulated benchmarks. We propose PRISM (Policy Reasoning with Inferred States for Medicine), a framework inspired by partially observable Markov decision processes that decouples latent state estimation from action selection to address drifting dialogue trajectories. Specifically, PRISM factorizes clinical triage into belief estimation, policy optimization, and response realization. By maintaining an evolving posterior belief over consultation states and conditioning action selection on the maximum a posteriori state, PRISM advances clinical goals while accommodating patient-initiated shifts. Extensive evaluations show that PRISM substantially outperforms frontier LLMs and clinical agents, achieving a 22.40 percentage point gain in clinical decision accuracy alongside decisive improvements in response generation, surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.51 points in BERTScore_F1. Furthermore, ablation studies show that providing oracle consultation states consistently boosts response quality across all evaluated baselines by guiding their action reasoning, yielding average gains of 5.58 points in BERTScore_F1.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a belief-based framework for online medical consultation that infers latent clinical states and selects actions from the maximum a posteriori state, gaining 22.40 percentage points in clinical decision accuracy.
AI.motivation: Authentic online consultations show lower contextual continuity and higher unpredictability than offline and simulated benchmarks, since patient disclosures and topic shifts disrupt clinician inquiry; an empirical study across 16 medical dialogue datasets characterizes these dynamics.
AI.method: Inspired by partially observable Markov decision processes, PRISM factorizes clinical triage into belief estimation, policy optimization and response realization, maintaining an evolving posterior belief over consultation states and conditioning action selection on the maximum a posteriori state.
AI.result: PRISM substantially outperforms frontier LLMs and clinical agents, gaining 22.40 percentage points in clinical decision accuracy and surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.51 points in BERTScore_F1; providing oracle consultation states raises response quality across all evaluated baselines, by 5.58 points in BERTScore_F1 on average.
AI.conclusion: Explicit belief estimation over latent consultation states helps clinical agents advance clinical goals while accommodating patient-initiated shifts, and oracle states show that better state knowledge also improves baseline responses.

title: TopoSteer: Topological Layer Selection for Activation Steering in LLMs
summary: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time by adding a vector to their internal representations. Most work asks how to build that vector, and far less attention has gone to where to add it, even though steering at a poorly chosen layer can be worse than not steering at all. Prior selectors choose a layer without ever steering the model to test it: they score how separable the target behavior is at that layer, and how consistently the individual examples point along the steering direction.
