We argue that what matters is not the separability of the two activation clouds, nor the alignment of individual displacements with their mean, but the extent of the cloud of per-example displacements that mean-difference steering averages. We propose a topology-based layer selection method, called TopoSteer, which scores a layer by the total H_0 persistence of its displacement cloud, computed as the length of the cloud's Euclidean minimum spanning tree. We show that the score focuses on the displacement cloud's relative geometry, while class separation affects it only through standardization. We also provide a theoretical explanation for our method by proving that, as example-level variation increases, TopoSteer and discriminability move in opposite directions, so the two criteria can rank layers in opposite ways. Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer provides a principled alternative to discriminability- and separability-based layer selection and yields more effective steering without requiring held-out validation.

AI.tldr: TopoSteer chooses the layer for activation steering by the total H0 persistence of the per-example displacement cloud, computed as the length of its Euclidean minimum spanning tree, rather than by class separability.
AI.motivation: Steering at a poorly chosen layer can be worse than not steering, yet existing layer selectors score separability or alignment without steering the model, and miss the extent of the displacement cloud that mean-difference steering averages.
AI.method: Each layer is scored by the total H0 persistence of its displacement cloud, the length of the cloud's Euclidean minimum spanning tree; class separation affects the score only through standardization.
AI.result: The authors prove that as example-level variation increases, TopoSteer and discriminability move in opposite directions, so the two criteria can rank layers in opposite ways; across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer gives more effective steering without requiring held-out validation.
AI.conclusion: Topological displacement geometry provides a principled alternative to discriminability- and separability-based layer selection for activation steering.

title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
summary: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

AI.tldr: Legible fine-tuning writes new facts in a form the model reads at the bridge layer, reducing the two-hop curse without multi-hop training data and reaching 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE.
AI.motivation: A model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it in two-hop questions; this is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, whereas the authors argue the reasoning is intact and the way facts are written is wrong.
AI.method: One loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity while keeping the same relation's other subjects unchanged; phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, with no multi-hop training data, across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3.
AI.result: Legible composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge on MQuAKE two-hop-curse questions; it reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four writer families; it also lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the Balesni et al. benchmark, and at 14B.
AI.conclusion: Writing new facts in a read-equivalent form, rather than as answers to be said, is a practical remedy for the two-hop curse.

title: The Structure of Disagreement in Emotion Annotation
summary: Calculating inter-annotator agreement is an established practice in NLP, and disagreement-aware work increasingly retains the distribution of human judgments rather than reducing annotations to a single gold label. Keeping the distribution, however, does not explain why annotators disagree. This paper examines the types of disagreement that occur in emotion annotation, starting from multilabel annotations of 1,677 sentence-level units from Ernest Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea and testing the patterns they reveal against individual-level annotations from BRIGHTER and GoEmotions. Across the three datasets, we find three main recurring disagreement structures. Emotion categories overlap systematically; annotators differ both in how broadly they apply labels and in how they treat particular category boundaries, while sparse participation and explicit abstention can look like disagreement. Where intensity is rated, disagreement over whether an emotion is present can be separated from disagreement over its intensity once recognized. Similar aggregate disagreement can therefore arise from qualitatively different annotation processes. Hard aggregation removes most of this structure, while annotator vote-share representations keep marginal label frequencies but not the co-occurrence, annotator-specific, or procedural patterns that produced them. We argue that disagreement should be understood in terms of its underlying patterns before it is summarized, aggregated, or used as a modeling target, and propose a vocabulary for disagreement structure.

AI.tldr: Analyses emotion annotation disagreement in three datasets and finds three recurring structures: overlapping emotion categories, differing label breadth and boundaries, and separable disagreement over presence versus intensity.
AI.motivation: Retaining the distribution of human judgments does not explain why annotators disagree, so the types of disagreement need to be understood before they are summarized or modeled.
AI.method: Multilabel annotations of 1,677 sentence-level units from The Old Man and the Sea are tested against individual-level annotations from BRIGHTER and GoEmotions.
AI.result: Emotion categories overlap systematically; annotators differ in how broadly they apply labels and in how they treat category boundaries, while sparse participation and explicit abstention can look like disagreement; where intensity is rated, disagreement over presence can be separated from disagreement over intensity; hard aggregation removes most of this structure, and vote-share representations keep marginal frequencies but not co-occurrence, annotator-specific or procedural patterns.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement should be understood in terms of its underlying patterns before it is summarized, aggregated or used as a modeling target, and the paper proposes a vocabulary for disagreement structure.

title: Revisiting LLM Homogeneity Through a Multidimensional Lens
summary: Concerns about LLM homogeneity are typically quantified with embedding similarity, which reduces two texts to a single score. We revisit homogeneity with 25 interpretable metrics spanning five dimensions: semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic & presentational. A human study shows that perceived similarity depends on both content (what responses say) and form (how they say it), yet embedding similarity correlates less with human meaning judgments than sentence-level matching ($\rho=0.417$ vs. $0.606$) and not significantly with form judgments ($\rho=0.140$). Across 18 contemporary LLMs, models say similar things in different words: they share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but remain distinct in lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Across releases from 2024 to 2026, models become more like themselves but not more like one another: among significantly changing metrics, intra-model distances decrease for 17 of 22, and inter-model distances increase for 14 of 21. Across two post-training pipelines, model-specific conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped by preference optimization. These results suggest that homogeneity is multidimensional and evolving, and that embedding similarity alone can overstate cross-model homogeneity while concealing diverging intra- and inter-model trends.

AI.tldr: Using 25 interpretable metrics across five dimensions, the study finds that LLMs say similar things in different words, and that embedding similarity can overstate cross-model homogeneity.
AI.motivation: LLM homogeneity is typically quantified by embedding similarity, which reduces two texts to one score and correlates less well with human meaning and form judgments than other measures.
AI.method: Twenty-five metrics span semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural and stylistic-presentational dimensions; a human study compares perceived similarity with embedding similarity and sentence-level matching across 18 contemporary LLMs and releases from 2024 to 2026, and two post-training pipelines are examined.
AI.result: Embedding similarity correlates less with human meaning judgments than sentence-level matching (rho=0.417 versus 0.606) and not significantly with form judgments (rho=0.140); models share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but remain distinct in lexical, structural and interactional conventions; intra-model distances decrease for 17 of 22 significantly changing metrics, while inter-model distances increase for 14 of 21; model-specific conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped by preference optimization.
AI.conclusion: Homogeneity is multidimensional and evolving: models are becoming more like themselves but not more like one another, and embedding similarity alone can overstate cross-model homogeneity while concealing diverging trends.

title: Can Large Language Models Extend Their Agentic Capabilities to Goal Pursuit in Open-Ended Multi-Turn Interaction?
summary: Goal pursuit in open-ended dialogue requires agents to adapt their actions to interaction feedback across successive exchanges. We investigate whether agentic capabilities developed for multi-step tool use carry over to dialogue organized through the model's native tool interface, and how this changes interaction behavior. We define Tool-Mediated Interaction (TMI) as a training-free protocol that represents dialogue actions as tool calls and counterpart responses as tool results, maintaining a continuous reasoning-action-observation loop with retained reasoning and interaction history. We evaluate TMI across social interaction, emotional support, persuasion, and price negotiation using two models and 15,678 main-experiment episodes. Across both models, TMI improves social goal attainment, emotional-support preference, donation amounts, and buyer negotiation margins over conversational baselines with and without thinking. A Qwen ablation further shows that TMI outperforms ordinary conversation with retained reasoning on all four primary outcomes. Behavioral analyses associate the improvements with task-specific patterns in initial proposals and responses to interaction feedback. Alongside these gains, TMI reduces mean reasoning tokens per decision by 42.0-81.5% relative to the thinking baseline and lowers mean cross-turn phrase reuse across all eight model-environment pairs. These findings show that interaction organization shapes both goal attainment and reasoning across dialogue turns.

AI.tldr: Tool-Mediated Interaction treats dialogue actions as tool calls and counterpart replies as tool results, improving goal attainment across four dialogue tasks while cutting reasoning tokens per decision by 42.0-81.5%.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether agentic capabilities developed for multi-step tool use carry over to open-ended goal pursuit in dialogue, and how this would change interaction behavior.
AI.method: TMI is a training-free protocol that maintains a continuous reasoning-action-observation loop with retained reasoning and interaction history; it is evaluated on social interaction, emotional support, persuasion and price negotiation with two models across 15,678 main-experiment episodes, plus a Qwen ablation.
AI.result: Across both models TMI improves social goal attainment, emotional-support preference, donation amounts and buyer negotiation margins over conversational baselines with and without thinking; the Qwen ablation shows TMI outperforms ordinary conversation with retained reasoning on all four primary outcomes; mean reasoning tokens per decision fall by 42.0-81.5% relative to the thinking baseline, and cross-turn phrase reuse decreases across all eight model-environment pairs.
AI.conclusion: Interaction organization shapes both goal attainment and reasoning across dialogue turns.

title: Halal-NeSyNet: Clause-Scoped Neuro-Symbolic Cross-Attention for Automated Food Ingredient Auditing and Risk-Aware Halal Logistics Triage
summary: Verifying that a packaged food is Halal requires reading ingredient declarations and E-number additives before goods enter certified warehouses. Dual-origin additives such as E471, E422, E441 and E920 are Mushbooh (doubtful) unless a botanical, microbial or certified-Halal qualifier appears in the same ingredient clause, so a plant-based qualifier on one clause must not clear an unqualified additive in another. We call a failure to respect this scope cross-clause modifier confounding and build a benchmark of 3,199 items (277 Open Food Facts records and 2,922 template-generated clause-swap items, labelled by an explicit 50-code rule base rather than by a certification authority) with a 540-item counterfactual suite. We propose Halal-NeSyNet, which couples a DistilBERT encoder with a 16-dimensional rule-derived symbolic vector through cross-attention and gated fusion, trained with an asymmetric false-Halal risk loss. Over five seeds, text-only TF-IDF baselines reach 86.25-86.71 % accuracy with 13.42-21.73 % false-Halal leakage and 6.33-26.00 % counterfactual triad consistency, whereas Halal-NeSyNet reaches 97.04+/-0.34 % and 99.67+/-0.50 %. Gradient boosting given the same symbolic vector reaches 96.25+/-1.24 % (+0.59 points from Halal-NeSyNet, 95 % CI [-1.11, +2.28]), so most of the gain comes from clause-scoped symbolic features and not from the network, and the risk loss did not help. Holding out whole template families, text-only models fall to 61.91-78.35 %, Halal-NeSyNet to 90.87+/-11.76 % and logistic regression with the symbolic vector to 91.11+/-2.88 %, with far more spread for Halal-NeSyNet. A three-lane receiving simulation auto-clears 49.33 % of cargo at 0.76 % green-lane contamination. Because labels and features come from one rule engine and 91.3 % of the items are templated, the results measure fidelity to a rule policy, not religious certification.

AI.tldr: Halal-NeSyNet audits food ingredient declarations by fusing a DistilBERT encoder with a 16-dimensional rule-derived symbolic vector, reaching 97.04% accuracy, but the results measure fidelity to a rule policy rather than religious certification.
AI.motivation: Halal verification requires reading E-number additives whose status depends on qualifiers in the same ingredient clause, and text-only classifiers fail to respect this clause scope, which the authors call cross-clause modifier confounding.
AI.method: A benchmark of 3,199 items (277 Open Food Facts records and 2,922 template-generated clause-swap items), labelled by a 50-code rule base, comes with a 540-item counterfactual suite; the model couples DistilBERT with the symbolic vector through cross-attention and gated fusion and is trained with an asymmetric false-Halal risk loss.
AI.result: Over five seeds, text-only TF-IDF baselines reach 86.25-86.71% accuracy with 13.42-21.73% false-Halal leakage, while Halal-NeSyNet reaches 97.04+/-0.34% accuracy and 99.67+/-0.50% counterfactual triad consistency; gradient boosting on the same symbolic vector reaches 96.25+/-1.24%, so most of the gain comes from the clause-scoped symbolic features and the risk loss did not help; under held-out template families, text-only models fall to 61.91-78.35% and Halal-NeSyNet reaches 90.87+/-11.76%; a receiving simulation auto-clears 49.33% of cargo at 0.76% green-lane contamination.
AI.conclusion: Because labels and features come from one rule engine and 91.3% of items are templated, the results measure fidelity to a rule policy and not religious certification.

title: FinForesight: A Diagnostic Backtesting Benchmark for Deep Research Systems in Financial Forecasting
summary: Anticipating financial outcomes requires synthesizing evolving evidence and reasoning under uncertainty, making deep research systems promising tools for forecasting. Yet evaluating forecasting ability is challenging because historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or information retrieved after the forecast date. Live forecasting avoids direct access to realized outcomes, but feedback arrives only after events resolve. To obtain timely feedback and assess historical scores, we introduce FinForesight, a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. Across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, the benchmark evaluates four forecasting tasks: valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately from forecasting performance. Our harness-compatible framework restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff, and live evaluations to test whether controlled backtests approximate future performance. Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results. Forecasting attribution and robustness analyses reveal how scores respond to retrieval policy and how predictions respond to prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. The code and benchmark data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: FinForesight is a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for deep research systems in financial forecasting across Chinese, US and Hong Kong markets, restricting retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date.
AI.motivation: Historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or post-date information, while live forecasting gives feedback only after events resolve.
AI.method: Four forecasting tasks (valuation, return ranking, event direction and future financial fundamentals) and two capability diagnostics (counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately) are evaluated; a harness-compatible framework limits evidence to the forecast date, and pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff and live evaluations are compared.
AI.result: Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results; attribution and robustness analyses show how scores respond to retrieval policy, prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Stronger retrieval controls bring post-cutoff backtests closer to live performance; the code and benchmark data are publicly available.

title: BanglishDepYT: Depression Detection in Native Bengali Social Media with Emotion-Preserving Preprocessing and Domain-Adaptive Pretraining
summary: Depression affects millions of Bengali speakers across South Asia, yet automated detection systems have relied almost entirely on datasets translated from English. Such datasets cannot capture the emoticons, romanized Bengali words, and elongated spellings that characterize real expressions of distress. We introduce BanglishDepYT, a Bengali depression dataset collected natively from YouTube, comprising 191,000 unlabeled comments and 1,000 samples verified through dual bilingual annotation. We propose EPH (Emotion-Preserving Hybrid preprocessing), which converts emoticons to semantic tags, preserves Banglish tokens, protects negation words, and normalizes emotional elongation. A key finding is that preprocessing choice substantially affects performance on informal text: standard cleaning reduces the Banglish Survival Rate to zero (SVM F1: 0.7062), while EPH preserves signals (CESS: 0.9996 vs. 0.6694) and raises SVM F1 to 0.8570, an improvement of 0.1508. We further apply domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT), continuing SahajBERT pretraining on unlabeled in-domain comments. DAPT-SahajBERT achieves the highest mean F1 (0.8161) and MCC (0.6272), significantly outperforming the baseline (F1: 0.7805, p = 0.0013, d = 1.450) and matching MuRIL (p = 0.589). These results suggest that targeted domain pretraining is a competitive alternative to large-scale multilingual pretraining. LLM-assisted annotation using Qwen2.5-7B achieves substantial human agreement (kappa = 0.611), enabling pseudo-labeling of 96,071 comments. Semi-supervised training improves AUC from 0.8499 to 0.8731 (p = 0.044), offering a scalable path to expanding annotation. All code, models, and datasets are publicly released to support reproducible research.

AI.tldr: BanglishDepYT introduces a Bengali depression dataset collected natively from YouTube and an emotion-preserving preprocessing method, with DAPT-SahajBERT reaching the highest mean F1 of 0.8161.
AI.motivation: Depression detection for Bengali has relied on datasets translated from English, which cannot capture emoticons, romanized Bengali and elongated spellings used to express distress.
AI.method: The dataset has 191,000 unlabeled comments and 1,000 samples verified through dual bilingual annotation; EPH preprocessing converts emoticons to semantic tags, preserves Banglish tokens, protects negation and normalizes elongation; SahajBERT is further pretrained on unlabeled in-domain comments (DAPT), and Qwen2.5-7B assists annotation and pseudo-labels 96,071 comments for semi-supervised training.
AI.result: Standard cleaning reduces the Banglish Survival Rate to zero (SVM F1 0.7062), while EPH raises SVM F1 to 0.8570, an improvement of 0.1508; DAPT-SahajBERT achieves mean F1 0.8161 and MCC 0.6272, significantly above the baseline (F1 0.7805, p = 0.0013) and matching MuRIL (p = 0.589); LLM-assisted annotation reaches kappa 0.611 with human annotators; semi-supervised training raises AUC from 0.8499 to 0.8731 (p = 0.044).
AI.conclusion: Targeted domain pretraining and preprocessing that preserves informal signals are competitive with large-scale multilingual pretraining, and LLM-assisted pseudo-labeling offers a scalable path to expanding annotation.

title: EEG-HealthLLM: Hierarchical Adaptation of Large Language Models for Unified Heterogeneous EEG Health Assessment
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive means for neurological and mental health assessment, yet existing EEG models are typically developed for individual tasks and are difficult to unify across heterogeneous signal configurations and assessment objectives. Large language models (LLMs) offer a common interface for multiple tasks, but adapting heterogeneous EEG signals to a shared LLM raises a key challenge: how to preserve task-specific signal characteristics while enabling effective language-side parameter sharing. To address this problem, we propose EEG-HealthLLM, a unified and parameter-efficient framework for heterogeneous EEG health assessment. We introduce an Asymmetric Hierarchical Adaptation Strategy: task-specific EEG adapters preserve heterogeneous spatio-temporal dynamics, while a unified shared LoRA is injected into the LLM backbone (e.g., Phi-3) to capture shared high-level assessment semantics across tasks. We further establish EEG-HealthBench by reorganizing five existing EEG resources into paradigms covering epileptic seizure detection, major depressive disorder assessment, anxiety risk assessment, depressive symptom risk assessment, and emotional state assessment under a unified subject-independent protocol. Extensive experiments show that EEG-HealthLLM achieves an average balanced accuracy (BAC) of 69.58%, ranking first among the evaluated methods in both average BAC and macro-F1. Compared with independent single-task LoRA adaptation, it improves average BAC from 67.70% to 69.58% while reducing the aggregate language-side adapter footprint by 80.0%. Further analyses reveal task-dependent cross-task interactions and trade-offs, supporting the proposed hierarchical adaptation strategy. The implementation is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: EEG-HealthLLM unifies heterogeneous EEG health assessment with task-specific EEG adapters and one shared LoRA in an LLM backbone (Phi-3 as an example), reaching 69.58% average balanced accuracy.
AI.motivation: EEG models are typically built for individual tasks and are hard to unify across heterogeneous signal configurations, and adapting heterogeneous EEG to a shared LLM must preserve task-specific signal characteristics while enabling language-side parameter sharing.
AI.method: An asymmetric hierarchical adaptation strategy uses task-specific EEG adapters to preserve spatio-temporal dynamics and a unified shared LoRA in the LLM backbone to capture shared high-level assessment semantics; EEG-HealthBench reorganizes five existing EEG resources into five paradigms (epileptic seizure detection, major depressive disorder, anxiety risk, depressive symptom risk and emotional state assessment) under a subject-independent protocol.
AI.result: EEG-HealthLLM achieves an average balanced accuracy of 69.58%, ranking first among evaluated methods in average BAC and macro-F1; compared with independent single-task LoRA adaptation (67.70%), it reduces the aggregate language-side adapter footprint by 80.0%; task-dependent cross-task interactions and trade-offs are reported.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical adaptation strategy supports unified EEG health assessment with a much smaller language-side footprint, with trade-offs that depend on the task.

title: CST: Lightweight Risk Triage with Source-Grounded Evidence for Web Discussions
summary: Web communities rely on moderators to catch harmful messages such as insults, hate speech, and scams, but no one can read every message. Existing tools give each message a risk score, which tells moderators where to look but not what to read or how to check it. Yet meaning depends on context: the same reply, "I agree.", can support or oppose removing someone from a group. Moderators therefore need source-grounded evidence, not just scores: a few key messages kept with their original wording and replies. We present CST, a lightweight triage pipeline that first decides where to look, then what to show. It scores risk by pairing character patterns, which capture exact wording, with sentence meaning from a fixed multilingual model, so it handles several languages and runs on an ordinary CPU. It then groups related messages and picks from each group in turn, so a small reading budget covers different parts of a discussion, and links every pick back to the original thread. Across six tasks from five datasets in several languages, CST ranks harmful messages more accurately than a fully fine-tuned multilingual model and, under the same budget, finds more of them than reading by score alone. In a user study, reviewers needed at least 27% less time with CST's grouped evidence while keeping decision accuracy above 94%. CST turns risk scores into evidence that moderators can read quickly and check in context. Code and dataset reconstruction resources will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CST is a lightweight, CPU-friendly triage pipeline that scores message risk and then selects grouped, source-linked evidence so that moderators read a small, diverse set of original messages.
AI.motivation: Risk scores tell moderators where to look but not what to read or how to check it, and meaning depends on context, so moderators need source-grounded evidence.
AI.method: Risk is scored by pairing character patterns with sentence meaning from a fixed multilingual model; related messages are grouped, picks are drawn from each group in turn, and every pick is linked back to the original thread.
AI.result: Across six tasks from five datasets in several languages, CST ranks harmful messages more accurately than a fully fine-tuned multilingual model and, under the same budget, finds more of them than reading by score alone; in a user study reviewers needed at least 27% less time with the grouped evidence while keeping decision accuracy above 94%.
AI.conclusion: CST turns risk scores into evidence that moderators can read quickly and check in context; code and dataset reconstruction resources will be released.

title: EarlySelectKV: Anticipatory KV Selection via Cross-Layer Query Proxies
comment: Published in EMNLP 2026. 20 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: Query-conditioned sparse KV selection reduces long-context inference cost by attending to a subset of historical KV entries at each decoding step. Existing selectors must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates and generating indices, placing routing on the immediate pre-attention path. We introduce EarlySelectKV, a training-free transformation that uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute selected KV indices while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention. Tests with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki show no consistent pattern of quality degradation across the evaluated settings. In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018 points on LongBench, approximately -0.01 points on RULER, and +0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings. In a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing, ES-RocketKV improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool. This makes routing timing an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: EarlySelectKV uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute sparse KV indices before the target-layer query is available, with no consistent quality degradation and up to 12.4% higher end-to-end throughput in a TensorRT-LLM deployment.
AI.motivation: Query-conditioned sparse KV selection must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates, which places routing on the immediate pre-attention path.
AI.method: A training-free transformation precomputes selected KV indices from proxy queries derived from earlier hidden states while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention; it is tested with RocketKV, Quest and Loki.
AI.result: In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018 points on LongBench, about -0.01 points on RULER and +0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings; in a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing it improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool.
AI.conclusion: Routing timing becomes an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding; the code is publicly available.

title: Less but Sufficient: Relation Knowledge Selects Compact Knowledge-Graph Contexts, and What External Checks Can and Cannot Catch
summary: Large language models (LLMs) read knowledge-graph facts ranked by relevance, leaving open whether they suffice or conflict. Our checks use relation knowledge, written by hand or learned from training questions labelled with their relation paths. It selects a compact context of facts yielding an answer, and derives it; a derivability check tests whether an answer follows, a consistency check whether facts conflict, and a validation-chosen routing gate decides where the derived answer replaces the LLM's. Seven open LLMs read the compact context better in exact match than relevance-ranked facts; on ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) they match SubgraphRAG's facts at a quarter of the prompt tokens, and stronger LLMs read SubgraphRAG's better. Where the routing gate passes, ours leads SubgraphRAG's in exact match in all 53 LLM, benchmark and prompt settings. A precision gate, returning the derived answer only when the check passes with exactly one derived entity, answered 18 and 5 percent of held-out WebQSP and CWQ questions in a pre-specified test, right for 90 and 96 percent. The consistency check judges facts by path evidence only where another path joins their entities, true of 2.5 percent of named-entity facts in our compact WebQSP and CWQ contexts.

AI.tldr: A relation-knowledge method selects compact knowledge-graph contexts for LLMs, matching SubgraphRAG's facts on ComplexWebQuestions at a quarter of the prompt tokens, and uses derivability and consistency checks with a validation-chosen routing gate.
AI.motivation: LLMs read relevance-ranked knowledge-graph facts without knowing whether those facts suffice or conflict.
AI.method: Relation knowledge, written by hand or learned from relation-labelled training questions, selects and derives a compact context; a derivability check tests whether an answer follows, a consistency check tests whether facts conflict, and a validation-chosen routing gate decides where the derived answer replaces the LLM's.
AI.result: Seven open LLMs read the compact context better in exact match than relevance-ranked facts; on CWQ they match SubgraphRAG's facts at a quarter of the prompt tokens; where the routing gate passes, the method leads SubgraphRAG in exact match in all 53 LLM, benchmark and prompt settings; a precision gate answered 18% and 5% of held-out WebQSP and CWQ questions, correct for 90% and 96%; the consistency check judges facts by path evidence only where another path joins their entities, which holds for 2.5% of named-entity facts.
AI.conclusion: The derived compact contexts and precision-oriented gate help, but the external checks apply to only a small share of facts.

title: A Bounded Evaluation Protocol for Representational Systematicity
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Multiple studies have shown that neural networks can be behaviorally systematic, producing correct outputs for novel combinations of familiar parts. Whether they are also representationally systematic, that is, whether they represent these parts and their roles and use them to produce the outputs, remains hard to test, because each kind of evidence can mislead on its own: correct outputs can come from shortcuts, a decodable signal need not be used, an intervention can act through unintended pathways, and a failed search does not show absence. We propose a bounded evaluation protocol for representational systematicity (Bounded-RS): for an explanation that attributes a systematic behavior to a declared representation, it tests on a matched behavioral contrast whether that representation is recoverable and whether it is causally used, checks the validity of this evidence, and assigns the explanation one of four bounded states, Unsupported, Present-only, Causal-use, or Undetermined, through control-calibrated scores, gates, and stop rules. On a semantic-parsing testbed of 96 matched sets that we release, the tested role-filler Binding explanation of fine-tuned T5 models is Causal-use and the distributed Geometry explanation is Unsupported within its declared search space, verdicts that hold across calibration-compatible parameter configurations, training seeds, and T5-base. On 41 cases with known causal status, full adjudication licenses a false Causal-use in 1 of 34 noncausal cases, against 13 when recoverability is taken as use, without missing any causal case. Bounded-RS thus turns the question of representational systematicity, debated since Fodor and Pylyshyn, into comparable and falsifiable verdicts on declared explanations, each reported with the evidence pattern that licenses it and, for a negative, the search space that bounds it.

AI.tldr: Bounded-RS is an evaluation protocol that assigns one of four bounded verdicts (Unsupported, Present-only, Causal-use or Undetermined) to explanations of representational systematicity, tested on fine-tuned T5 models in a semantic-parsing testbed.
AI.motivation: Behavioral systematicity does not show whether networks represent and use parts and their roles, and each kind of evidence (correct outputs, decodable signals, interventions) can mislead on its own.
AI.method: For an explanation that attributes systematic behavior to a declared representation, the protocol tests on matched behavioral contrasts whether the representation is recoverable and causally used, checks the validity of this evidence, and assigns a bounded state through control-calibrated scores, gates and stop rules; a 96-set semantic-parsing testbed is released.
AI.result: The role-filler Binding explanation of fine-tuned T5 is Causal-use and the distributed Geometry explanation is Unsupported within its declared search space, with verdicts holding across calibration-compatible configurations, training seeds and T5-base; on 41 cases with known causal status, full adjudication licenses one false Causal-use in 34 noncausal cases, against 13 when recoverability is taken as use, with no causal case missed.
AI.conclusion: The protocol turns representational systematicity into comparable, falsifiable verdicts on declared explanations, each reported with the evidence pattern that licenses it and, for a negative, the search space that bounds it.

title: MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents
summary: LLM-based role-playing agents are fluent at imitating a character's style, yet struggle to make role-consistent decisions over long narrative horizons. Such decisions are shaped by experiences spanning many prior scenes, which are often partial and may point in different directions. Existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context, but do not reason about how past events shape a character's current motivations and behavior. We propose MemRole, a framework that makes this memory-to-decision process explicit. It introduces Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a reasoning schema that decomposes hidden reasoning into context understanding, memory activation, and response strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset whose character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools limit each character to what it could plausibly know at the current narrative point. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we propose Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD): the model critiques its own rollouts against the reference under a data-driven rubric, and a critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model distills token-level guidance back into the policy. MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4, and achieves the best character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.

AI.tldr: MemRole trains role-playing agents to reason from memories to decisions through a three-part reasoning schema and self-refining on-policy self-distillation, with MemRole-32B gaining 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing.
AI.motivation: Role-playing agents imitate style well but make inconsistent decisions over long narrative horizons, and existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context without reasoning about how past events shape a character's motivations.
AI.method: Long-Horizon Memory Thinking decomposes hidden reasoning into context understanding, memory activation and response strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset with character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools; SR-OPSD has the model critique its own rollouts against the reference under a data-driven rubric and distills token-level guidance from a critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model.
AI.result: MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4 on the reported evaluation, and achieves the best character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.
AI.conclusion: Making the memory-to-decision process explicit, together with self-refining distillation, improves role consistency over long horizons in the reported evaluations.

title: Shared relations, specific choices: conditional sensitivity and competing pathways in language models
summary: How does a relational representation shared across queries drive a query-specific choice? Controlled entity-binding experiments with GPT-2 Small, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B reveal a low-dimensional relational background that is predominantly shared across query roles and transfers to new names. Same-domain interactions persist when another attribute domain is queried. After removing this component, restoring independently trained relation directions brings output contrasts closer to their original values than sign-reversed or equal-norm random controls in all three models. Yet a transferable relational representation need not have a transferable functional sign. In Qwen2.5, fixing model weights, the training-mean relation vector and edit dose yields opposite selection effects across binary and lexical-mapping prompts with different answer vocabularies. A factorial contrast of downstream sensitivities across attribute-query combinations determines the shared direction's local signed selection gain. In a separate eight-condition protocol, mean local gain is positive in Qwen2.5 and negative in Llama3.2. Late-component clamps resolve opposing pathway contributions: in Llama3.2, negative transmission through selected attention-only paths is partially offset by positive transmission through paths traversing both selected attention and MLP sets. Source-coordinate analyses establish distributed factor coverage, hidden-receiver readouts reveal layout-dependent combination, and instance-geometry interventions separate response direction from amplitude. These findings show how conditional sensitivity and competing pathways give shared relational structure its effect on specific choices.

AI.tldr: In GPT-2 Small, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B, a low-dimensional relational background shared across queries drives query-specific choices, and competing pathways determine how it affects selection.
AI.motivation: How a relational representation shared across queries drives a query-specific choice is not yet understood.
AI.method: Controlled entity-binding experiments, factorial contrasts of downstream sensitivities across attribute-query combinations, an eight-condition protocol, late-component clamps, source-coordinate analyses and instance-geometry interventions.
AI.result: The relational background is predominantly shared across query roles and transfers to new names; restoring independently trained relation directions brings output contrasts closer to their original values than sign-reversed or equal-norm random controls in all three models; the training-mean relation vector yields opposite selection effects in Qwen2.5 across binary and lexical-mapping prompts; mean local gain is positive in Qwen2.5 and negative in Llama3.2, where negative transmission through attention-only paths is partly offset by positive transmission through paths traversing both attention and MLP sets.
AI.conclusion: Conditional sensitivity and competing pathways determine the effect shared relational structure has on specific choices, and a transferable relational representation need not have a transferable functional sign.

title: LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environments via Modular Recombination
summary: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet existing environments are designed for specific tasks and fail to generalize to new ones. Recent methods automate environment construction with LLMs. However, they generate each environment from scratch, neither reusing parts shared across environments nor carrying a fix from one environment to the rest. To address this, we propose a new paradigm of evolving environment atoms, which composes environments from reusable atoms (intent, rule, data and server) and evolves the atoms when an environment fails to give reliable feedback (e.g., an application lacks a tool the task requires). To instantiate this paradigm, we introduce LegoEnv, which builds 5,465 verified environments over 223 applications, and one round of evolution raises the share of solvable environments from 71.6% to 88.3%. On AutomationBench, SFT on these environments lifts Qwen3.6-27B from 16.0% to 32.0%, and RL with their verifiers lifts Qwen3.8-27B from 37.6% to 40.3%. Further analyses show steady gains with corpus size, transfer to unseen applications, and failures concentrated in a few shared root causes.

AI.tldr: LegoEnv composes LLM agent environments from reusable atoms (intent, rule, data and server) and evolves atoms when an environment fails to give reliable feedback, building 5,465 verified environments over 223 applications.
AI.motivation: Existing environments are designed for specific tasks and generalize poorly, and recent LLM-based construction methods generate each environment from scratch, without reusing shared parts or carrying a fix from one environment to the rest.
AI.method: Environments are composed from reusable atoms (intent, rule, data and server), and atoms are evolved when an environment fails to give reliable feedback, for example when an application lacks a tool that the task requires.
AI.result: One round of evolution raises the share of solvable environments from 71.6% to 88.3%; on AutomationBench, SFT on these environments lifts Qwen3.6-27B from 16.0% to 32.0%, and RL with their verifiers lifts Qwen3.8-27B from 37.6% to 40.3%; further analyses show steady gains with corpus size, transfer to unseen applications, and failures concentrated in a few shared root causes.
AI.conclusion: Evolving reusable environment atoms offers a route to scalable agent training, with failures concentrated in a few shared root causes.

title: Don't Guess, Ask Wisely: Benchmarking and Training Proactive Elicitation in Open-Domain LLM Conversations
summary: When user queries are incomplete, large language models should ask targeted questions before committing to an answer, a capability we call proactive elicitation, yet evaluation on real user-assistant queries across seven LLMs (8B to frontier) shows that fewer than 11% of underspecified queries trigger a follow-up question. To benchmark and train this capability, we introduce VagueBench, where each seed query is annotated with structured intent and detail units then degraded into intent-vague and fully-vague variants via controlled removal of linguistic cues, yielding known hidden information sets for evaluating both when and what to ask. We propose DialogGRPO, an offline reinforcement learning method that organizes multi-turn elicitation as a dialogue-state directed acyclic graph, where candidate questions at each node receive dense turn-level rewards combining immediate information gain with lookahead value through group-relative comparison, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without runtime simulation. DialogGRPO elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries with substantial gains in both recovery efficiency and answer coverage, without over-asking on complete queries, outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines, and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.

AI.tldr: VagueBench and DialogGRPO benchmark and train proactive elicitation, asking targeted questions when queries are underspecified; DialogGRPO elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries.
AI.motivation: Across seven LLMs, fewer than 11% of underspecified real user queries trigger a follow-up question, so models usually answer without asking.
AI.method: VagueBench degrades annotated seed queries into intent-vague and fully-vague variants with known hidden information sets; DialogGRPO is an offline reinforcement learning method that organizes elicitation as a dialogue-state directed acyclic graph, giving candidate questions dense turn-level rewards that combine immediate information gain with lookahead value through group-relative comparison.
AI.result: DialogGRPO elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries with substantial gains in recovery efficiency and answer coverage, avoids over-asking on complete queries, outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines, and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.
AI.conclusion: Turn-level credit assignment on a dialogue-state graph can teach LLMs when and what to ask without runtime user simulation.

title: TAC-CoT: Tool-Empowered Implicit Chain-of-Thought via Interleaving Explicit Tokens
summary: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

AI.tldr: TAC-CoT interleaves compact latent reasoning segments with textual tool calls, observations and final answers, improving accuracy by up to 8.8 points while cutting model forward passes by up to 6.8x.
AI.motivation: Explicit chain-of-thought is costly to generate, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface that agentic tool use requires.
AI.method: Explicit reasoning traces are replaced by compact continuous latent segments, with textual tokens kept only for tool calls, observations and final answers, so that tool use does not require verbalizing every intermediate step.
AI.result: On agentic math and QA benchmarks, TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points and reduces model forward passes by up to 6.8x, and it improves tool-use quality in both single-tool and multi-tool settings.
AI.conclusion: Interleaving latent reasoning with explicit tool interaction offers an efficient alternative to fully verbalized CoT for agentic systems.

title: Tracing How Language Models Integrate Temporal Anchors into Factual Recall
summary: Factual recall in language models is typically framed as retrieving a factual association: a subject--relation pair maps to a single object. However, many facts are context-dependent: the same pair maps to different objects depending on a condition such as time. We introduce anchored factual recall, in which the model receives an explicit conditioning expression, an anchor, and must select the object valid under it. This raises questions that single-object recall does not: where the anchor enters the computation, what it changes, and how that change selects the answer. Focusing on temporal anchors, we answer them with causal interventions on four open-weight models on English prompts and identify two routes. In a subject-mediated route, the anchor resolves the final subject-token representation to the queried year, and the relation redistributes the readout of this state across attention heads. In a direct route] the final position attends to the anchor, and upper-layer MLPs turn this signal into a preference for the time-appropriate object. The two routes are parallel channels: their contributions add up, most queries use both, and their balance depends on the query, e.g., on the relation, consistently across models. This reframes mechanistic accounts of factual recall from retrieving a single stored object to selecting among context-dependent alternatives.

AI.tldr: In four open-weight models, temporal anchors are integrated into factual recall through two parallel routes, a subject-mediated route and a direct attention route, that together select the object valid under the anchor.
AI.motivation: Factual recall is usually framed as retrieving a single object for a subject-relation pair, but many facts are context-dependent, with the same pair mapping to different objects depending on a condition such as time.
AI.method: Causal interventions on four open-weight models with English prompts identify where the anchor enters the computation and what its effect on the answer is, focusing on temporal anchors.
AI.result: In the subject-mediated route the anchor resolves the final subject-token representation to the queried year and the relation redistributes the readout of this state across attention heads; in the direct route the final position attends to the anchor and upper-layer MLPs turn this signal into a preference for the time-appropriate object; the two routes add up, most queries use both, and their balance depends on the query, for example on the relation, consistently across models.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic accounts of factual recall should describe selection among context-dependent alternatives rather than retrieval of a single stored object.

title: Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs
comment: Under review at the ACL Rolling Review (ARR) October 2026 cycle
summary: Traditional interactive narrative systems offer strong authorial control and structural coherence but often restrict player agency. In contrast, LLM-driven narratives enable open-ended generation and greater flexibility, yet frequently suffer from inconsistency and diminished narrative control. To navigate this trade-off, we propose a hybrid narrative framework that dynamically balances pre-authored content with real-time LLM generation via semantic similarity alignment. Additionally, sustaining narrative quality over extended gameplay remains a core challenge in LLM-based storytelling. To address this, we introduce a self-evolving, feedback-driven optimization framework that leverages in-context learning to iteratively refine prompts, eliminating the need for manual prompt engineering. Through a case study and participant-based evaluation, we show that our framework enhances narrative coherence while preserving player agency, effectively aligning generated content with both authorial intent and evolving player behavior.

AI.tldr: A hybrid narrative framework balances pre-authored content with real-time LLM generation through semantic similarity alignment, and refines prompts through in-context feedback to keep narrative quality over extended gameplay.
AI.motivation: Traditional interactive narratives offer authorial control but restrict player agency, while LLM-driven narratives are flexible but often inconsistent and hard to keep under narrative control, and their quality degrades over extended gameplay.
AI.method: Semantic similarity alignment balances pre-authored content with real-time LLM generation, and a self-evolving, feedback-driven optimization framework uses in-context learning to iteratively refine prompts without manual prompt engineering.
AI.result: A case study and a participant-based evaluation show that the framework enhances narrative coherence while preserving player agency, and aligns generated content with both authorial intent and evolving player behavior.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a way to combine authorial control and player agency in LLM-based interactive storytelling.

title: Better Answers, Weaker Evidence Control: Evidence Bypass in On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) can improve answer accuracy while weakening responsiveness to supporting evidence. We investigate this separation in scientific-document question answering through matched document interventions that change the supported answer while preserving the question and unrelated context. We identify evidence bypass: a student retains an originally correct answer after the document changes to support a different one. On QASPER with a Qwen3-4B student, standard OPD raises original-document accuracy by 3.4 percentage points, lowers counterfactual accuracy by 5.3 points, and increases bypass by 15.7 points; the same directional pattern appears on PeerQA. Controlled perturbations localize the shift to answer-critical evidence, and bypass grows with the student's pre-distillation closed-book preference for the original answer. A factorized study of teacher targets, privileged information, divergence, and supervision density finds that explicitly supplying the teacher with annotated answer-critical spans yields the largest joint improvement in evidence response and claim support. These findings motivate Evidence-Paired OPD (EP-OPD), which combines on-policy supervision on matched documents supporting different answers to the same question with an answer-level margin that favors each document's supported answer over its paired alternative. Across both datasets and two student sizes, EP-OPD recovers 54-66% of standard OPD's counterfactual-accuracy loss while preserving 80-85% of its original-document accuracy gain. Our results establish evidence responsiveness as a distinct training and evaluation target alongside answer accuracy. Our code is publicly available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: On-policy distillation raises answer accuracy on scientific-document QA but weakens evidence responsiveness; the proposed Evidence-Paired OPD recovers much of the counterfactual-accuracy loss while keeping most of the accuracy gain.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation can improve answer accuracy while weakening a student's responsiveness to supporting evidence, and this separation needed investigation.
AI.method: Matched document interventions change the supported answer while keeping the question and unrelated context; on QASPER and PeerQA with a Qwen3-4B student, the study identifies evidence bypass and factorizes teacher targets, privileged information, divergence and supervision density; Evidence-Paired OPD (EP-OPD) pairs on-policy supervision on documents supporting different answers with an answer-level margin.
AI.result: Standard OPD raises original-document accuracy by 3.4 points but lowers counterfactual accuracy by 5.3 points and raises bypass by 15.7 points; explicitly supplying the teacher with annotated answer-critical spans gives the largest joint improvement in evidence response and claim support; EP-OPD recovers 54-66% of standard OPD's counterfactual-accuracy loss while preserving 80-85% of its original-document accuracy gain across both datasets and two student sizes.
AI.conclusion: Evidence responsiveness is a distinct training and evaluation target alongside answer accuracy.

title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue
summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).

AI.tldr: TrackMem is a per-speaker graph memory that tracks revised figures, entity- and lens-specific perspectives and chronological actions in long financial dialogues, reaching 73.9% macro accuracy on the failure-mode split of FinLoCoMo.
AI.motivation: Memory systems that retrieve the most similar or most recent passages return superseded values and miss rules and stances in financial dialogue, where figures are revised and stances shift without being restated.
AI.method: TrackMem keeps the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order; FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits (one following the LoCoMo categories, one targeting four failure modes), is introduced for evaluation.
AI.result: With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits; on the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gain on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
AI.conclusion: Explicitly tracking evolving state, rather than relying on similarity or recency retrieval, helps memory systems answer questions in financial dialogue.

title: Retrieval-Enhanced Cultural Evaluation for Social Media Translation Training
summary: Social media translation requires preserving meaning while capturing the cultural nuances of user-generated content (UGC). However, gaps in the cultural knowledge of LLM-based evaluators can lead to inaccurate assessments and unreliable training rewards. To improve these signals, we use retrieval-enhanced cultural evaluation to train CUE-MT, a family of social media translation models. A calibrated, domain-specific Judger guides supervised data refinement and is augmented by an Agent for hard-example mining and reinforcement learning. The Agent retrieves relevant external evidence as needed and distills it into concise hints that the Judger uses to score translations and assign rewards. Across 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B backbones, CUE-MT outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines of comparable size on CUE-MT-Bench and three public benchmarks. Human evaluation on CUE-MT-Bench shows cultural effectiveness gains of 7.44-15.12 percentage points over the strongest external baseline in each size group. Retrieval improves the Judger's four-way classification accuracy by 8.07 percentage points over a matched no-retrieval baseline that uses LLM-generated hints alone. Training ablations further support the combination of hard-example mining and Agent-enhanced rewards.

AI.tldr: The paper uses retrieval-enhanced cultural evaluation to train CUE-MT, a family of social media translation models whose rewards come from a judge that is augmented with retrieved cultural evidence.
AI.motivation: LLM-based evaluators have gaps in cultural knowledge, which leads to inaccurate assessments and unreliable training rewards for social media translation of user-generated content.
AI.method: A calibrated, domain-specific Judger guides supervised data refinement, and an Agent performs hard-example mining and reinforcement learning by retrieving external evidence and distilling it into concise hints that the Judger uses to score translations and assign rewards.
AI.result: Across 9B, 27B and 35B-A3B backbones, CUE-MT outperforms open-source baselines of comparable size on CUE-MT-Bench and three public benchmarks, with human-rated cultural effectiveness gains of 7.44 to 15.12 percentage points over the strongest external baseline in each size group, and retrieval improves the Judger's four-way classification accuracy by 8.07 points over a no-retrieval baseline that uses LLM-generated hints alone.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-grounded cultural evaluation provides more reliable training rewards for social media translation, and the ablations support combining hard-example mining with Agent-enhanced rewards.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
summary: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models built for edge deployment, which outperform much larger medical baselines on seven closed-ended medical benchmarks and HealthBench-Hard.
AI.motivation: The strongest open medical LLMs are too large for private edge devices, while compact medical models trail substantially on knowledge-intensive tasks, and long reasoning traces increase latency, energy use and KV-cache memory on such devices.
AI.method: The recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused teacher, followed by a four-stage post-training curriculum of two SFT stages and two RL stages with hard-sample mining, and an edge evaluation over GGUF quantization variants and real inference on laptop and smartphone hardware.
AI.result: MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B on seven closed-ended medical benchmarks while being 6.75 times smaller, and MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points; on HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points and MedPsy-1.7B by 11.66 points; response length falls 1.7 times (1.7B) and 3.2 times (4B) versus Qwen3 backbones, Q4_K_M stays within 1 point of BF16 with about 69% lower disk footprint, and MedPsy-4B has 75% lower median end-to-end latency than its backbone with peak RAM below 5 GB.
AI.conclusion: Compact medical models trained with this recipe can reach the accuracy of much larger models while reducing generation length, latency and energy, making private on-device medical assistance more practical.

title: Scaling Makes It Possible: How Large Models Master Impossible Languages
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, including 6 pages of supplementary information
summary: While language models (LMs) excel in natural language tasks, their ability to learn impossible languages--those that violate the structural, cognitive, or logical constraints that make human languages learnable and functional--remains debatable. This controversy is further fueled by a divide between linguistic theorists and empirical researchers working with small-scale LMs. To address this controversy, we introduce semantic coherence. This concept measures how effectively semantic information is expressed in language structures and examines the learning capabilities of LMs across multiple scales. By fine-tuning billion-parameter LMs on impossible language samples, we demonstrate that larger LMs achieve similar performance on impossible and possible languages, whereas million-parameter LMs exhibit significant degradation when trained on impossible languages. This performance gap widens as semantic complexity increases. We further show that scaling up the LM size fundamentally shifts the learning focus from grammatical rules to semantic understanding, with billion-scale LMs exhibiting a threefold reduction in sensitivity to low-level linguistic perturbations while maintaining stable performance under high-level semantic perturbations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that billion-parameter language models learn impossible languages about as well as possible languages, whereas million-parameter models degrade, and it attributes this to a shift from grammatical rules to semantic understanding as scale increases.
AI.motivation: Whether language models can learn impossible languages is contested, and the debate is split between linguistic theorists and researchers who work with small-scale models.
AI.method: The authors introduce semantic coherence, a concept measuring how effectively semantic information is expressed in language structures, and fine-tune LMs of several scales on impossible-language samples to compare their learning across scales.
AI.result: Billion-parameter LMs perform similarly on impossible and possible languages, while million-parameter LMs degrade significantly on impossible languages, and the gap widens as semantic complexity increases; billion-scale models show a threefold reduction in sensitivity to low-level linguistic perturbations while staying stable under high-level semantic perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Scaling changes what language models learn, moving the focus from grammatical rules to semantics, which reconciles the conflicting findings of theorists and small-model researchers.

title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?
summary: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \textbf{\ourmethod}, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at this http URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Switch-SWE, a benchmark that tests whether coding agents can resume an unfinished repository task after working on other unfinished tasks from the same repository, and it proposes a context-management module that improves resumption.
AI.motivation: Existing repository-level benchmarks score a single issue-to-patch episode and do not measure whether an agent can recover a task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work in the same repository.
AI.method: The benchmark has 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, each rendered as matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical requirements and executable verifiers, where the switched session interleaves stages from other unfinished tasks and only the final focus patch is scored; a plug-in context-management module selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries.
AI.result: Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points (range 6.0 to 15.0), trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state, and on OpenCode the module improves focus-task completion under task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents do not reliably hold focus across task switches, and explicit task-state management is a practical way to reduce this loss.

title: CULTURE-CMT: Benchmarking Contextualized Social Media Translation
summary: Social-media comments are interactions, yet they are often translated and evaluated as isolated text. This mismatch is especially problematic when meaning depends on surrounding discussion, community-specific slang, or culturally situated expressions. We introduce CULTURE-CMT, a Chinese-English benchmark for contextualized social-media comment translation that restores the post and conversational context naturally available to users. Its 572 manually verified examples are organized into Slang, Context, and Both, enabling diagnostic analysis of distinct and interacting sources of translation difficulty. To support scalable evaluation, we further develop a retrieval-augmented cultural-effectiveness Judger that combines a calibrated scoring model with dynamically retrieved cultural knowledge. CULTURE-CMT reveals several non-trivial patterns. Providing interaction context improves most model configurations, but does not eliminate culturally ineffective translations. Examples requiring both contextual grounding and culturally situated language remain substantially more difficult than either source of difficulty alone. Moreover, larger models are not consistently better, and thinking produces highly model-dependent gains, including occasional degradation. In contrast, a 27B model adapted on benchmark-disjoint social-media data achieves the lowest observed invalidity rate among the evaluated configurations under thinking inference with context. Together, these results suggest that realistic social-media translation is not simply a matter of scaling models or reasoning longer, but of learning to translate meaning as it is constructed within evolving online interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CULTURE-CMT, a Chinese-English benchmark of 572 manually verified examples for translating social media comments with their post and conversational context, together with a retrieval-augmented cultural-effectiveness Judger.
AI.motivation: Social media comments are usually translated and evaluated in isolation, which fails when meaning depends on surrounding discussion, community slang or culturally situated expressions.
AI.method: Examples are organized into Slang, Context and Both categories to diagnose distinct and interacting sources of difficulty, and a Judger combines a calibrated scoring model with dynamically retrieved cultural knowledge to support scalable evaluation.
AI.result: Providing interaction context improves most model configurations but does not remove culturally ineffective translations, examples needing both context and culturally situated language are harder than either alone, larger models are not consistently better, and thinking gives model-dependent gains including occasional degradation; a 27B model adapted on benchmark-disjoint social media data has the lowest invalidity rate among the evaluated configurations under thinking inference with context.
AI.conclusion: Realistic social media translation is not simply a matter of scaling models or reasoning longer, but of learning to translate meaning as it is constructed within evolving online interactions.

title: How Green Is Your Manifesto? Scoring Environmental Positions in the 2024 EU Elections with an LLM Panel
summary: Locating political parties on environmental and climate policy is central to the study of party competition, yet the established instruments, expert surveys and the hand coding of manifestos, are costly, periodic, and slow to extend to new documents. We ask whether a panel of large language models can serve as a cheaper and reproducible alternative.
