Treating each manifesto as a set of sentences, three models from independent providers score every sentence on two dimensions, environmental protection and climate change, separating a party's position on an issue from the salience it gives it, and the judgments are averaged to the manifesto level. Agreement across the models is retained as a built-in reliability signal. We apply the panel to 41 manifestos from the 2024 European Parliament election, covering Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the European party families, and validate it against the 2024 Chapel Hill Expert Survey for the 25 parties with a like-for-like expert benchmark, using the other manifestos as diagnostic cases. The panel recovers the expert ordering of parties with strong rank agreement on both dimensions, while reading them as systematically greener than experts do, a gap we interpret as the distance between manifesto promise and governing record. Inter-model disagreement modestly flags where the instrument errs, and position and salience prove related for environmental protection but independent for climate change. The result is a transparent, low-cost, and multilingual instrument that complements rather than replaces expert and hand-coded approaches; the prompt, code, and manifesto-level results are released openly.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an LLM panel of three models from independent providers to score the environmental and climate positions of party manifestos, and validates it on the 2024 European Parliament election against the Chapel Hill Expert Survey.
AI.motivation: Expert surveys and hand-coded manifesto analysis are costly, periodic and slow to extend to new documents, so a cheaper and reproducible alternative is needed for locating parties on environmental policy.
AI.method: Each manifesto is treated as a set of sentences that three LLMs score on environmental protection and climate change, separating position from salience, with judgments averaged to the manifesto level and inter-model agreement used as a reliability signal.
AI.result: Applied to 41 manifestos from the 2024 European Parliament election, the panel recovers the expert ordering of the 25 validated parties with strong rank agreement on both dimensions while reading parties as systematically greener than experts, inter-model disagreement flags where the instrument errs, and position and salience are related for environmental protection but independent for climate change.
AI.conclusion: The LLM panel is a transparent, low-cost and multilingual instrument that complements rather than replaces expert and hand-coded approaches, and the prompt, code and results are released.

title: Consolidating Reasoning with Test-Time Training
comment: NeurIPS 2026, 25 pages, test-time training, reasoning aggregation, meta-learning
summary: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires finalizing solutions from reasoning that is distributed across the individual attempts of many agents. However, useful intermediate reasoning can remain unexploited when collaboration is limited to voting on conclusions reached among individual agents, or aggregating long, noisy collections of reasoning trajectories in context. In this work, we propose TTT-Consolidate, a framework that uses multi-agent reasoning trajectories as adaptation data to improve a model's subsequent reasoning. TTT-Consolidate jointly consolidates trajectories into parametric representations through test-time training, then generates a new solution by conditioning on the consolidated information. We meta-learn how to consolidate using bi-level optimization at training time, where an inner loop encodes reasoning trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter, and an outer loop learns meta-parameters for the inner loop such that the consolidation is helpful for the model to synthesize a final solution. As no large-scale corpus of diverse reasoning trajectories exists for training aggregation methods, we construct the OpenParallelThinking corpus composed of 12,810 math problems paired with a mixture of trajectories from six LLMs. Evaluated on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, TTT-Consolidate outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points, even under matched compute and runtime settings, with the gap widening at larger model scales. TTT-Consolidate also recovers from unsuccessful individual trajectories more robustly, an ability that improves as the number of available (even incorrect) trajectories increases. Finally, we demonstrate that TTT-Consolidate benefits from both SFT and RL-based outer loop objectives. We will release TTT-Consolidate and OpenParallelThinking for use in future work on reasoning aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TTT-Consolidate, which turns multi-agent reasoning trajectories into a LoRA adapter through test-time training and then generates a final solution conditioned on that adapter.
AI.motivation: Aggregating multi-agent reasoning by voting on conclusions or by concatenating long, noisy trajectories in context leaves useful intermediate reasoning unexploited, and no large corpus exists for training aggregation methods.
AI.method: The method meta-learns consolidation with bi-level optimization, where the inner loop encodes trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter and the outer loop learns meta-parameters so that the consolidated information helps synthesize the final solution, and the authors build the OpenParallelThinking corpus of 12,810 math problems with trajectories from six LLMs.
AI.result: On challenging math and STEM benchmarks, TTT-Consolidate outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points under matched compute and runtime, the gap widens at larger scales, it recovers from unsuccessful trajectories more robustly, and it benefits from both SFT and RL outer-loop objectives.
AI.conclusion: Consolidating distributed reasoning into parameters is an effective alternative to voting or in-context aggregation, and the authors plan to release the method and corpus.

title: FOLLIE: Automated Reasoning over the First Dataset of Sentences with their First-Order Logical Representation for French
summary: FOLLIE (for First-Order Logic for Language Inference and Entailment for French) connects French sentences, compositional first-order representations and automated natural language inference (NLI). The first French NLI-ready, NL-to-FOL resource, it contains 19,983 inference records and 36,987 non-empty sentence-slot--formula mappings from six heterogeneous NLI sources, retaining French lexical material and source problem structure. Its silver annotations are produced by a neural--symbolic pipeline, with 111 separately identified LLM-assisted additions. The construction combines morphosyntactic analysis, probability-conditioned categorial multitagging, grammatical proof search, discourse representation and first-order semantic construction. Stage-wise experiments show substantial gains in derivation coverage; analyses of conjunction distributions, logical-operator incidence and scope alternation characterise the resulting resource. We then develop an automatic inference engine whose input-conditioned background theories address lexical relations, quantification, quantities, event structure and temporal dependencies. Prover9 supplies proofs for entailment and contradiction, while Mace4 supports bounded consistency checks. Three-way accuracies are 65.37% on all 335 FraCaS-FR problems, 70.33% on 300 GQNLI-FR problems and 71.35% on 9,399 eligible SICK-FR records pooled across splits. Agreement with reference labels among committed decisions is 93.53%, 100.00% and 98.66%, at commitment coverage of 41.49%, 37.00% and 15.05%, respectively. Worked constructions, axiom schemas and proof analyses explain these outcomes and identify the contributions of scope, reference, lexical knowledge and numerical structure. FOLLIE provides a French experimental basis for studying the representations and assumptions that connect sentence interpretation to deductive inference.

AI.tldr: The paper presents FOLLIE, the first French natural language inference resource pairing sentences with first-order logic representations, together with an automatic inference engine that reaches about 65 to 71 percent three-way accuracy on three French NLI benchmarks.
AI.motivation: French lacked an NLI-ready natural-language-to-first-order-logic resource and an automatic inference pipeline that connects sentence interpretation to deductive inference.
AI.method: The resource is built with a neural-symbolic pipeline that combines morphosyntactic analysis, probability-conditioned categorial multitagging, grammatical proof search, discourse representation and first-order semantic construction, and the inference engine uses input-conditioned background theories with Prover9 for proofs and Mace4 for bounded consistency checks.
AI.result: The resource contains 19,983 inference records and 36,987 non-empty sentence-slot formula mappings from six NLI sources, with 111 LLM-assisted additions, and three-way accuracies are 65.37% on FraCaS-FR, 70.33% on GQNLI-FR and 71.35% on eligible SICK-FR records; agreement with reference labels on committed decisions is 93.53%, 100.00% and 98.66% at coverages of 41.49%, 37.00% and 15.05%.
AI.conclusion: FOLLIE provides an experimental basis for French studies of how sentence representations and assumptions connect to deductive inference, with accuracy high on committed decisions but limited by coverage.

title: HaloGuard 2.0: An Open-Weights Constitutional Output Guard for Multilingual Response Safety
summary: An input guard decides whether a request reaches the model, but never sees what the model says. Harm that emerges during generation, because a jailbreak passed the input layer or a benign request drifted into operational detail, is visible only on the output side and only as tokens arrive. We present HaloGuard 2.0, an open-weight streaming output guard that assigns a safe/unsafe probability to every response token in a single forward pass, so a deployment can stop the stream once harm is confirmed. The guard reuses the constitution of HaloGuard 1.0, our input guard, to organise a 478,532-response training corpus, and supervises each token from the point where the response becomes harmful. We find that a guard trained on conventionally shaped data learns a shortcut specific to streaming: it judges the prompt instead of the response, and handles only 13.9% of matched safe/unsafe response pairs correctly. We correct this with a second phase on 106,043 counterfactual responses built around the base guard's own failure modes, and release the equal-weight average of the base and corrective models. On six English response-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 2.0-0.8B reaches a macro F1 of 83.6 (83.3 on held-out halves of the decision-rule search), up from 72.8, with 38% fewer false positives. It matches the strongest full-response guards with 5-10x fewer parameters and is 2.6 points above the strongest streaming guard, Qwen3Guard-Stream-4B. A multilingual variant, HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B, trained on PolyGuardMix, reaches 83.1 F1 on the response labels of PolyGuardPrompts across 17 languages, 5.0 points above the strongest baseline. On one H100 the guard costs 0.37 ms per token per stream when moderating 64 concurrent responses. Both guards are hardened continuously through the weekly red-teaming protocol of HaloGuard 1.0, extended here to the output layer.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HaloGuard 2.0, an open-weight streaming output guard that scores every response token for safety, and a multilingual variant, reaching strong macro F1 on six English response-safety benchmarks and 17-language response labels at low per-token cost.
AI.motivation: Input guards cannot see what a model generates, so harm that emerges during generation after a jailbreak or drift into operational detail is visible only on the output side and only as tokens arrive.
AI.method: A streaming guard assigns a safe or unsafe probability to each token in one forward pass so a stream can be stopped once harm is confirmed; it is trained on a 478,532-response corpus organized by the HaloGuard 1.0 constitution, and a second phase on 106,043 counterfactual responses corrects a shortcut in which the guard judged the prompt instead of the response, with the release being the equal-weight average of the base and corrective models.
AI.result: HaloGuard 2.0-0.8B reaches macro F1 of 83.6 on six English response-safety benchmarks, up from 72.8, with 38% fewer false positives, and is 2.6 points above the strongest streaming guard, Qwen3Guard-Stream-4B; the multilingual HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B reaches 83.1 F1 on PolyGuardPrompts response labels across 17 languages, 5.0 points above the strongest baseline, and the guard costs 0.37 ms per token per stream with 64 concurrent responses on one H100.
AI.conclusion: Output-side streaming moderation can match full-response guards with 5 to 10 times fewer parameters, and the authors state that both guards are hardened continuously through weekly red-teaming.

title: GatedV: Self-Gated Values for Transformer Language Models
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, Code and experimental results: this https URL
summary: Standard attention forms query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices through learned linear projections of input hidden states. Architectures such as GAU and Mega incorporate nonlinear transformations into attention. In this paper, we propose GatedV, a simple attention variant that applies SiLU only to V before aggregation without introducing additional trainable parameters. We evaluate GatedV against a standard decoder-only Transformer using matched parameter counts, paired initializations, and equal training-token budgets. At 2.33M parameters, GatedV reduces mean held-out perplexity from 59.1 to 57.9 (2.0%), with improvements across all five paired seeds. At 26.16M parameters, following an equal-budget learning-rate search, mean held-out perplexity falls from 20.2 to 19.7 (2.4%), with improvements across all three paired seeds. Small-model ablations show that the tested affine rescaling of values does not fully reproduce GatedV's gains. A short interleaved benchmark on NVIDIA DGX Spark measures approximately 0.7% higher full-context forward latency for the larger model, based on synchronized wall-clock timings. These findings suggest that value-only self-gating can improve language modeling performance without increasing parameter count or redesigning the attention-weighting mechanism.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GatedV, an attention variant that applies SiLU only to the value matrix before aggregation, which lowers held-out perplexity in decoder-only Transformers without adding trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Standard attention uses linear projections for queries, keys and values, while architectures such as GAU and Mega add nonlinear transformations to attention, and the question is whether a simpler value-only gate helps.
AI.method: GatedV applies SiLU to V before aggregation with no additional parameters, and it is compared with a standard decoder-only Transformer under matched parameter counts, paired initializations and equal training-token budgets.
AI.result: At 2.33M parameters, mean held-out perplexity falls from 59.1 to 57.9 (2.0%) across all five paired seeds, and at 26.16M parameters it falls from 20.2 to 19.7 (2.4%) across all three paired seeds; a tested affine rescaling of values does not reproduce the gains, and full-context forward latency is about 0.7% higher for the larger model on an NVIDIA DGX Spark.
AI.conclusion: Value-only self-gating can improve language modeling without increasing parameter count or redesigning attention weighting, at a small latency cost.

title: Detailed Derivation of The Backpropagation Algorithm
comment: 41 pages, 2 figures, 2 algorithms. Code: this https URL
summary: Backpropagation is the standard method for computing the gradients that train neural networks, but it is usually presented in a compact vector form that skips the intermediate steps. This tutorial derives backpropagation step by step for a fully connected feedforward network with sigmoid activations and a squared-error loss. Using a running example with three layers, we first differentiate the error with respect to a single weight by following its path through the network with the chain rule. We then show how summing over all paths leads to the error terms $\delta$ and to the four general backpropagation equations in matrix form. Every term is annotated with its dimensions, so each equation can be checked for consistency. The derivation is then extended to $m$ training examples, where the weight gradients become a single matrix product and the bias term corresponds to broadcasting. It is also extended to mini-batch gradient descent, including why the gradient of a mini-batch estimates the full gradient. Batch and mini-batch training are both given as algorithms. Finally, each equation is linked to the corresponding line of a NumPy implementation trained on the AHDBase dataset of handwritten Arabic digits, and the complete code is included.

AI.tldr: The paper is a tutorial that derives backpropagation step by step for a fully connected sigmoid network with squared-error loss, extending the derivation to m training examples and mini-batch gradient descent, and links each equation to a NumPy implementation trained on AHDBase.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation is usually presented in compact vector form that skips intermediate steps, which makes the individual equations hard to check and to connect with code.
AI.method: The derivation uses a three-layer running example with the chain rule over paths, sums over paths to obtain the error terms delta and the four general backpropagation equations in matrix form with dimensions annotated, then extends to m examples, mini-batches and batch and mini-batch algorithms.
AI.result: The tutorial shows that the gradient of a mini-batch estimates the full gradient and that the weight gradients for m examples become a single matrix product with bias handled by broadcasting, and each equation is linked to a line of a NumPy implementation trained on the AHDBase handwritten Arabic digit dataset, with the complete code included.
AI.conclusion: A dimension-annotated, step-by-step derivation makes each backpropagation equation verifiable and connects it directly to implementation.

title: Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space
summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. We show, with interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) on the NARCBench collusion benchmark, that colluding agents' J-space holds the collusion itself: before replying, 86% of colluders represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse. In a steganographic card-counting task, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count, and causal interventions alter its count. We also introduce the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT), an unsupervised method for detecting collusion between agents. We evaluate J-PACT on four open-weight models: GPT-OSS-20B, Llama-3.3-70B-IT, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios, and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the J-space of colluding LLM agents holds the collusion itself and introduces J-PACT, an unsupervised method that detects collusion between agents and names the colluding pair.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in multi-agent systems can coordinate in ways that escape human oversight, and the J-space has been used to uncover deception in single models but not to detect or steer collusion between agents.
AI.method: Interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) using the NARCBench collusion benchmark and a steganographic card-counting task test whether the J-space encodes collusion and hidden counts, with causal interventions, and the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT) is introduced as an unsupervised detector evaluated on four open-weight models.
AI.result: Before replying, 86% of colluding agents represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count that causal interventions can alter, and J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.
AI.conclusion: Collusion between agents is visible in internal representations, and an unsupervised contrast can detect it without labels.

title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Dataset, rule texts and harness available at this https URL
summary: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as runtime classifiers for a 28-rule coding-agent policy engine, and finds that writing rule boundaries as examples and counterexamples raises recall and lowers false alarms.
AI.motivation: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets or message the wrong person faster than a human can review, and the question is whether a decision model can catch these risks at runtime.
AI.method: A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules with a sealed holdout, and a single shared preamble was used in both conditions while explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples were compared with a baseline; further tests replaced concrete names with generic descriptions and wrote boundaries as prose, and a follow-up used 16 new scenarios.
AI.result: Explicit boundaries raised recall by 5.5 to 26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21; Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2% and its unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions, with a median latency of 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests; the follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models.
AI.conclusion: Explicit policy boundaries improve runtime detection of risky agent actions with fewer false alarms, and the dataset, rule texts and harness are released.

title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
summary: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes 6,959 paper revision trajectories from five AI conferences and finds that AI reviewers often leave scores unchanged after substantive revisions and that a brief negative user opinion can erase the gain.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether AI reviewers' judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision, and this matters for using them to assess scientific manuscripts.
AI.method: The authors use PaperTrajectory-2026, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate overall quality judgments, and they compare independent assessments from eight AI reviewers across manuscript versions, relating annotated major improvements and revision dimensions to score changes and testing the effect of user opinions.
AI.result: Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, agreement on the direction of score changes is weak, revision dimensions show only reviewer-specific associations with limited predictive value, and a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse the advantage of a higher neutral score, with substantial variation across reviewers.
AI.conclusion: Substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in AI review scores, and scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, which motivates assessments tied to manuscript evidence.

title: Current state of LLMs for Arabic dialectal machine translation
summary: This work presents an evaluation of large language models (LLMs) for English to dialectal Arabic machine translation on the MADAR dataset. We evaluate both translation directions (English to Arabic and vice-versa) on 16 Arabic dialects. Our experiments cover a diverse set of models, including specialized Arabic models (Jais, Nile), multilingual models (Gemma, Command-R, Mistral, Aya), and commercial APIs (GPT-4.1). We employ multiple evaluation metrics: BLEU, CHRF, COMET (both reference-based and reference-less variants) and GEMBA (LLM-as-a-judge), as well as a small-scale manual evaluation, to assess translation quality. We discuss the challenges of automatic MT evaluation, especially in the context of Arabic dialects. We also evaluate the ability of LLMs to classify the dialect used in a text. The study offers insights into the capabilities and limitations of current LLMs for dialectal Arabic machine translation, particularly highlighting the difficulty of handling dialectal diversity, although the results may be influenced by possible training data contamination, which is always a concern with LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates large language models on English-to-dialectal-Arabic and dialectal-Arabic-to-English machine translation across 16 Arabic dialects on the MADAR dataset, and also tests their dialect classification.
AI.motivation: Dialectal Arabic machine translation is under-studied, and automatic MT evaluation is especially hard for Arabic dialects, so the current capabilities and limits of LLMs need to be documented.
AI.method: The study covers specialized Arabic models (Jais, Nile), multilingual models (Gemma, Command-R, Mistral, Aya) and a commercial API (GPT-4.1), scored with BLEU, CHRF, COMET (reference-based and reference-less), GEMBA LLM-as-a-judge and a small manual evaluation, plus a dialect classification task.
AI.result: The abstract reports no specific numbers and states that the study highlights the difficulty of handling dialectal diversity, while results may be influenced by possible training data contamination.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have clear capabilities and limits for dialectal Arabic machine translation, and dialectal diversity remains a major challenge, with the caveat that contamination may inflate results.

title: GRIPS: An Empirical Study of Pre-SQL Grounding Information for SQL Generation
summary: Text-to-SQL systems answer natural language questions over structured data, but can fail before SQL generation by linking question mentions to the wrong table, column, value, or relation. Even valid SQL can then return an incorrect answer. This raises a central question: What pre-SQL information helps a SQL generator, and when does additional information cease to help? We investigate this question on TempTabQA-C and BIRD. Among the audited SQL Static failures, grounding errors form the largest category on both benchmarks. We introduce GRIPS (Grounding Representation and Input Processing for SQL generation), a three-stage method that derives structured pre-SQL information to make these decisions explicit before query generation. Across GPT-5-nano and Llama-70B, GRIPS-Adaptive improves over SQL Static in 18 of 20 settings, with an average accuracy gain of 11.8 percentage points, while reducing model-call token usage by 47.8%. Our controlled analysis shows which grounding information can improve SQL generation, whereas adding more pre-SQL information does not consistently help. By separating question-input grounding from SQL generation, GRIPS makes text-to-SQL more accurate, efficient, and easier to diagnose.

AI.tldr: The paper presents GRIPS, a three-stage method that derives structured pre-SQL grounding information for text-to-SQL, and shows that grounding information helps SQL generation while adding more pre-SQL information does not consistently help.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SQL systems often fail before SQL generation by linking question mentions to the wrong table, column, value or relation, and grounding errors are the largest failure category on TempTabQA-C and BIRD.
AI.method: GRIPS (Grounding Representation and Input Processing for SQL generation) derives structured pre-SQL information in three stages so that decisions are explicit before query generation, and GRIPS-Adaptive is compared with SQL Static across GPT-5-nano and Llama-70B.
AI.result: GRIPS-Adaptive improves over SQL Static in 18 of 20 settings with an average accuracy gain of 11.8 percentage points while reducing model-call token usage by 47.8%, and a controlled analysis shows which grounding information helps.
AI.conclusion: Separating question-input grounding from SQL generation makes text-to-SQL more accurate, efficient and easier to diagnose, and more pre-SQL information is not automatically better.

title: A Capitulation Direction Emerges With Scale and Is Causally Load-Bearing Where Validation Is Strong: Eight Models, Two Families, and Five Measurement Hazards
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures. Code, data and pre-registration: this https URL
summary: Sycophancy in language models is well documented as a behaviour but poorly localised as a mechanism. We ask whether capitulation under user pushback, the abandonment of a correct answer when a user objects, corresponds to a linear direction in the residual stream, and whether such a direction emerges with scale. Across eight instruction-tuned models spanning 0.5B to 14B parameters in two families, under a pre-registered protocol with leave-one-question-out cross-validation, within-question permutation nulls, and a positive control, we find no usable direction below 7B and a direction that clears our validation gate at 7B, 8B and 14B. Ablating that direction in Qwen2.5-7B reduces the rate at which the model reverses a correct answer by 4.8 percentage points, roughly a quarter in relative terms, while the identical intervention on a gate-failing direction and on a marginally passing one produces no effect. Probe quality, not statistical significance, predicts causal relevance. Behaviourally, pushback destroys three to five times more correct answers than it repairs at 1B and reaches parity by 7B, falsifying our own pre-registered prediction, and a sign-reversing crossover between pushback types survives an order of magnitude of scale in Qwen and holds at 8B in Llama, with marginalisation over five paraphrases per type. We additionally quantify five measurement hazards, including a numerical-precision effect that changes roughly one episode label in ten.

AI.tldr: The paper finds a linear capitulation direction in the residual stream of instruction-tuned models that emerges around 7B parameters and is causally relevant where probe validation is strong, and it documents several measurement hazards.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy is well documented as a behaviour but poorly localized as a mechanism, and the paper asks whether capitulation under user pushback corresponds to a linear direction that emerges with scale.
AI.method: Eight instruction-tuned models from 0.5B to 14B parameters in two families are tested under a pre-registered protocol with leave-one-question-out cross-validation, within-question permutation nulls and a positive control, and the direction is ablated in Qwen2.5-7B.
AI.result: No usable direction is found below 7B, and a direction clears the validation gate at 7B, 8B and 14B; ablating it reduces the rate of reversing correct answers by 4.8 percentage points, roughly a quarter in relative terms, while ablating gate-failing or marginal directions has no effect; pushback destroys three to five times more correct answers than it repairs at 1B and reaches parity by 7B, which falsifies the authors' own prediction.
AI.conclusion: Probe quality rather than statistical significance predicts causal relevance, and the authors identify five measurement hazards, including a numerical-precision effect that changes about one episode label in ten.

title: Does a Norwegian further-trained model give more outdated legal values than its base model? A preregistered paired comparison of Borealis 2 and Gemma 4
comment: Preregistered: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23858965. Data and code: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23870450, this https URL
summary: We compare how often two released language models give outdated numeric values from Norwegian statutes and regulations: NbAiLab/borealis2-26b-a4b-preview (Borealis 2), which the National Library of Norway further trained from google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (Gemma 4), and Gemma 4 itself. The study was preregistered (doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23858965) and uses the closed norregel benchmark, scored deterministically against a value history. On the 411 of 503 primary items where both models gave an interpretable answer, Borealis 2 alone was outdated on 10 items and Gemma 4 alone on 11 (d = -0.2 percentage points, 95% cluster bootstrap interval [-2.7, +2.5], exact one-sided McNemar p = 0.668). By the preregistered rule this is no effect of interest: the whole interval lies within the smallest effect of interest of +/-10 percentage points. Among the secondary measures, only the share of answers giving a value that took effect after the question date differs after Holm correction; Gemma 4 gave such answers more often. An exploratory comparison of two smaller Borealis models had no discordant pairs and is not informative. The design compares released models and does not isolate the effect of any part of their training.

AI.tldr: A preregistered paired comparison finds no meaningful difference in outdated Norwegian legal values between the Norwegian further-trained model Borealis 2 and its base model Gemma 4.
AI.motivation: It is unknown whether further training of Gemma 4 into the Norwegian model Borealis 2 changes how often it gives outdated numeric values from Norwegian statutes and regulations.
AI.method: The authors compare Borealis 2 and Gemma 4 on the closed norregel benchmark, scored deterministically against a value history, with a preregistered design, a cluster bootstrap interval and an exact one-sided McNemar test on items where both models gave interpretable answers.
AI.result: On 411 of 503 primary items, Borealis 2 alone was outdated on 10 items and Gemma 4 alone on 11, a difference of -0.2 percentage points with a 95% cluster bootstrap interval of [-2.7, +2.5] and McNemar p = 0.668; the whole interval lies within the smallest effect of interest of plus or minus 10 points, and only one secondary measure differs after Holm correction, with Gemma 4 giving answers about values that took effect after the question date more often.
AI.conclusion: By the preregistered rule there is no effect of interest, and because the design compares released models it does not isolate the effect of any part of training.

title: MemShift: Separating Detection from Repair in LLM-Derived Personal Memory
summary: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person's records under the person's own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MemShift, a benchmark that separates detection from repair when an LLM-derived personal memory value must change, and finds that detection helps only as far as repair allows.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks that score only final answers cannot tell whether a memory failed to notice a change or failed to repair its value, and they state every change as new text.
AI.method: MemShift defines five shifts (source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch and export), where the first three fork a synthetic world into branches, gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge, and a reference memory with known detection and repair validates the measure; four open-weight LLMs are evaluated.
AI.result: The LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, detection helps only as much as repair allows, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation.
AI.conclusion: Separating detection from repair reveals failures that answer-only scoring hides, and program-based recomputation over typed records is a strong remedy.

title: Which Words a Model Fears: From a Refusal Direction to a Vocabulary-Wide Fear Lexicon
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures. Code: this https URL ; data: this https URL
summary: Whether an aligned language model refuses depends in part on which words a prompt contains, regardless of whether those words carry the request's meaning. Harm words shift the hidden state at the generation boundary along a component shared across prompts and words, which crossed differencing extracts as a single direction. In eight models, writing along this direction raises and lowers refusal monotonically with dose, ahead of random and KL-matched directions. Used as a ruler over the full vocabulary, the direction gives every word a shift, from "feared" words at one end to "courage" words at the other; a word's shift is predictable from its own representation, and appending a feared word to a benign prompt is enough to make the model refuse it. Two held-out tests validate the ranking in all eight models: refusal after inserting an unseen word rises with its table shift, and replacing a prompt's most feared word by its most courageous meaning-preserving synonym significantly raises the answer rate on benign and harmful prompts alike, by an amount that follows the shift the replacement actually causes.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that refusal in aligned language models depends on a vocabulary-wide fear direction, a shared component of harm words that can be read as a ranking of every word and that can be used to predict and change refusals.
AI.motivation: Whether a model refuses depends partly on which words a prompt contains regardless of their meaning, and the mechanism behind this word-level sensitivity is not understood.
AI.method: A refusal direction is extracted by crossed differencing of hidden states at the generation boundary, writing along it is tested in eight models with random and KL-matched directions as controls, and the direction is used as a ruler to score the full vocabulary, with two held-out tests inserting unseen words and replacing feared words with courageous synonyms.
AI.result: Writing along the direction raises and lowers refusal monotonically with dose in all eight models, a word's shift is predictable from its own representation, appending a feared word to a benign prompt makes the model refuse it, and the held-out tests validate the ranking in all eight models, with replacement by a more courageous synonym significantly raising the answer rate on benign and harmful prompts.
AI.conclusion: Refusal behavior is sensitive to lexical fear signals that can be mapped across the vocabulary, which has implications for how alignment and refusals depend on word choice.

title: VisCodeBench: a new benchmark dataset for Text-to-Vis reflecting real-world practice
comment: Accepted to COLM 2026. this https URL
summary: Generating visualisations from natural language requests (text-to-vis) enables users to explore data more efficiently. While LLMs can complete simple visualisation requests, their performance on challenging ones is not well covered by existing benchmarks. We introduce VisCodeBench, an end-to-end text-to-vis benchmark with 2,672 samples from three different domains: educational, scientific, and general audience scenarios with varying levels of complexity. We benchmark three visualisation systems---Codex, Claude Code, and LIDA---paired with a range of open and commercial LLMs across seven metrics covering execution, chart content, and visual quality. While basic execution is near-solved for strong systems, no system comes close to reproducing the reference data, with the best displayed data similarity reaching only $0.81$ and falling to $0.69$ on our hardest subset for this metric. We further find that frontier models separate on chart correctness and efficiency, with ClaudeCode-Opus-4.7 improving chart correctness by around 5 points over Codex-GPT-5 while running roughly 20 seconds faster. Separately, we find that system design matters as much as the underlying model: despite both running on GPT-5, Codex clearly outperforms LIDA, showing that the surrounding prompting, execution, and refinement pipeline can shape outcomes as much as the model itself. Finally, latency remains a practical obstacle, as even the strongest systems take 39-78 seconds to produce results. VisCodeBench is available at \href{this https URL}{this https URL} and accessed via a leaderboard; the full dataset is kept private to prevent LLM training use.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VisCodeBench, a text-to-visualization benchmark of 2,672 samples that shows strong systems execute requests well but reproduce the reference data poorly and are slow.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks do not cover challenging visualization requests well, so they do not reflect how text-to-vis systems perform on realistic, complex tasks.
AI.method: VisCodeBench has samples from educational, scientific and general audience domains with varying complexity, and three systems (Codex, Claude Code and LIDA) are paired with several open and commercial LLMs and scored on seven metrics covering execution, chart content and visual quality, with the full dataset kept private.
AI.result: Basic execution is near-solved for strong systems, the best displayed data similarity is 0.81 and falls to 0.69 on the hardest subset, ClaudeCode-Opus-4.7 improves chart correctness by around 5 points over Codex-GPT-5 while running about 20 seconds faster, Codex clearly outperforms LIDA although both run on GPT-5, and even the strongest systems take 39 to 78 seconds.
AI.conclusion: System design such as prompting, execution and refinement matters as much as the underlying model, and latency remains a practical obstacle for text-to-vis.

title: Beyond Accuracy: How Quantization Affects Coding Agents
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Small Language Models for Agentic Systems (SLM-Agents), Paris, France
summary: Agents are increasingly used for coding tasks, but the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) limits where they can run. Quantization reduces model size, but its effects on coding agents that execute and revise programs remain underexplored. We compare BF16 with 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct (7B, 14B, and 32B) and Devstral-Small-2507 (24B) on OJBench coding problems across three seeds. We detect no statistically significant accuracy loss for any of the coding agents. However, final accuracy can conceal substantial behavioral changes: AWQ reduces Qwen-7B one-shot solves from 17 to 0 while increasing loop-based solves from 10 to 25. All Qwen-32B successes involve tool use, whereas Devstral rarely makes a valid executor call. Failure profiles also differ: Qwen-32B produces far more compilation errors than the smaller Qwen models, rising slightly under quantization, while Devstral's failures shift significantly from runtime errors toward wrong answers and timeouts. These findings indicate that quantization robustness in coding agents should be assessed through solution trajectories, tool use, and failure modes, in addition to final accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ quantization shows no statistically significant accuracy loss for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct and Devstral-Small coding agents on OJBench, yet it substantially changes their behavior and failure modes.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces the cost of running LLM coding agents, but its effects on agents that execute and revise programs remain underexplored.
AI.method: The authors compare BF16 with 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct at 7B, 14B and 32B and Devstral-Small-2507 at 24B on OJBench coding problems across three seeds, and analyze solution trajectories, tool use and failure types.
AI.result: No statistically significant accuracy loss is detected for any agent, but AWQ reduces Qwen-7B one-shot solves from 17 to 0 while increasing loop-based solves from 10 to 25, all Qwen-32B successes involve tool use while Devstral rarely makes a valid executor call, Qwen-32B produces many more compilation errors than smaller Qwen models, and Devstral's failures shift from runtime errors toward wrong answers and timeouts.
AI.conclusion: Quantization robustness in coding agents should be judged by solution trajectories, tool use and failure modes as well as final accuracy.

title: EviCast: Forecasting Retrieval Gains Through Shared Response Calibration
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) extends large language models with external evidence, yet relevant evidence does not ensure that a generator can use it. Indiscriminate retrieval can degrade task performance while adding retrieval and long-context inference costs. Existing methods neither determine before large-scale execution whether a generator, task distribution, and retriever configuration is worth deploying nor diagnose multiple candidate retrievers under a shared budget. We introduce EviCast, a framework that forecasts retrieval value through interventional evidence-state decomposition. EviCast measures a generator's response to controlled evidence states once and combines this shared profile with the offline evidence-state distribution of each candidate retriever, yielding the end-to-end net utility and its 95% lower confidence bound without executing every RAG configuration. A state-refinement analysis characterizes when its binary and topology-aware instantiations are exact and when shared calibration is statistically more efficient than per-retriever calibration. In frozen evaluations, EviCast correctly decides all 14 HotpotQA retrieval configurations with a forecast error of 2.75 F1 points while reducing diagnostic generation calls by 80%, and it attains the lowest forecast error among seven predictors in the low-budget regime. Its topology-aware instantiation, EviCast-T, captures the complementarity between terminal and bridge evidence, correctly deciding all 16 configurations on MuSiQue and HotpotQA and 23 of 24 after prospective transfer to a third dataset. These results show that retrieval deployment depends on both evidence availability and the generator's ability to convert evidence structure into stable net utility. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EviCast, a framework that forecasts the net utility of a retrieval-augmented generation configuration from a shared calibration of the generator's responses to controlled evidence states, without executing every configuration.
AI.motivation: Relevant evidence does not ensure that a generator can use it, indiscriminate retrieval can degrade performance while adding cost, and existing methods do not decide before large-scale execution whether a configuration is worth deploying.
AI.method: EviCast measures the generator's response to controlled evidence states once and combines that profile with the offline evidence-state distribution of each candidate retriever to produce end-to-end net utility and its 95% lower confidence bound, with binary and topology-aware instantiations, the latter called EviCast-T.
AI.result: On HotpotQA, EviCast correctly decides all 14 retrieval configurations with a forecast error of 2.75 F1 points while reducing diagnostic generation calls by 80%, and it has the lowest forecast error among seven predictors in the low-budget regime; EviCast-T decides all 16 configurations on MuSiQue and HotpotQA and 23 of 24 after prospective transfer to a third dataset.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval deployment depends on both evidence availability and the generator's ability to turn evidence structure into stable net utility, and forecasting can avoid costly exhaustive evaluation.

title: Solver-Like Behavior in Large Language Models as Formalizers
summary: In the LLM-as-formalizer paradigm, a large language model translates a problem into a formal program and leaves the search to a solver, gaining the solver's guarantees. Formalizers are now often reasoning models that write a long reasoning trace before the program, yet they are judged only by the program's output. We find that the trace routinely does the solver's job, assigning, testing and ruling out values until it often reaches the full answer; we call this solver-like behavior (SLB). We define an ontology of SLB over the trace, the program and its output, and use LLM judges, checked against human labels, to label 2,000 generations from three reasoning models on four constraint satisfaction datasets, each formalized in a declarative and an imperative formal language. SLB appears in 85% of traces and takes 24% of reasoning tokens, yet the program usually recomputes the answer, so the effort is redundant. The 9% of programs that inherit the trace's answer also inherit its errors, and pass output-based evaluation whenever that answer is correct. The amount of SLB is not associated with accuracy, and SLB is more common in imperative Python than in declarative Z3 or PDDL. Cautionary prompts reduce it by only a quarter, but hiding the problem's values behind placeholders, which the program receives only at run time, removes 97% of it without loss of accuracy. Formalizers should therefore be evaluated by how their programs are reached, not only by what they output.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies solver-like behavior (SLB) in the reasoning traces of LLM formalizers, where the trace solves the problem itself, and finds that the subsequent program usually redundantly recomputes the answer, while hiding problem values removes most of it without loss of accuracy.
AI.motivation: In the LLM-as-formalizer paradigm the program is judged only by its output, so the solving that occurs in long reasoning traces before the program goes unevaluated.
AI.method: The authors define an ontology of SLB over the trace, the program and its output, and use LLM judges checked against human labels to label 2,000 generations from three reasoning models on four constraint satisfaction datasets, each formalized in a declarative and an imperative language.
AI.result: SLB appears in 85% of traces and takes 24% of reasoning tokens, the program usually recomputes the answer, the 9% of programs that inherit the trace's answer also inherit its errors, SLB is not associated with accuracy and is more common in imperative Python than in declarative Z3 or PDDL, cautionary prompts reduce it by only a quarter, and placeholders for problem values that the program receives at run time remove 97% of it without loss of accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Formalizers should be evaluated by how their programs are reached, not only by their outputs, since much of the reasoning effort is redundant and can carry errors.

title: Diagnosing Model--Item Interactions in Language Model Benchmarks with LSIRM
summary: Language models with similar benchmark accuracy can succeed on different items. Overall scores do not show where their performance differs or which item properties might explain those differences. We demonstrate how the latent space item response model (LSIRM) can help evaluators investigate these patterns and their consequences for model comparison. We analyze 1,348 language models on 5,761 BBH items and compare ways of presenting and scoring answers across BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MuSR. We examine LSIRM maps, which summarize differences in performance across models and items, alongside item properties and records of correct and incorrect responses. In BBH, nearby items on these maps often share the same correct answer, such as "Yes" or "No." Across the four benchmarks, this pattern is stronger when answers are scored using option labels, such as A, B, C, and D, than when using the text of the options. We then estimate each model's tendency to perform better or worse on items with particular correct answers and quantify how this tendency contributes to its score. This separates an estimated contribution associated with correct answers from the remaining differences in item performance. Two models' total numbers of correct answers differed by only 14 out of 5,761 items. Excluding the estimated answer-category contribution from their scores moved their ranks hundreds of places in opposite directions, while keeping all other estimates unchanged. The approach helps evaluators identify differences hidden by overall accuracy and understand how the choice of what to include in a score affects model rankings.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the latent space item response model (LSIRM) to show that models with similar benchmark accuracy succeed on different items, and that answer-category tendencies can change model rankings when they are removed from scores.
AI.motivation: Overall benchmark scores hide where models differ and which item properties explain those differences, so evaluators need a way to investigate model-item interactions.
AI.method: The authors analyze 1,348 language models on 5,761 BBH items with LSIRM maps, compare option-label and option-text answer scoring across BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro and MuSR, and estimate each model's tendency to perform better or worse on items with particular correct answers, separating that contribution from the remaining item performance.
AI.result: On BBH, nearby items often share the same correct answer such as Yes or No, this pattern is stronger under option-label scoring than option-text scoring across the four benchmarks, and for two models whose correct counts differed by only 14 of 5,761 items, removing the estimated answer-category contribution moved their ranks hundreds of places in opposite directions.
AI.conclusion: Scoring choices and answer-category tendencies can change model rankings, so evaluators should examine item-level patterns beyond overall accuracy.

title: As Expected? Efficient LLM Planning via Expectation-Observation Consistency Verification
summary: LLM planning often relies on reactive executors (e.g., ReAct) that generate a single action at each step to remain grounded in the latest observations, incurring substantial inference cost. Batched executors reduce this cost by predicting multiple actions in a single model invocation, yet they are prone to compounding errors, as intermediate observations are ignored. We propose an expectation-observation consistency verification (EOCV) mechanism for batched executors, preserving grounding while improving efficiency. The mechanism generates expectations of action outcomes and compares them with the resulting observations. Consistency permits continued execution, whereas mismatches trigger early termination and replanning from the current observation. Experiments on text-based and multimodal benchmarks across multiple backbones show broadly comparable average task performance between EOCV and reactive executors, with a 29-35% reduction in average weighted token usage. Moreover, the mechanism is model-agnostic and remains effective when integrated into state-of-the-art planners.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes expectation-observation consistency verification (EOCV) for batched LLM executors, which keeps grounding while cutting token usage by 29 to 35% by stopping execution and replanning when predicted and actual observations differ.
AI.motivation: Reactive executors such as ReAct are grounded but expensive, while batched executors predict multiple actions per call and are prone to compounding errors because intermediate observations are ignored.
AI.method: The mechanism generates expectations of action outcomes and compares them with the resulting observations, continuing execution when they are consistent and triggering early termination and replanning from the current observation when they mismatch.
AI.result: On text-based and multimodal benchmarks across multiple backbones, EOCV has broadly comparable average task performance to reactive executors with a 29 to 35% reduction in average weighted token usage, and it remains effective when integrated into state-of-the-art planners.
AI.conclusion: Expectation checking makes batched execution efficient while preserving grounding, and the mechanism is model-agnostic.

title: GigaSpeech 3: Scaling Multi-Dialect Arabic Speech Recognition with Weakly Labeled Data
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 11 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing
summary: Dialectal Arabic speech recognition remains constrained by the scarcity of dialect-resolved transcribed speech despite the abundance of web audio. We introduce GigaSpeech 3, a corpus of 39,000 hours and 10 million weakly transcribed speech segments covering Algerian, Egyptian, Iraqi, Saudi, and Syrian Arabic. Starting from 60 hours of manual transcription per dialect, we train labeling models using speech-recognition-biased self-supervised learning and apply them to dialect-matched web audio. Data selection and four rounds of noisy-student refinement for Saudi and Syrian Arabic yield the final corpus. We validate its utility through dialect-specific and multi-dialect speech recognition training and cross-domain evaluation. On GigaSpeechBench, the final dialect-specific models outperform their labeling models across all five dialects and achieve a macro-average word error rate of 23.86%, a 16.6% relative reduction from the strongest third-party system covering all five dialects, while outperforming the best third-party result on three dialects. A multi-dialect model using self-predicted dialect identities achieves a macro-average word error rate of 25.51% while also supporting Modern Standard Arabic. Across eight conditions from three external corpora, a GigaSpeech 3-trained Zipformer achieves the lowest word error rate among six evaluated models in every condition, while adapting the Qwen3 speech recognizer on GigaSpeech 3 improves performance across all eight conditions. We release the corpus and recipes as a foundation for dialect-aware Arabic speech processing.

AI.tldr: The paper releases GigaSpeech 3, a corpus of 39,000 hours and 10 million weakly transcribed segments for five Arabic dialects, and shows that dialect-specific models trained on it reach a macro-average word error rate of 23.86% on GigaSpeechBench.
AI.motivation: Dialectal Arabic speech recognition is limited by the scarcity of dialect-resolved transcribed speech despite abundant web audio.
AI.method: The authors start from 60 hours of manual transcription per dialect, train labeling models with speech-recognition-biased self-supervised learning, apply them to dialect-matched web audio, and use data selection and four rounds of noisy-student refinement for Saudi and Syrian Arabic.
AI.result: Dialect-specific models outperform their labeling models on all five dialects and reach a macro-average WER of 23.86%, a 16.6% relative reduction from the strongest third-party system covering all five dialects, while a multi-dialect model with self-predicted dialect identities reaches 25.51% and also supports Modern Standard Arabic, and a GigaSpeech 3-trained Zipformer has the lowest WER among six models in all eight evaluated conditions from three external corpora.
AI.conclusion: The corpus and recipes provide a foundation for dialect-aware Arabic speech processing, and adapting the Qwen3 recognizer on the corpus improves performance across all eight conditions.

title: Chain on Demand: Deferred Evidence Organization for Long-Term Conversational Memory
summary: Long-term conversational memory faces a timing mismatch: write-time summaries and graphs organize history before a future query is known, while independent retrieval can allocate a limited evidence budget to redundant or fragmented turns. We introduce Chain on Demand (CoD), a query-time evidence organization framework over an unchanged turn-level memory. Given a broad candidate pool, CoD constructs a temporary evidence chain by allocating a fixed anchor budget according to query relevance, lexical diversity relative to selected anchors, and newly covered query terms, followed by deterministic restoration of each selected anchor's same-session neighborhood. The resulting chain is used only for the current query, while the underlying conversational memory remains unchanged. In a paired comparison over all 1,986 LoCoMo questions, CoD achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial questions and 76.3% on all 1,986 questions. On LongMemEval-S, one fixed configuration that indexes both user and assistant turns obtains 86.6% across all 500 questions. These results show that long-term memory can preserve the original conversation while deferring evidence organization until the information need is known.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Chain on Demand (CoD), a query-time framework that builds a temporary evidence chain from an unchanged turn-level memory, and reports higher accuracy on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S.
AI.motivation: Write-time summaries and graphs organize conversational history before a future query is known, while independent retrieval can spend a limited evidence budget on redundant or fragmented turns.
AI.method: From a broad candidate pool, CoD allocates a fixed anchor budget according to query relevance, lexical diversity relative to selected anchors and newly covered query terms, then restores each anchor's same-session neighborhood deterministically, using the chain only for the current query while the memory remains unchanged.
AI.result: In a paired comparison over all 1,986 LoCoMo questions, CoD achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial questions and 76.3% on all 1,986 questions, and on LongMemEval-S one fixed configuration that indexes both user and assistant turns obtains 86.6% across all 500 questions.
AI.conclusion: Long-term memory can preserve the original conversation while deferring evidence organization until the information need is known.

title: Same Sentence, Different Construct: Identity-Swapped Rationales Reveal Measurement Non-Invariance in LLM Hate Speech Classifiers
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as measurement instruments for socially consequential constructs such as hate speech, and are typically validated by their aggregate agreement with human labels. A valid instrument must also apply the same construct to every group it measures. We test this requirement using 421 \hc{} templates that are instantiated identically for seven protected groups, so that only the identity term varies. Four LLM classifiers each exceed 0.95 balanced accuracy, yet within identical templates two of them miss hateful statements about women at markedly higher rates than the same statements about other groups (excess false-negative rates of 8.3 and 4.4 percentage points), a gap first reported for fine-tuned classifiers in 2021. We show how the construct shifts. Comparing rationales within each template, we find that models invoke protected-group status for other groups but recast the identical statement about women as personal dislike or as aimed at an individual, in 22 of 30 missed templates for one model. Adding the benchmark's own definition, which lists sex as a protected characteristic, does not close the gap, and the contrast persists. Apparent false-positive disparities, by contrast, largely vanish under identity control and trace to reclaimed slurs present only for some groups. Errors shared by all models concentrate where model and benchmark definitions diverge, and pairwise counterfactual accuracy adds little beyond endpoint accuracy. We argue that validating LLM measurement requires identity-controlled tests of measurement invariance that examine both decisions and the criteria models state for them.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLM hate speech classifiers with high aggregate accuracy can apply the construct inconsistently across protected groups, missing hateful statements about women at higher rates in identical templates, and it argues for identity-controlled measurement invariance tests.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used as measurement instruments for constructs such as hate speech and are validated by aggregate agreement with human labels, which does not ensure that the same construct is applied to every group.
AI.method: The authors use 421 templates instantiated identically for seven protected groups so that only the identity term varies, evaluate four LLM classifiers, compare rationales within each template, and test whether adding the benchmark's own definition closes the gap.
AI.result: All four classifiers exceed 0.95 balanced accuracy, yet two of them show excess false-negative rates of 8.3 and 4.4 percentage points for statements about women, and in 22 of 30 missed templates for one model the rationale recasts the statement as personal dislike or as aimed at an individual; adding the definition does not close the gap, and apparent false-positive disparities largely vanish under identity control.
AI.conclusion: Validating LLM measurement requires identity-controlled tests of measurement invariance that examine both decisions and the criteria models state for them.

title: Ranked but Not Stopped: Detecting Prompt-Injection Hijacks from Typed Decision Models' Output Probabilities
summary: Programs that use a language model as a classifier act on its most probable label. Text injected into the input can move that label to one the attacker chooses, a hijack. A monitor that does not know the attacker's label can read the model's own confidence and raise an alarm when the top probability is low. We test this monitor on AG News topic classification with five systems, three of them served through a provider's API. Pooled over five families of injected text, low confidence ranks hijacked answers above clean ones on four of the five systems (AUROC 0.86-0.90). Ranking them does not stop many of them. A threshold set so that at most 5% of clean answers to separate calibration articles alarm falls among the least confident clean answers, and every more confident hijack passes. In our main gate run on the three API-served systems, the monitor misses 51-70% of the hijacks caused by a plain injected note (per-system point estimates). When the note adds one handwritten sentence that calls the target certain and asks for full probability, the monitor misses 99-100% of the hijacks, although low confidence still ranks them at AUROC 0.70-0.79. Confidence monitors should be tested at their operating alarm rate, against attackers who claim certainty.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that low-confidence monitoring can rank prompt-injection hijacks above clean answers on AG News, but at a 5% alarm rate it misses most hijacks, and it misses nearly all of them when the injection claims certainty.
AI.motivation: A program that uses a language model as a classifier acts on its top label, so injected text can move the label to an attacker's choice, and a monitor that reads the model's own confidence might detect this without knowing the target label.
AI.method: The authors test a confidence monitor on AG News topic classification with five systems, three served through a provider's API, pooling over five families of injected text, calibrating an alarm threshold so that at most 5% of clean answers alarm, and testing a plain injected note and a note that adds a handwritten sentence claiming certainty.
AI.result: Low confidence ranks hijacked answers above clean ones on four of five systems with AUROC 0.86 to 0.90, but at the 5% operating threshold the monitor misses 51 to 70% of hijacks from a plain note on the three API systems, and 99 to 100% of hijacks when the note claims certainty, although AUROC remains 0.70 to 0.79.
AI.conclusion: Confidence monitors should be tested at their operating alarm rate and against attackers who claim certainty, since ranking ability does not translate into effective alarms.

title: Tune the Baseline First: Most of Muon's Scaled Weight Decay Gain Is a Tuning Gap, but Its Small Real Advantage Grows With Model Size
comment: 9 pages,8 figures, code and data:this https URL
summary: Scaled weight decay for Muon (Muon-SW) has been reported to train language models more efficiently than constant decoupled weight decay, but such comparisons usually reuse one learning-rate (LR) and weight-decay (WD) setting for both methods. We re-run the comparison under the MAI-Base-2 protocol: LR and WD are tuned jointly through their product for each method, on a source-scaled mixture-of-experts (MoE) scaling ladder (1.9M to 15M active parameters) that holds tokens per active parameter and data repetition fixed across sizes. We find: (1) Most of the gain is a tuning gap. At the shared setting Muon-SW wins by 0.035 bits per byte (BPB), a 1.52x compute saving; after both methods are tuned, the gap is 0.0026 BPB (95% CI [0.0018, 0.0034]), a 1.03x saving, so about 90% of the advantage disappears. (2) The small advantage that remains is real: at the smallest size, all four paired seeds favour Muon-SW at the tuned settings. (3) That advantage grows with model size: across an 8x range of active parameters, the tuned gap rises from 0.0036 to 0.0051 BPB while the untuned gap shrinks from 0.035 to 0.024, so the surviving share rises from about 10% to 21%. (4) The best weight decay moves with scale: the optimal LRWD product grows for both methods, faster for Muon-SW (ratio 1.40 to 1.91), and a law fitted on the two smallest sizes overshoots the third by 1.3-1.5x, costing up to 0.002 BPB. The whole study runs on one NVIDIA T4 GPU; we release the code and all run results.

AI.tldr: The paper re-runs the comparison of scaled weight decay for Muon against constant decoupled weight decay with both methods tuned jointly, finds that most of the reported gain is a tuning gap, and shows that the small remaining advantage grows with model size.
AI.motivation: Earlier comparisons of Muon-SW reused one learning-rate and weight-decay setting for both methods, which may have exaggerated its advantage.
AI.method: Learning rate and weight decay are tuned jointly through their product for each method on a source-scaled mixture-of-experts ladder from 1.9M to 15M active parameters, with tokens per active parameter and data repetition held fixed, and paired seeds are used at the smallest size.
AI.result: At a shared setting Muon-SW wins by 0.035 bits per byte (1.52x compute saving), but after tuning the gap is 0.0026 BPB (95% CI [0.0018, 0.0034], 1.03x saving), so about 90% of the advantage disappears; the tuned gap rises from 0.0036 to 0.0051 BPB across an 8x range of active parameters, and the optimal LR-WD product grows faster for Muon-SW, with a fitted law overshooting the third size by 1.3 to 1.5x.
AI.conclusion: Most of the reported advantage of Muon-SW is a tuning artifact, but a small real advantage remains and grows with scale, and the whole study runs on one NVIDIA T4 GPU with code and results released.

title: FindLink: Learning to Assess Scientific Connections from Source-Grounded Premises
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures. Dataset: this https URL
summary: Scientific discovery from the literature requires assessing connections among findings obtained under different study conditions. Source attribution makes individual findings traceable, but does not determine what they jointly support. We introduce GI-TraceBench, a benchmark of 10,282 questions in gastrointestinal oncology that unifies provenance question answering, knowledge discovery, and hypothesis evaluation through shared Paper, Claim, and Evidence Span records. We further propose FindLink, a two-stage framework for provenance-grounded scientific reasoning. Premise Grounding constructs source-bound premises with explicit study context and support status. Structured Reasoning organizes these premises into support plans that represent both supported relations and unresolved conditions, then generates evidence-conditioned answers using deterministic compiler feedback. The compiler verifies structural and source-binding consistency, but does not assess scientific entailment. On the 1,545-question fixed-evidence test set, FindLink improves the balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone. A retrained variant without Structured Reasoning achieves slightly higher premise-identifier F1, but substantially lower relation and evidence-sufficiency F1. These results indicate that scientific reasoning requires not only identifying grounded premises, but also assessing what connections those premises support.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GI-TraceBench, a 10,282-question gastrointestinal oncology benchmark, and FindLink, a two-stage framework that grounds premises in source evidence and assesses what they jointly support, improving balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Source attribution makes individual findings traceable but does not determine what findings jointly support, which is needed for scientific discovery across studies with different conditions.
AI.method: Premise Grounding builds source-bound premises with explicit study context and support status, and Structured Reasoning organizes them into support plans that represent supported relations and unresolved conditions and generates evidence-conditioned answers checked by a deterministic compiler that verifies structural and source-binding consistency but not scientific entailment.
AI.result: On the 1,545-question fixed-evidence test set, FindLink improves the balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone, and a variant without Structured Reasoning has slightly higher premise-identifier F1 but substantially lower relation and evidence-sufficiency F1.
AI.conclusion: Scientific reasoning requires assessing what connections grounded premises support, not only identifying the premises.

title: Re$^3$Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads
summary: Attention-based rerankers score each candidate by the attention mass that retrieval heads route to it from the question, but the question, serving as a fixed query, carries limited information for locating relevant evidence. We propose Re$^3$Rank, a listwise reranker built on reasoning-conditioned retrieval heads (RRHeads). A generator first writes a reasoning trace over the question and the candidates, and a scorer then uses the trace tokens as the attention query of a few selected RRHeads, reading relevance as continuous scores. We present a straight-through estimator to propagate the ranking loss through the discrete trace, so that the generator and the scorer can be trained jointly for ranking. Averaged over 9 benchmarks, Re$^3$Rank outperforms 11 baseline rerankers: our 4B variant exceeds the strongest baseline by 3.11 NDCG@10 points on average, and even our 0.6B variant surpasses rerankers with up to 32B parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Re$^3$Rank, a listwise reranker whose scorer uses attention heads queried by a reasoning trace written by a generator, and reports gains over 11 baseline rerankers averaged over nine benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Attention-based rerankers use the question as a fixed query for retrieval heads, which carries limited information for locating relevant evidence.
AI.method: A generator writes a reasoning trace over the question and candidates, a scorer uses the trace tokens as the attention query of selected reasoning-conditioned retrieval heads (RRHeads) to produce continuous relevance scores, and a straight-through estimator propagates the ranking loss through the discrete trace so the two components train jointly.
