AI.result: Averaged over nine benchmarks, the 4B variant exceeds the strongest of 11 baseline rerankers by 3.11 NDCG@10 points, and the 0.6B variant surpasses rerankers with up to 32B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning retrieval heads on reasoning traces improves listwise reranking and lets small rerankers outperform much larger ones.

title: From Language to Country to Valence: A Multilingual Audit of Stereotype Bias Across LLMs
comment: 10 pages. Author preprint; conference review ongoing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for education, recruitment, workplace decision support, and other consequential applications, making pre-deployment social-bias detection essential. Yet major benchmarks are English-centred or translated, focus mainly on negative stereotypes, and may miss linguistic and cultural variation. We investigate gender, racial, and religious bias using 12,000 locally written Reddit posts in English, Spanish, French, and German. Only search terms are translated, preserving local context. The dataset is balanced by language and category; English gender is additionally balanced by stereotype valence. Three open-weight and three proprietary API-based models are evaluated with a two-blank design that reduces grammatical-gender cues. Religion has the highest absolute choice imbalance in every model-language condition. Spanish is highest for gender, whereas German is highest for race and religion. The evaluated API models score below the open-weight models throughout. Negative English-gender items exceed positive items; Australian and Mexican contexts exceed their Canadian and Spanish counterparts. These descriptive differences measure choice concentration, not stereotype endorsement or causal country effects. The crossed patterns show how aggregate scores can conceal category- and context-specific behaviour, motivating closer inspection before deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper audits stereotype bias in six LLMs across gender, race and religion using 12,000 locally written Reddit posts in English, Spanish, French and German, and finds that religion has the highest absolute choice imbalance in every model-language condition.
AI.motivation: Major bias benchmarks are English-centred or translated, focus mainly on negative stereotypes and may miss linguistic and cultural variation before LLMs are deployed in consequential applications.
AI.method: The dataset of 12,000 locally written Reddit posts is balanced by language and category, search terms alone are translated, English gender items are also balanced by stereotype valence, and three open-weight and three proprietary API models are evaluated with a two-blank design that reduces grammatical-gender cues.
AI.result: Religion shows the highest absolute choice imbalance in every model-language condition, Spanish is highest for gender while German is highest for race and religion, API models score below open-weight models throughout, and negative English-gender items exceed positive ones, with Australian and Mexican contexts exceeding Canadian and Spanish counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate scores can conceal category- and context-specific behavior, so closer inspection is needed before deployment, and the descriptive differences measure choice concentration rather than stereotype endorsement or causal country effects.

title: They Know Where It Is, But Not What It Says: A Bilingual Hallucination Benchmark of Hadith Recall in Open LLMs
summary: Large language models are increasingly consulted for religious knowledge, including the recall of specific Hadith (recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him). Unlike open-ended generation, Hadith recall is a high-stakes, verifiable task: a reference (collection, chapter, and Hadith number) has exactly one correct text, and any deviation from it constitutes a fabrication that can be mistaken for authentic scripture. This study introduces a bilingual (English/Arabic) benchmark that probes five open-weight, locally-deployable language models (Mistral-7B, Gemma3-4B, Jais-7B, ALLaM-7B, and Phi4-mini-3.8B) across all six canonical Sunni Hadith collections (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Da'ud, Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Sunan an-Nasa'i, Sunan Ibn Majah), sampling 500 Hadith per collection (3,000 per model per language, 30,000 responses total). Each model is given only the bibliographic reference and asked to reproduce the exact Hadith text, with no retrieval augmentation, and is scored on lexical fidelity (BLEU) and semantic fidelity (multilingual cosine similarity), with refusals flagged separately. Across all five models and both languages, 0% of 30,000 responses achieve both high lexical and high semantic fidelity, i.e., an exact, verifiable match to the source text. Arabic responses fare uniformly worse than English. These findings suggest that current open-weight LLMs, used without retrieval grounding, are unreliable and potentially dangerous sources for exact religious-text recall, and that deployment for Islamic scholarship should mandate retrieval-augmented generation over a verified corpus rather than parametric memory. The complete code, prompts, evaluation pipeline, and scored outputs are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a bilingual English and Arabic benchmark showing that five open-weight LLMs without retrieval never reproduce Hadith text exactly, with 0% of 30,000 responses achieving both high lexical and high semantic fidelity.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly consulted for religious knowledge, and Hadith recall is a high-stakes, verifiable task in which any deviation from the single correct text is a fabrication that may be mistaken for authentic scripture.
AI.method: The benchmark gives Mistral-7B, Gemma3-4B, Jais-7B, ALLaM-7B and Phi4-mini-3.8B only the bibliographic reference and asks them to reproduce the Hadith text, sampling 500 Hadith from each of six canonical Sunni collections per model and language, and scores responses with BLEU for lexical fidelity and multilingual cosine similarity for semantic fidelity, with refusals flagged separately.
AI.result: Across all five models and both languages, 0% of 30,000 responses achieve both high lexical and high semantic fidelity, and Arabic responses fare uniformly worse than English.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs used without retrieval grounding are unreliable sources for exact religious-text recall, and deployment for Islamic scholarship should use retrieval-augmented generation over a verified corpus.

title: Scalaris: A Scalable Enterprise Memory Architecture for Conversational AI Assistants
summary: Enterprise conversational systems require memory to personalize interactions, retain information across sessions, and maintain conversational coherence. At enterprise scale, however, memory must not only retrieve relevant information accurately but also provide it efficiently to the answer-generation model. Existing memory systems face a trade-off between retrieval accuracy and context efficiency. Retrieving more context can improve recall but increases inference cost and latency. We present Scalaris, a scalable enterprise memory architecture that addresses this trade-off through a unified long-term and short-term memory design. We propose that user interactions and assistant responses possess distinct characteristics and roles in a conversation: user interactions capture evolving knowledge about the user and provide value across sessions, whereas assistant responses must be stored efficiently so that only information relevant to the current query is retrieved. We therefore treat them separately and support each with specialized representations and ingestion/retrieval pipelines. Scalaris reaches 92.2 % accuracy on LongMemEval-S and 90.77 % on LoCoMo using Qwen3-32B, state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, while supplying the answer-generation model with approximately 10 times fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight, a leading memory system for conversational AI. When integrated with our proprietary closed-source AI assistants, Scalaris improved overall response quality by 36 %. Together, these results establish Scalaris as a cost-effective framework for building scalable, personalized conversational AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Scalaris, an enterprise memory architecture that treats user interactions and assistant responses separately and reports state-of-the-art accuracy on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with about ten times fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight.
AI.motivation: Enterprise conversational memory faces a trade-off between retrieval accuracy and context efficiency, since retrieving more context improves recall but raises inference cost and latency.
AI.method: Scalaris provides a unified long-term and short-term memory design in which user interactions capture evolving knowledge about the user and assistant responses are stored efficiently, each with specialized representations and ingestion and retrieval pipelines.
AI.result: Scalaris reaches 92.2% accuracy on LongMemEval-S and 90.77% on LoCoMo using Qwen3-32B, supplies the answer model with about 10 times fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight, and improves overall response quality by 36% when integrated with the authors' proprietary closed-source assistants.
AI.conclusion: Separating user and assistant memory supports a cost-effective framework for scalable, personalized conversational AI.

title: ICJ-Graph: A Citation Graph and a Layered Document Corpus of the International Court of Justice
summary: We present ICJ-Graph, a machine-readable resource connecting documents of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to cited cases, legal provisions and United Nations resolutions. Court decisions, written pleadings and oral records form distinct document layers, preserving the distinction between the Court's reasoning and the parties' submissions. The collection contains 6,396 ICJ documents and 505 documents from other courts and legal bodies, together with 12,375 provisions and 20,291 UN resolutions. The data files contain text, metadata and embeddings. The accompanying pipeline lets users load the graph and generate embeddings for use in their own retrieval systems. To illustrate the resource's use, we evaluate five models on citation prediction for 199 decisions using documents available before each decision. Tools designed for citation research improve citation-prediction F1 over answering without tools for all five models across case, provision and resolution citations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ICJ-Graph, a machine-readable resource linking International Court of Justice documents to cited cases, legal provisions and UN resolutions, with layered document types and embeddings, and shows that tools improve citation prediction for five models.
AI.motivation: Legal citation research needs a resource that separates the Court's reasoning from the parties' submissions and connects documents to the cases, provisions and resolutions they cite.
AI.method: The collection contains 6,396 ICJ documents and 505 documents from other courts and legal bodies, with 12,375 provisions and 20,291 UN resolutions, organized into decision, pleading and oral-record layers with text, metadata and embeddings, and five models are evaluated on citation prediction for 199 decisions using only documents available before each decision.
AI.result: Tools designed for citation research improve citation-prediction F1 over answering without tools for all five models across case, provision and resolution citations.
AI.conclusion: The resource supports retrieval and citation research on ICJ materials, and tool use helps models predict citations.

title: SYNC: A Training-Free Inference Controller for Dynamic Layer Selection in Multi-Persona Alignment
summary: Steering vectors align a model at inference time without touching its weights, but eliciting several personas at once is a different problem from eliciting one. Prior multi-persona steering approaches predetermine both how persona vectors are combined and the specific layers at which they are injected. Moreover, this static commitment introduces substantial offline search costs to identify suitable target layers, despite the fact that optimal intervention strengths vary dynamically across both decoding steps and distinct personas. We introduce SYNC (SensitivitY-guided iNference Control), a novel training-free inference control framework compatible with pre-existing steering vectors. SYNC dynamically estimates each layer's sensitivity to every persona via cosine similarity trajectories, assigning each persona to its optimal injection layer at every decoding step. Across two models, two persona profiles and steering vectors from both unsupervised and supervised extraction, SYNC leads on 21 of 28 persona configurations, significantly on 15. Code is available at \href{this https URL}{this https URL}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SYNC, a training-free inference controller that dynamically chooses the injection layer for each persona at each decoding step when steering several personas at once, and leads on most persona configurations tested.
AI.motivation: Prior multi-persona steering predetermines how persona vectors are combined and which layers receive them, which costs substantial offline search and ignores that optimal intervention strengths vary across decoding steps and personas.
AI.method: SYNC estimates each layer's sensitivity to every persona from cosine similarity trajectories and assigns each persona to its optimal injection layer at every decoding step, and it is compatible with existing steering vectors from unsupervised and supervised extraction.
AI.result: Across two models, two persona profiles and steering vectors from both extraction methods, SYNC leads on 21 of 28 persona configurations and is significantly better on 15.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, sensitivity-guided layer selection is an effective training-free way to steer multiple personas at inference time.

title: LLMs Cannot Be Neutral: Gender Sensitivity Across Candidates, Evaluators, and Models
comment: This manuscript is under review at FAccT'2027
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate candidates for professional roles, raising concerns about their sensitivity to demographic identities. We examine how candidate and evaluator gender assignments affect decisions by LLM-as-a-Judge (LaJ) models and decision language models (DLMs). In a hypothetical city council voting task, eight models evaluated 240 synthetic professional narratives from NVIDIA's US and French Nemotron-Personas datasets under independently varied gender assignments, producing 30,720 judgments. Explicit candidate gender labels increased Yes-vote probability by 1.05-1.73 percentage points relative to unspecified gender, while only the nonbinary evaluator assignment showed a significant increase (1.26 points). Identity matching showed no significant overall association. Yes-vote rates varied across models (81.3-97.2%), and 2.5-3.3% of decisions reversed relative to the unspecified-identity baseline. Under direct substitutions between explicit gender identities, DLMs exhibited fewer decision reversals than LaJ models (1.18% vs. 3.38%), indicating lower observed decision-level gender sensitivity among the tested DLMs. These findings demonstrate that gender sensitivity depends on candidate and evaluator identities and the evaluation model, while highlighting the importance of examining individual decision consistency alongside aggregate differences.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that LLM evaluators' decisions in a hypothetical city council voting task are sensitive to candidate and evaluator gender, with small but significant shifts and 2.5 to 3.3% of decisions reversing under gender substitutions.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to evaluate candidates for professional roles, which raises concern about their sensitivity to demographic identities, so the paper examines how candidate and evaluator gender assignments affect decisions.
AI.method: Eight models, including LLM-as-a-Judge models and decision language models (DLMs), evaluated 240 synthetic professional narratives from NVIDIA's US and French Nemotron-Personas datasets under independently varied gender assignments, producing 30,720 judgments.
AI.result: Explicit candidate gender labels increased Yes-vote probability by 1.05 to 1.73 percentage points relative to unspecified gender, only the nonbinary evaluator assignment showed a significant increase of 1.26 points, identity matching showed no significant overall association, Yes-vote rates ranged from 81.3% to 97.2% across models, and under direct substitutions DLMs reversed fewer decisions than LLM-as-a-Judge models (1.18% vs. 3.38%).
AI.conclusion: Gender sensitivity depends on candidate and evaluator identities and on the evaluation model, so individual decision consistency should be examined alongside aggregate differences.

title: MicroMouse: Masking Harmful Supervision in Long CoT via Relative Potential
summary: Even successful long CoTs may contain harmful supervision, motivating the need for methods that can automatically identify and mask such signals during SFT. Inspired by the MicroMouse maze-solving process, we view a long CoT as a search trajectory from the input problem toward the target answer. This perspective motivates maintaining a goal-relative measure, analogous to a MicroMouse's spatial coordinates, to quantify how close the current reasoning state is to the target answer. Building on this perspective, we propose MicroMouse, an automated selective-SFT framework for masking harmful supervision in long CoTs. In MicroMouse we introduce a Relative Potential (REP) to measure how closely each reasoning state supports the gold answer. Unlike the perplexity of the gold answer alone, REP measures relative support by contrasting the gold answer with a matched foil. This contrast cancels likelihood variations shared by the pair, yielding a more stable signal of progress toward the target answer. By tracking the REP trajectory, MicroMouse identifies consecutive potential decreases as erroneous exploration and post-peak reasoning as redundant wandering, and masks these harmful supervision during SFT. Extensive experiments across multiple student model scales and reasoning benchmarks show that MicroMouse consistently outperforms Full-CoT SFT and existing selective-SFT baselines, yielding average relative gains of 5.5% in greedy accuracy and 2.6% in Pass@1 relative to Full-CoT SFT. Meanwhile, MicroMouse improves reasoning efficiency by reducing average output length by 8.8%, while identifying harmful supervision in only 1.7 seconds per long CoT on average.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MicroMouse, a selective-SFT framework that uses a Relative Potential measure to identify and mask harmful supervision in long chain-of-thought traces, outperforming full-CoT SFT while shortening outputs.
AI.motivation: Even successful long CoTs can contain harmful supervision, so automatic methods are needed to identify and mask such signals during SFT.
AI.method: A long CoT is viewed as a search trajectory toward the gold answer, and the Relative Potential (REP) contrasts the gold answer with a matched foil to measure how closely each reasoning state supports the answer, with consecutive potential decreases marked as erroneous exploration and post-peak reasoning marked as redundant wandering, and those steps masked during SFT.
AI.result: Across multiple student model scales and reasoning benchmarks, MicroMouse gains on average 5.5% relative in greedy accuracy and 2.6% relative in Pass@1 over Full-CoT SFT, outperforms existing selective-SFT baselines, reduces average output length by 8.8%, and identifies harmful supervision in 1.7 seconds per long CoT on average.
AI.conclusion: Contrast-based relative potential tracking provides a stable, efficient signal for masking harmful supervision in long CoT SFT.

title: EffComp: Efficient Prompt Compression via Hybrid Reinforcement & Supervised Learning
summary: Prompt compression is aimed at reducing input prompt lengths to enable cheaper, faster, and potentially higher-quality LLM predictions. However, existing prompt compression methods are often limited by modest compression gains, a risk of hallucination, and/or high compression latency. We propose EffComp, an Efficient prompt Compression framework for RAG-based question answering (QA). EffComp employs BERT-style document reranker and sentence selector models to allow fast extractive prompt compression at the sentence level. Its extractive nature prevents hallucinations in the compressed prompts. Additionally, the training process using a hybrid reinforcement and supervised learning approach is designed to optimize the compression ratio while preserving LLM accuracy. Experiments on various QA datasets demonstrate that EffComp outperforms state-of-the-art prompt compression methods achieving the best trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency. This makes it practical for real-world applications.

AI.tldr: EffComp is an extractive prompt compression framework for RAG-based QA that selects sentences with BERT-style reranker and sentence selector models. Trained with a hybrid of reinforcement and supervised learning, it reportedly gives the best trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt compression methods offer only modest compression gains, risk hallucination, and/or incur high compression latency.
AI.method: EffComp uses a BERT-style document reranker and a sentence selector to perform fast sentence-level extractive compression, so the compressed prompt contains only source text. A hybrid reinforcement and supervised learning procedure optimises the compression ratio while preserving LLM accuracy.
AI.result: Across various QA datasets, EffComp reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art prompt compression methods, achieving the best compression ratio versus accuracy trade-off with minimal latency.
AI.conclusion: Extractive compression can be both fast and accurate for RAG QA, which the authors argue makes prompt compression practical for real-world applications.

title: PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge. We introduce PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone's intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without altering its original inference pathway or generation behavior. Specifically, dynamic layer gating selectively aggregates residual-stream representations across layers to extract safety-relevant signals during both prefill and autoregressive decoding. To balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, PGuard supports multiple representation-modeling architectures, including a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules. Its design also accounts for the execution characteristics of LLM serving frameworks, such as SGLang, optimizing computation and data access to minimize additional runtime and synchronization overhead. As a result, PGuard incurs only 0.82-2.26% end-to-end overhead on the hundred-billion-parameter backbone Qwen3.5-122B-A10B served by SGLang. Extensive evaluations across more than 30 benchmarks spanning text and multimodal safety, jailbreaks, cyber and CBRN risks, multilingual scenarios, and real-world traffic demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among native guardrails. On text queries with Qwen3.5-9B, PGuard achieves an average F1 score of 0.836, approaching dedicated external guardrails, while supporting deployment-time configuration of category-specific thresholds and enforcement actions.

AI.tldr: PGuard is a native, streaming, plug-in guardrail that detects unsafe content at the token level from the backbone model's own intermediate representations. It reports 0.82-2.26% end-to-end overhead on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B under SGLang and an average F1 of 0.836 on text queries with Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.motivation: As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving mode, safety monitoring is usually an external serving dependency, which adds cost and latency and is not integrated into the model during generation.
AI.method: PGuard uses dynamic layer gating to aggregate residual-stream representations across layers during prefill and autoregressive decoding, without changing the inference path or generation behaviour. It offers a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules, and is designed to fit the execution characteristics of SGLang.
AI.result: PGuard incurs 0.82-2.26% end-to-end overhead on the 122B-parameter Qwen3.5-122B-A10B served by SGLang. Across more than 30 benchmarks it reportedly reaches state-of-the-art performance among native guardrails. On text queries with Qwen3.5-9B it achieves an average F1 of 0.836, approaching dedicated external guardrails, and it supports category-specific thresholds and enforcement actions at deployment time.
AI.conclusion: Safety detection can be built into the backbone model as a near-free, configurable capability, rather than remaining a separate external serving component, though its accuracy is still somewhat below dedicated external guardrails.

title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: The work has been published in EMNLP 2026
summary: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TRIO is a retrieval-augmented generation approach that coordinates three agents (query extension, judge, and answer) through iterative refinement, each optimised toward its own objective. The paper reports that it outperforms state-of-the-art RAG approaches on multiple benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Current RAG methods are still unsatisfactory because of inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations.
AI.method: A query extension agent expands ambiguous queries, with a reward based on improved answer quality. A judge agent labels expanded queries as sufficient or insufficient using unanimity voting, and these labels serve as ground truth for training. An answer agent is optimised with dynamic matching-based rewards and curriculum learning to improve evidence use and answer accuracy.
AI.result: The abstract reports that TRIO is effective across multiple benchmark datasets compared with state-of-the-art approaches, but gives no specific numbers in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the individual optimisation objectives of several cooperating agents is presented as a promising route to better retrieval and answer quality in RAG.

title: Window-Aware Scheduling for Health Messaging under Platform Delivery Constraints: Evidence from an AI-Powered WhatsApp Maternal and Infant Health Chatbot in Nigeria
summary: WhatsApp lets a business send free-form messages only within 24 hours of a user's last message; outside this customer service window, only pre-approved templates are delivered. Health chatbots inherit this rule, but its cost is rarely measured. We analyse 98,607 messages sent to 3,696 mothers by a WhatsApp maternal health chatbot in Nigeria, with a largely separate export as replication. No free-form message failed with the window open (0 of 35,500), and failure jumped by 93.0 percentage points (95% CI 87.0 to 99.1) at exactly 24 hours. Two flows produced 66.1% of failures, including an offer to speak with a medical professional that, as built, reached 0.3 in 100 mothers whose window had closed. We formalise window-aware scheduling as a decision problem with an action of known zero value. Model-based offline evaluation, with bounds for unconfirmed delivery, estimates that sending the offer as an approved template would reach 81.5 to 86.8 in 100 such mothers, against 16.6 for waiting and 11.6 for a reply prompt. In a calibrated simulation, tabular Q-learning converges to the same template rule and does not beat it in any of 13 stress tests, and opting out does not rise with message volume. The main gain comes from respecting the platform rule, and it needs no learning. All outcomes are deliveries, not health outcomes.

AI.tldr: In a WhatsApp maternal health chatbot in Nigeria, free-form messages failed only after the 24-hour customer service window closed, and the authors argue that sending pre-approved templates is the main gain. A Q-learning agent converged to the same template rule and did not beat it in any of 13 stress tests.
AI.motivation: WhatsApp allows free-form messages only within 24 hours of a user's last message, and health chatbots inherit this rule, but its cost is rarely measured.
AI.method: The authors analysed 98,607 messages sent to 3,696 mothers, with a largely separate export used as replication. They formalised window-aware scheduling as a decision problem with an action of known zero value, ran model-based offline evaluation with bounds for unconfirmed delivery, and ran a calibrated simulation with tabular Q-learning.
AI.result: No free-form message failed with the window open (0 of 35,500), while failure jumped by 93.0 percentage points (95% CI 87.0 to 99.1) at exactly 24 hours. Two flows produced 66.1% of failures. Sending the medical professional offer as an approved template was estimated to reach 81.5 to 86.8 in 100 such mothers, against 16.6 for waiting and 11.6 for a reply prompt. Tabular Q-learning converged to the template rule and did not beat it in any of 13 stress tests, and opt-outs did not rise with message volume.
AI.conclusion: Respecting the platform delivery rule yields most of the gain and needs no learning. The outcomes measured are deliveries, not health outcomes.

title: Omni-Life: Benchmarking Omnimodal Real-Time AI Assistants in People's Daily Lives
summary: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.

AI.tldr: Omni-Life is a benchmark of 400 videos for real-time omnimodal assistants, testing whether they give timely and appropriate help and stay silent when no help is needed. The best configurations handle at most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance completely correctly.
AI.motivation: Audiovisual understanding alone does not show whether real-time omnimodal assistants can provide timely and appropriate help in everyday life.
AI.method: The benchmark combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. It has 290 videos requiring assistance (555 required intervention events) and 110 videos requiring silence. Twelve configurations of mainstream real-time omnimodal models are assessed on event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. Task reminders and response-latency tolerance are also studied.
AI.result: At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. Reminders improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add about 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10 s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Existing models remain insufficient for reliable real-life assistance, and the authors call for better instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when help is not needed.

title: Tug of Watts: A study on the Energy - Accuracy Trade-off of Large Language Models on Medical Question Answering Tasks
comment: Accepted to "Workshop on GREEN-AI: Grounding Research on Energy- and resource-Efficient Networks for sustainable AI", Co-Located with CIKM 2026, November 08, 2026, Rome, Italy
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in medical question answering (QA) systems. While recent works aim at incrementally improving the downstream task accuracy, an empirical estimation of the models' energy consumption and the associated carbon footprints is often overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate how practitioners can estimate energy consumption and arrive at reliable emission estimates for medical QA tasks available in the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard by investigating 13 LLMs from 3 model families ranging from 270M to 14B parameters. We discuss how one can critically interpret energy versus accuracy trade-offs for a set of models for a given task. With this work, we underline that reporting disjoint energy and accuracy metrics alone does not suffice for careful trade-off assessments, but it also demands systematic construction and interpretation of joint trade-off metrics. We envisage such studies aiding practitioners in adopting better and more efficient models for their task and helping them become active participants in building sustainable LLM pipelines.

AI.tldr: This study estimates the energy consumption and carbon footprint of 13 LLMs (270M to 14B parameters, from 3 families) on medical question answering tasks from the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard. It argues that energy and accuracy must be reported together through joint trade-off metrics.
AI.motivation: Medical QA work focuses on incremental accuracy gains, while energy consumption and carbon emissions are often overlooked, and reporting energy and accuracy separately is not enough for trade-off assessment.
AI.method: The authors show how practitioners can estimate energy use and reliable emission estimates for medical QA tasks, then evaluate 13 LLMs from 3 model families and discuss how to interpret energy versus accuracy trade-offs for a given task.
AI.result: The abstract reports no specific numbers. It presents a methodology for estimating energy and emissions and for interpreting joint trade-offs across the 13 models.
AI.conclusion: Joint energy-accuracy trade-off metrics are needed for careful model selection and for building more sustainable LLM pipelines in medical QA.

title: Maswao: An automatically collected, prepared, and benchmarked dataset for the South African Sign language
summary: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.

AI.tldr: Maswao is a sign language dataset for South African Sign Language (SASL) built automatically from public news broadcasts, with ASR-derived text and weak sentence alignment. Transformer models outperform recurrent baselines on sign-to-text translation, reaching BLEU-4 1.54 and ChrF 18.09.
AI.motivation: Most sign languages lack the large-scale datasets that have driven progress in sign language processing, so they fall behind languages such as American, British, and German Sign Language.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that collects SASL video from public news broadcasts, transcribes the audio with ASR, crops the signing area, and uses gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion as sentence boundaries, producing a weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpus. They benchmark sign-to-text translation with recurrent neural networks and Transformer models.
AI.result: The best Transformer achieves BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, with ChrF 18.09 and ROUGE-L 10.51. Transformers outperform the recurrent baselines.
AI.conclusion: Automatic collection with minimal human labour can produce a usable sign language dataset, and the task remains promising for further investigation for under-resourced sign languages.

title: A State Change Is Local, Its Consequences Are Not: Dependency-Aware State Revision for Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long-lived agents rely on persistent memory of users, tasks and decisions, and this memory must stay consistent with a world that keeps changing. When an upstream fact changes, however, memory systems can revise the contradicted memory itself while the beliefs, plans and actions derived from it remain accepted, even though they have lost their support. We therefore formulate dependency-aware state revision, which asks not only what changed but also which dependent states should no longer be trusted. To address it, StateGraph maintains an evolving state dependency graph whose edges are recovered from interaction histories. Its core design is counterfactual verification: each candidate edge is tested by asking whether the dependent state would survive the loss of its premise, which separates support dependence from semantic relatedness, and revision then invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path survives. To test this design, we introduce StateChangeBench, a controlled benchmark of 50 author-constructed cases annotated with cascade depth, hard negatives and action consequences. On it, StateGraph's Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 percentage points at depth 1 and 26.0 at depth 3+. On public long-term memory benchmarks, its point estimates are comparable to or higher than those of the evaluated baselines on most datasets. These results provide initial evidence that explicit dependency tracking can improve selective memory revision under changing conditions.

AI.tldr: StateGraph is a memory system for long-lived agents that revises dependent states when an upstream fact changes, using a state dependency graph verified by counterfactual tests. On the new StateChangeBench it beats a CUPMem reimplementation by 6.9 Impact-F1 points at depth 1 and 26.0 points at depth 3 and above.
AI.motivation: Memory systems revise a contradicted fact but leave beliefs, plans, and actions derived from it trusted, even though they have lost their support.
AI.method: StateGraph keeps an evolving state dependency graph with edges recovered from interaction histories. Each candidate edge is checked by counterfactual verification, asking whether the dependent state would survive the loss of its premise, which separates support dependence from semantic relatedness. A dependent state is invalidated only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path survives.
AI.result: On StateChangeBench, a benchmark of 50 author-constructed cases, StateGraph's Impact-F1 margin over the CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 points at depth 1 and 26.0 points at depth 3+. On public long-term memory benchmarks, its point estimates are comparable to or higher than the baselines on most datasets.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dependency tracking appears to improve selective memory revision under changing conditions, though the evidence is described as initial.

title: PlagiaCorpus: A Bilingual, Adversarial, and Cross-Lingual Dataset for Forensic Plagiarism Detection
summary: PlagiaCorpus is a bilingual Arabic-English dataset for benchmarking plagiarism and text-reuse detection, including reuse produced by large language models (LLMs) and reuse across languages. It contains 198,643 text records: a source corpus of 34,885 passages drawn from English and Arabic Wikipedia and two openly licensed book collections, and 163,758 queries (147,381 for training and 16,377 for testing). The queries cover five reuse classes of increasing difficulty, namely verbatim copying, character-level obfuscation, same-language paraphrasing by two different LLMs, and English--Arabic translation with structural paraphrasing, together with a Safe class of non-reused passages. Every positive query is linked to its source passage, and the train/test split is grouped by source passage so that no passage contributes queries to both splits. The release was curated through language identification, removal of LLM generation artefacts, and exact and cross-lingual de-duplication. Technical validation reports per-class length statistics, automatic checks of the train/test split, and inter-annotator agreement on a manually rated sample. The dataset is distributed in JSON and Parquet formats under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license.

AI.tldr: PlagiaCorpus is a bilingual Arabic-English dataset of 198,643 text records for plagiarism and text-reuse detection, including LLM-generated reuse and cross-lingual reuse. It is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 in JSON and Parquet.
AI.motivation: Plagiarism detection benchmarks need to cover LLM-generated reuse, cross-language reuse, and adversarial obfuscation, which existing resources do not jointly provide, according to the abstract's framing.
AI.method: The corpus contains 34,885 source passages from English and Arabic Wikipedia and two openly licensed book collections, plus 163,758 queries (147,381 for training and 16,377 for testing). The queries cover five reuse classes: verbatim copying, character-level obfuscation, same-language paraphrasing by two different LLMs, English-Arabic translation with structural paraphrasing, and a Safe class of non-reused passages. The train/test split is grouped by source passage, and the release was curated through language identification, artefact removal, and exact and cross-lingual de-duplication.
AI.result: The abstract reports technical validation covering per-class length statistics, automatic checks of the split, and inter-annotator agreement on a manually rated sample, but gives no detection results.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is intended as a forensic benchmark for plagiarism and text-reuse detection across languages and against LLM-generated text.

title: Distilling Literary Sentiment from LLM Annotations into an Ordinal BERT Model
summary: The scarcity of human-annotated literary corpora limits the development of domain-specific sentiment analysis models. This study investigates whether LLM-generated annotations can supervise smaller models for literary sentiment analysis. We fine-tune five BERT models using ordinal regression on 10,889 literary sentences annotated by Gemma 4 31B on a ten-point sentiment scale. The models are evaluated against 1,923 human-annotated sentences from Hemingway's "The Old Man and the Sea", alongside the teacher model and conventional baselines. BERT-large achieves a Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.589, approaching the teacher's 0.604. Although a constant-neutral predictor achieves the lowest overall mean absolute error (MAE), BERT-base outperforms the teacher on non-neutral sentences, achieving an MAE of 0.726 versus 1.116. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLM-generated supervision for developing smaller literary sentiment models, while highlighting the limitations of aggregate error metrics on predominantly neutral datasets.

AI.tldr: Ordinal BERT models fine-tuned on LLM-generated labels for literary sentiment reach a Kendall's tau of 0.589 (BERT-large) against the teacher's 0.604. BERT-base beats the teacher on non-neutral sentences, with an MAE of 0.726 versus 1.116.
AI.motivation: Human-annotated literary sentiment corpora are scarce, which limits domain-specific sentiment models.
AI.method: Five BERT models were fine-tuned with ordinal regression on 10,889 literary sentences labelled by Gemma 4 31B on a ten-point sentiment scale. They were evaluated on 1,923 human-annotated sentences from Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, alongside the teacher model and conventional baselines.
AI.result: BERT-large reaches a Kendall's tau of 0.589, close to the teacher's 0.604. A constant-neutral predictor has the lowest overall MAE, but BERT-base outperforms the teacher on non-neutral sentences, with an MAE of 0.726 versus 1.116.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated supervision can help develop smaller literary sentiment models, and aggregate error metrics can be misleading on predominantly neutral datasets.

title: Finding Errors Is Not Enough: Selective Model Escalation for Entity-Targeted Sentiment Analysis
summary: Improving a sentiment classifier with limited resources involves more than simply deciding how much data to collect or which model to train. A labelled collection may lack examples of an important class. Once trained, a classifier may benefit from another model even when that model is weaker on its own. We study these decisions in document-level Entity-Level Sentiment Analysis (ELSA), primarily using South Slavic news. We first compare acquisition orders as collections grow. We then use uncertainty to choose which predictions to revisit, how many to process, and whether an alternative encoder or local LLM can correct them. Finally, we select complete routing policies on development data for held-out evaluation. Minority-prioritised acquisition helps at some very small training sizes, but not consistently thereafter. On SentiCoref, an oracle correcting all errors in the least-confident 10% without harming correct predictions would add 9.14 Macro-F1 points; however the best evaluated action gains only 0.90. Encoder averaging helps on AspectBench and NewsMTSC but harms SentiCoref, where selective LLM assistance is more promising. Both development-selected policies route 30% of records to the encoder-assisted LLM, yielding observed gains of 1.02 points on SentiCoref (interval includes zero) and 1.71 on NewsMTSC, at substantially different inference costs.

AI.tldr: For entity-level sentiment analysis on South Slavic news, the paper finds that selectively escalating uncertain predictions to an encoder-assisted LLM gives only small gains. Development-selected policies route 30% of records to that LLM and gain 1.02 points on SentiCoref (interval includes zero) and 1.71 on NewsMTSC.
AI.motivation: Improving a sentiment classifier with limited resources involves choosing what data to collect and which model to use, and a weaker model may still help a stronger one on uncertain cases.
AI.method: The authors compare acquisition orders as training collections grow, then use uncertainty to choose which predictions to revisit, how many to process, and whether an alternative encoder or local LLM should correct them. Routing policies are selected on development data and evaluated on held-out data.
AI.result: Minority-prioritised acquisition helps at some very small training sizes but not consistently afterwards. An oracle correcting all errors in the least-confident 10% would add 9.14 Macro-F1 points on SentiCoref, but the best evaluated action gains only 0.90. Encoder averaging helps on AspectBench and NewsMTSC but harms SentiCoref. Both selected policies gain 1.02 points on SentiCoref (interval includes zero) and 1.71 on NewsMTSC, at substantially different inference costs.
AI.conclusion: Gains from selective model escalation are modest relative to the errors available to fix, and the best strategy depends on the dataset.

title: VERS: Steering Reasoning Models by Editing Their Activation Explanations
comment: 36 pages. Code and checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Reasoning language models write a chain of thought before they answer, and many checks in it do not change the final answer. Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) explain a model's activations in text and rebuild activations from text, and editing an explanation can steer a model at a single token. We study whether such edits can also steer how a model reasons. We build VERS (Verbalize, Edit, Reconstruct, Steer): it turns explanation edits at the doubt points of one reasoning trace into one fixed direction, and adds this direction at paragraph breaks. On the full GSM8K test, VERS cuts generated tokens by 45.8% at an accuracy change of -0.82 percentage points (pp); on MATH-500 it saves 31.3% at -3.05 pp. At half strength, its trade-off between tokens and accuracy lies between those of the published methods SEAL and DEER. With fitted affine maps and a strength tuned for each model, the direction transfers to larger Qwen3 models, up to 235B-A22B, and saves 30-35% of tokens. On competition problems, however, VERS loses 3-7 pp at every model size, and a fixed direction did not separate necessary checks from unneeded ones.

AI.tldr: VERS steers reasoning models by editing natural language explanations of activations at doubt points and adding a fixed direction at paragraph breaks. It cuts generated tokens by 45.8% on GSM8K with a -0.82 pp accuracy change, but loses 3-7 pp on competition problems at every model size.
AI.motivation: Many checks in a reasoning model's chain of thought do not change the final answer, and the authors ask whether edits to natural language autoencoder explanations can steer how a model reasons, not only a single token.
AI.method: VERS (Verbalize, Edit, Reconstruct, Steer) turns explanation edits made at the doubt points of one reasoning trace into one fixed direction, and adds this direction at paragraph breaks. Fitted affine maps and a per-model strength allow the direction to transfer to larger Qwen3 models.
AI.result: On the full GSM8K test, VERS cuts generated tokens by 45.8% at an accuracy change of -0.82 pp. On MATH-500 it saves 31.3% at -3.05 pp. At half strength its trade-off lies between those of SEAL and DEER. On Qwen3 models up to 235B-A22B it saves 30-35% of tokens. On competition problems it loses 3-7 pp at every model size.
AI.conclusion: Explanation-based steering can reduce reasoning length on some benchmarks, but a fixed direction does not separate necessary checks from unneeded ones, so it fails on harder competition problems.

title: Unlocking Criminal Court Decisions: Flexible Information Extraction for Empirical Legal Research
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Legal Knowledge and Information Systems (JURIX 2026)
summary: Criminal verdicts contain descriptions of criminal behavior that can support quantitative legal research, but structuring them requires attributes and extraction rules that cannot always be fully specified in advance. We present an LLM-based pipeline that builds a structured dataset through attribute exploration, text span extraction, and value normalization, guided by annotation instructions that legal experts can refine. We evaluate it on two traffic offenses: driving under the influence (DUI) and driving despite a ban (DDB). For DUI, revising the instructions was associated with higher extraction accuracy (from 52% to 70% of correctly extracted values) and higher agreement between human annotators. Repeated runs of the same model agreed with each other more than with the gold annotations, showing that consistent output is not necessarily correct, while disagreement between annotators and between models helped reveal unclear instructions. For DDB, where the instructions defined fixed categories and output formats, agreement was high for most attributes.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based pipeline extracts structured attributes from German criminal verdicts through attribute exploration, span extraction, and normalisation, with instructions that legal experts can refine. Revising the instructions raised DUI extraction accuracy from 52% to 70%.
AI.motivation: Criminal verdicts can support quantitative legal research, but the attributes and extraction rules cannot always be fully specified in advance.
AI.method: The pipeline builds a structured dataset through attribute exploration, text span extraction, and value normalisation, guided by annotation instructions that legal experts can refine. It is evaluated on two traffic offences, driving under the influence (DUI) and driving despite a ban (DDB).
AI.result: For DUI, revising the instructions was associated with extraction accuracy rising from 52% to 70% of correctly extracted values, and with higher human annotator agreement. Repeated runs of the same model agreed with each other more than with the gold annotations. For DDB, where categories and output formats were fixed, agreement was high for most attributes.
AI.conclusion: Consistent LLM output is not necessarily correct, and disagreement between annotators and between models helps reveal unclear instructions.

title: SAGE (Subjectivity-Aware Generation Estimator): A Linguistic Framework for AI-Generated Review Detection *
summary: We propose a simple, linguistically motivated approach to detecting AI-generated peer reviews based on the inherently human trait of subjectivity. We capture subjectivity at two levels: the semantic level of evaluative language and modality and the pragmatic level of speech acts. Using features derived from speech act annotations and model-predicted subjectivity scores, we train a lightweight classifier that achieves an AUROC of 0.9566 with only these linguistic features. Combining its output with the state-of-the-art detector Sem-Detect raises the TPR at 1% FPR of Sem-Detect on the APRDB benchmark from 0.874 to 0.985, outperforming the current state of the art. Our results show that linguistic features of subjectivity provide an explainable source of information for detecting AI-generated peer reviews and can be readily integrated into existing detection methods. The code and models are publicly available on GitHub (this https URL\_ text\_detection\_hub) and Hugging Face (this https URL), respectively.

AI.tldr: SAGE detects AI-generated peer reviews from linguistic subjectivity features, reaching an AUROC of 0.9566 on its own. Combined with the Sem-Detect detector, it raises TPR at 1% FPR on the APRDB benchmark from 0.874 to 0.985.
AI.motivation: Existing detection of AI-generated reviews may miss the subjectivity that is typical of human writing, and an explainable linguistic signal could complement it.
AI.method: Subjectivity is captured at a semantic level (evaluative language and modality) and at a pragmatic level (speech acts). Features come from speech act annotations and model-predicted subjectivity scores, and feed a lightweight classifier.
AI.result: The linguistic classifier reaches an AUROC of 0.9566. Combined with Sem-Detect, TPR at 1% FPR on APRDB rises from 0.874 to 0.985.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic subjectivity features give an explainable signal that can be added to existing AI-generated review detectors.

title: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
summary: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether a conservative fusion of NLI and LLM verifiers improves scientific claim verification, and finds that it hurts. Qwen3 8B reaches the highest Macro-F1 at 0.7937, and fusion lowers every model's score.
AI.motivation: NLI models struggle when evidence is spread across several sentences, while LLMs can reason across sentences but may draw unsupported conclusions. The authors hypothesise that labelling a claim Support or Contradict only when both agree combines their strengths.
AI.method: The benchmark has 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). The top five sentences per claim are retrieved by a hybrid of semantic and BM25 retrieval, then given to every verifier. A DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline is compared with Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B.
AI.result: Qwen3 reaches Macro-F1 0.7937, Llama 3.1 0.7204, Mistral 0.6388, and the NLI baseline 0.3157. Fusion lowers these to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991 respectively. Error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often overturn correct LLM predictions.
AI.conclusion: Conservative NLI-LLM fusion does not help here, because NLI disagreement tends to override correct LLM judgements.

title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.

AI.tldr: SPTA adapts the teacher in on-policy distillation to the student-generated prefixes it will be queried on, by training it with RLVR to continue from those prefixes. It improves average student performance on math reasoning benchmarks over standard OPD and over OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers.
AI.motivation: In on-policy distillation, student-generated prefixes can contain reasoning errors or unfamiliar patterns, which makes the teacher's token-level supervision less reliable, and this worsens for longer prefixes.
AI.method: Before distillation, student rollout prefixes of random lengths are collected and the teacher is trained with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to continue from them, rewarding correct final answers. The adapted teacher is then used for standard OPD with the distillation objective unchanged.
AI.result: SPTA improves average student performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks over standard OPD and over OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Teachers should be adapted to the states their students actually visit, not only to solve problems independently, so they give reliable guidance.

title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
summary: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DepthGraft is a hierarchical cross-layer KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer keys and values from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. It improves downstream performance on 0.5B to 16B models and cuts KV cache by about one third, with a 7.0% MMLU-Pro gain on the 16B MoE model.
AI.motivation: In Pre-LN architectures, depth-wise information dilution limits the use of deep layers, and existing cross-layer connections add computation or memory access.
AI.method: The authors revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient connection. Each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, which acts as a structural regulariser. DepthGraft builds deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs, distributing non-local gradient flow across sources while preserving early completion of prefill.
AI.result: On the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, 6.6% on CMMLU, and 6.4% on C3. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B show consistent downstream gains under both GQA and MLA, and KV cache is reduced by roughly one third.
AI.conclusion: The authors position DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining.

title: ACTOR: Action-Centered Temporal Organization for Literary Role-Playing Agents
summary: Large language agents for literary role-playing are typically modeled around dialogue generation, leaving characters' non-dialogue behaviors and their dynamic evolution over story time underrepresented. In this paper, we propose ACTOR (Action-Centered Temporal Organization for Literary Role-Playing Agents), an automated framework for constructing such behavior trajectories from raw novel texts. ACTOR extracts dialogue and persona-relevant non-dialogue behaviors, represents each behavior using a Thought-Action-Observation structure, and organizes behavior trajectories according to the internal temporal order of the story. We build a behavior dataset from 143 diverse literary works. For each source behavior, we generate counterfactual behaviors that are contextually plausible yet inconsistent with the character's persona. We find that existing models struggle to reliably infer character-consistent actions from historical behaviors and evolving character states. Using these behavior pairs, we train models with Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO), which augments DPO with a negative log-likelihood loss on the source behavior to jointly optimize behavior preference and generation. We further design a four-way next-behavior selection task to evaluate the model's ability to faithfully mimic character actions. Across 17,560 evaluation instances, the model trained on ACTOR's preference pairs achieves substantially improved accuracy. This result demonstrates that structured, temporally organized supervision enables models to leverage character profiles and prior behaviors to infer subsequent actions, greatly advancing literary role-playing beyond mere dialogue imitation. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ACTOR builds behaviour trajectories for literary role-playing agents from raw novels, using Thought-Action-Observation records ordered by story time. Models trained with Regularized Preference Optimization on its preference pairs substantially improve next-behaviour selection accuracy over 17,560 evaluation instances.
AI.motivation: Role-playing agents are usually built around dialogue, which leaves characters' non-dialogue behaviour and its evolution over story time underrepresented.
AI.method: ACTOR extracts dialogue and persona-relevant non-dialogue behaviours from 143 literary works and represents each as a Thought-Action-Observation structure, ordered by the story's internal temporal sequence. Counterfactual behaviours that are plausible in context but inconsistent with the persona are generated, and models are trained with Regularized Preference Optimization, which adds a negative log-likelihood term on the source behaviour to DPO. A four-way next-behaviour selection task evaluates the models.
AI.result: Across 17,560 evaluation instances, the model trained on ACTOR's preference pairs achieves substantially improved accuracy. The abstract gives no exact figures.
AI.conclusion: Structured, temporally organised supervision lets models use character profiles and prior behaviour to infer later actions, which moves role-play beyond dialogue imitation.

title: Written Once, Read Differently How Language Models Own Answers Steer Their Next Ones
summary: When a language model answers a yes/no question, that answer changes how it answers a different question about the same entity. We study this \emph{self-commitment} in 22 open-weight models from four families (0.5B--72B parameters), fixing the model's first answer and measuring the shift in its second across 3,600 question pairs about 120 entities. Each answer writes a \emph{commitment direction} into the residual stream. The similarity of two questions' directions predicts their coupling on held-out entities ($\rho = 0.43$--$0.85$), and ablating a single direction shared across topics leaves at most 17\% of the effect in every model. How this direction is read is far less stable: the reading circuit spreads across more attention heads as models grow, instruction tuning makes more questions read it in the opposite sense, and in one model changing only the system prompt reverses the circuit's sign. Ablating the direction while sparing the attention sink removes most of the coupling at under 1.3\% perplexity cost in 18 of 19 instruction-tuned models, though it shifts standalone answers in two. Without the sink spared, the direction's alignment with the leading principal component of ordinary text predicts which models pay a high cost. Written once, the commitment is read differently across scale, training and prompt.

AI.tldr: Across 22 open-weight models, a yes/no answer to one question shifts the answer to a related question about the same entity, and this coupling is carried by a single residual-stream direction. Ablating that direction removes most of the coupling in 18 of 19 instruction-tuned models at under 1.3% perplexity cost.
AI.motivation: Language models may carry commitments from their own earlier answers, and the authors ask how this self-commitment is written and read internally.
AI.method: The authors fix a model's first answer and measure the shift in its second answer over 3,600 question pairs about 120 entities. They test whether the similarity of two questions' commitment directions predicts coupling on held-out entities, ablate shared directions, and examine the attention heads that read the direction. Ablation is run with and without the attention sink spared.
AI.result: Direction similarity predicts coupling with rho between 0.43 and 0.85. Ablating a single shared direction leaves at most 17% of the effect in every model. Ablating the direction while sparing the attention sink removes most coupling at under 1.3% perplexity cost in 18 of 19 instruction-tuned models, though it shifts standalone answers in two. Reading is less stable, varying with scale, instruction tuning, and in one model with the system prompt.
AI.conclusion: A commitment is written once but read differently depending on scale, training, and prompt, so it cannot be treated as a single fixed mechanism.

title: Specificity Bias and the Wikipedia Paradox: An xAI Analysis of AI Text Detectors under Domain Shift
summary: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) demands reliable detection of human-authored versus synthetic text. However, current Transformer-based detectors often experience severe performance degradation during domain shifts and operate as opaque classifiers. This paper investigates the robustness and interpretability of fine-tuned Transformer models (DistilBERT, RoBERTa) by evaluating them against a custom out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset of hyper-local news synthesized via open-source LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma). To analyze model decision boundaries, we apply a tripartite Explainable AI (xAI) framework using SHAP. Our analysis reveals three key phenomena: First, detectors often rely on a "Call-to-Action" syndrome inherent to instruction-tuned LLMs rather than generic machine text. Second, we observe a "Specificity Bias," where LLMs successfully bypass detection by hallucinating specific named entities and mimicking conversational imperfection. Finally, we illustrate the "Wikipedia Paradox," wherein formal, objective human writing is frequently misclassified as AI due to its low statistical burstiness. These findings demonstrate that purely statistical detection paradigms face systematic limitations in highly structured human domains, emphasizing the critical need for semantically-aware, interpretable detection architectures.

AI.tldr: Transformer detectors of AI-generated local news, fine-tuned on DistilBERT and RoBERTa, degrade under domain shift and are analysed with SHAP. The authors report three failure patterns: reliance on call-to-action phrasing, a specificity bias that lets LLMs evade detection, and the Wikipedia Paradox, where formal human writing is flagged as AI.
AI.motivation: Current Transformer-based detectors degrade severely under domain shift and are opaque, so their robustness and interpretability need examination.
AI.method: Fine-tuned DistilBERT and RoBERTa detectors are tested on a custom out-of-distribution dataset of hyper-local news synthesised by Llama 3, Mistral, and Gemma. A tripartite explainable AI framework based on SHAP is used to analyse decision boundaries.
AI.result: The abstract reports three phenomena rather than numbers: detectors rely on a call-to-action syndrome typical of instruction-tuned LLMs, LLMs evade detection by hallucinating specific named entities and mimicking conversational imperfection (specificity bias), and formal human writing with low burstiness is misclassified as AI (Wikipedia Paradox).
AI.conclusion: Purely statistical detection has systematic limits in highly structured human domains, and semantically aware, interpretable detectors are needed.

title: MultiInpaintCOCO: Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in Multiple Languages
summary: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MultiInpaintCOCO extends the English InpaintCOCO fine-grained visual benchmark to 13 languages with 953 minimal-pair examples. Most models show a systematic bias toward English captions in cross-lingual retrieval, and Gemma 3 is the most English-biased while Qwen 3 is the least.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models struggle with fine-grained image details, and weaknesses in English are amplified in multilingual settings.
AI.method: The English InpaintCOCO dataset is extended to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating 953 minimal-pair examples. Several state-of-the-art models, including light CLIP-like encoders and large language models, are tested in multilingual multimodal retrieval.
AI.result: Performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, and data resource availability predicts performance better than typological similarity to English. Most models prefer the English caption when a correct non-English caption is compared with an incorrect English one. Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference, and Qwen 3 the least, despite similar monolingual accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual fine-grained visual understanding depends mainly on language resources, and cross-lingual retrieval carries architecture-dependent English bias.

title: Steering with Multilingual Lexicons for Sentiment Control in Low-Resource Languages
summary: Activation steering offers a lightweight mechanism for controlling model behavior, but existing methods depend on sentence-level contrastive data that is unavailable for most of the world's languages. We show that multilingual sentiment lexicons are a viable substitute across three model families: aggregated multilingual lexicons outperform English-derived steering vectors for mid- and low-resource languages, while monolingual lexicons remain stronger for languages a model has specialized in during pre-training. The steering efficacy is mechanistically dictated by both representational density and pre-training priors.
