Large-magnitude English vectors overwhelm the compact representations of low-resource languages, causing "linguistic collapse." This fragility is mitigated by the norm-dampening of multilingual aggregation. Architectural biases, including bilingual specialization penalty and latent numerical rigidity, also heavily constrain cross-lingual steering responsiveness. Ultimately, our work establishes lexicons as a practical steering signal and offers a comprehensive mechanistic account of cross-lingual steering dynamics.

AI.tldr: Multilingual sentiment lexicons serve as a practical substitute for sentence-level contrastive data when steering model activations for sentiment in low-resource languages. Aggregated multilingual lexicons outperform English-derived steering vectors for mid- and low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Activation steering needs sentence-level contrastive data, which is unavailable for most of the world's languages.
AI.method: Steering vectors are built from multilingual sentiment lexicons and tested across three model families, comparing aggregated multilingual lexicons, monolingual lexicons, and English-derived vectors.
AI.result: Aggregated multilingual lexicons outperform English-derived vectors for mid- and low-resource languages, while monolingual lexicons remain stronger for languages the model specialised in during pre-training. Large English vectors overwhelm the compact representations of low-resource languages, causing linguistic collapse, and multilingual norm-dampening mitigates this. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Lexicons are a practical steering signal, and the mechanistic account of cross-lingual steering is shaped by representational density, pre-training priors, and architectural biases.

title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?
summary: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (this https URL) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.

AI.tldr: IdeaTaste is a benchmark that scores LLMs by how closely their research proposals, written from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025, match what the same communities published in 2026. Six models reach only about 26% of human level on citation matching and 18% on idea matching.
AI.motivation: Research taste, the judgement of which problems and methods to pursue, shapes AI scientists' work but is much less understood than their ability to execute research.
AI.method: The benchmark spans six contemporary language models and four research areas, from established to emerging fields, with more than 90,000 proposals in total. Proposals are compared with the 2026 publications of the human communities in those areas, on cited literature and stated ideas. Blinded expert review is also conducted.
AI.result: LLM agents reach about 26% of human level on citation matching and 18% on idea matching. Richer field context and larger populations do not substantially close the gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success. Proposals whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst.
AI.conclusion: The main bottleneck in AI research taste is turning community directions into concrete approaches and research plans, rather than identifying the directions themselves.

title: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations
summary: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models.

AI.tldr: VIAS builds steering vectors that isolate individual organisational values by contrasting a prompt listing all values with one omitting a single target value. Combined with prompting, it lets Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-3.5-mini comply with all tagged values on 69.6%, 75.2%, and 72.6% of scenarios.
AI.motivation: Steering vectors built from fully compliant versus fully violating responses mostly capture a general compliance signal, which makes them hard to combine across several values.
AI.method: For each scenario, VIAS contrasts responses under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. A pair is kept only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. It is evaluated on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset tagged with a 21-value taxonomy.
AI.result: VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors. Combined with prompting, it complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models. Vectors alone do not give independent per-value control.
AI.conclusion: Value-isolating contrasts make steering vectors better suited to multi-value steering, and they are most useful when combined with prompting.

title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
summary: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.

AI.tldr: On a simulated enterprise text-to-SQL engagement, 15 models discover up to over 80% of withheld customer requirements, but only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria in delivery. The authors identify four bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether LLM coding agents can act as forward-deployed engineers who discover customer requirements and turn them into deployment decisions, as they can automate model post-training.
AI.method: A simulated customer, grounded in a real use case, starts with an ambiguous request. In the discovery phase the agent must find acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints. In the delivery phase it plans and executes a post-training recipe.
AI.result: The strongest model discovers over 80% of withheld requirements, and open-weight models discover 40-50%. Only 25% of delivery runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. The four bottlenecks are incomplete discovery (40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented), unreliable execution, underused compute budgets with few systematic comparisons, and benchmark accuracy that does not guarantee production readiness.
AI.conclusion: Suggested remedies are human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget, and production checks.

title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

AI.tldr: VeriHarm is a framework for building verifiable benchmarks of harmful success, where a coding agent completes a benign task yet causes unintended harm. Frontier agents average 95% task accuracy on VeriHarm-Bench but only 37% safe success.
AI.motivation: Coding agents with shell access can cause unintended harm while succeeding at a benign task, and conventional task-success metrics and safety evaluations do not measure this harmful success.
AI.method: VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behaviour while keeping the task benign and its objective intact. It then synthesises executable harm tests, which run alongside the original task-correctness tests to evaluate task accuracy and harmful outcomes together.
AI.result: Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, average 95% task accuracy on VeriHarm-Bench, but their safe success rate averages only 37%.
AI.conclusion: Successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, so task-success metrics alone may understate the safety risks of coding agents.

title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains
summary: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce NitiBench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 26 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it twenty of the 26 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.

AI.tldr: NitiBench+ is a temporal Thai legal QA benchmark of 1,670 items across 17 domains, graded against the law in force on the decision date. Reading the current text of amended law lowers the Bar-standard score by 0.25, and the best model scores 7.78 out of 10.
AI.motivation: Legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law, but courts decide cases under the law in force on the day, and many decisions cite law that has since changed.
AI.method: The authors checked 156,650 decisions from four Thai courts and found that up to 67% cite law since amended or repealed. Each cited section is stored with its text in force on the decision date and its current text, and the retrieval corpus holds every dated version. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric and on overlap between cited sections and the court's citations. Part I tests 13 open-weight models, and Part II ranks 26 models on a held-out test split of 500 items, in memory-only, court-sections-provided, and retrieval-agent settings.
AI.result: Reading current text of amended law lowers the Bar-standard score by 0.25, and missing repealed law lowers it by 0.79. The penalty is 0.45 on 428 rule-changed items and zero on 331 wording-only items, which Citation F1 does not capture. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool, only five open-weight models recall any Thai law. With search, twenty of the 26 models gain and six lose.
AI.conclusion: Legal benchmarks must track dates, and today's models still show a wide gap on Thai law when given the correct text.

title: ufakzeka-kulak: Building and Evaluating a 31.6M-Parameter Turkish Speech Recognizer from Scratch
comment: 9 pages (text on pages 1 to 8, references on pages 8 and 9). Model, card, attribution, code and demo: this https URL, this https URL, this https URL
summary: ufakzeka-kulak is an open Turkish speech-to-text model of 31.6M parameters, a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) and a CTC head, trained from scratch and released under Apache-2.0. It writes cased, punctuated Turkish with numbers as words. Its 4,977 training hours come from sources whose licences allow commercial use; 281 hours are human-transcribed, and for the other 4,696 the training text is an uploader subtitle or a machine transcript, kept only where a second, independent reading of the audio agrees with it. The recipe, checkpoint, labelling and export choices were made on development data, and the test sets were scored once, in a release gate fixed before training. With greedy TDT decoding the normalised word error rate (WER) is 0.0921 (95 percent interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both sets with paired intervals wholly below zero; Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. On conversational speech the WER is 0.3807. We also report punctuation and casing, degraded audio, and how closely each shipped export reproduces the trained model.

AI.tldr: ufakzeka-kulak is an open 31.6M-parameter Turkish speech recogniser, a FastConformer with TDT and CTC heads, trained from scratch on 4,977 hours under Apache-2.0. Its greedy TDT word error rate is 0.0921 on FLEURS Turkish and 0.0916 on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish, below Whisper base and Whisper small on both.
AI.motivation: The abstract frames the work as building a small, openly licensed Turkish speech-to-text model with training data whose licences allow commercial use.
AI.method: Training data includes 281 hours of human transcription and 4,696 hours whose text is an uploader subtitle or machine transcript, kept only where a second independent reading of the audio agrees. Recipe, checkpoint, labelling, and export choices were made on development data, and test sets were scored once under a release gate fixed before training.
AI.result: Normalised WER is 0.0921 (95% interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both, with paired intervals wholly below zero. Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. Conversational speech WER is 0.3807.
AI.conclusion: A small, openly licensed model can match or beat some larger Whisper variants on read Turkish speech, though it remains well behind on conversational speech and larger Whisper models are still better.

title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs is set by the monofact rate in training data, meaning the share of facts seen only once. In materials science and regulatory genomics, more monofacts yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families.
AI.motivation: It is unclear what enables reliable scientific discovery by LLMs and how that capacity traces back to training data.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical account in which monofacts set discovery capacity, then manipulate monofact rates in training sets in materials science and regulatory genomics. They test two open-weight model families across sampling strategies and reasoning budgets, and check whether training-set diversity alone explains the effect.
AI.result: More monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across both model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. The relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data.
AI.conclusion: Monofact rate in training data is a key factor governing discovery in language models.

title: Cultural Evolution Drives the Emergence of Conventions in Neural Emergent Communication
summary: Recent studies of language evolution with neural agents often use models where agents can either speak or listen, where there are only two agents in the population, or where agents can share internal representations. These choices prevent the study of how language emerges through cultural evolution, i.e. through the cumulative adaptation of individual behaviours to fit the communicative needs of the community. We tackle this issue with a new model that trains populations of bi-directional neural agents in a fully distributed fashion to solve a referential game. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple image datasets and show that it is able to scale to large populations. We also show that more conventional languages are easier to learn, providing a direct advantage for cultural transmission. Overall, this work provides a novel approach to neural emergent communication that opens up new directions for evolutionary linguistics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a fully distributed neural emergent communication model in which populations of bidirectional agents play a referential game, and shows that conventions emerge through cultural evolution. More conventional languages are also easier to learn, which gives them a transmission advantage.
AI.motivation: Many neural language evolution studies use agents that only speak or only listen, populations of two, or shared internal representations, which prevents the study of cumulative cultural evolution.
AI.method: The authors train populations of bidirectional neural agents in a fully distributed fashion to solve a referential game, evaluated on multiple image datasets and at large population sizes.
AI.result: The approach scales to large populations and works on multiple image datasets. The abstract reports no specific numbers. More conventional languages are shown to be easier to learn.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a new route to neural emergent communication and opens directions for evolutionary linguistics, with conventional languages gaining a direct transmission advantage.

title: "I Wrote, I Paused, I Rewrote": A Mixed-Methods Study of Learner Perceptions of Process-Aware LLM Feedback
summary: Large language models increasingly provide formative writing feedback, but most systems evaluate only the submitted text. Process-aware systems can additionally incorporate intermediate drafts and interaction records, yet access to these traces does not establish whether learners perceive the resulting feedback as useful, fair, or aligned with their own revision experience. We conducted a convergent mixed-method post-task evaluation with 43 undergraduate English-language learners. Participants completed a timed essay, received LLM-generated feedback based on the final essay, intermediate snapshots, and keystroke-derived records, and then answered six five-point Likert items and four open-ended questions. Ratings were concentrated above the neutral midpoint across all six items. Between 74.4% and 95.3% of participants selected ratings of 4 or 5, and all six one-sided exact sign tests remained significant after Holm correction. Perceived correspondence between the revision analysis and the participant's reported thought process was positively associated with overall perceived usefulness, Spearman's $\rho_s=.327$, 95% bootstrap CI $[.009,.609]$, $p=.032$, $n=43$. Qualitative responses were analysed through an LLM-assisted codebook development procedure followed by independent human coding of 14 binary codes. Participants frequently described the product feedback and revision rationale as accurate, while a smaller set reported misinterpretation of surface corrections, time constraints, or rhetorical intention. The findings distinguish perceived detection of revision activity from perceived interpretation of why revision occurred.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study with 43 undergraduate English learners finds that most rate process-aware LLM feedback, which uses drafts and keystroke records as well as the final essay, as useful and fair. Perceived correspondence with their own thought process predicts perceived usefulness (Spearman rho 0.327).
AI.motivation: Most LLM writing feedback evaluates only the submitted text. Access to drafts and interaction traces does not show whether learners perceive the resulting feedback as useful, fair, or aligned with their revision experience.
AI.method: A convergent mixed-method post-task evaluation used a timed essay, LLM feedback based on the final essay, intermediate snapshots, and keystroke-derived records, followed by six five-point Likert items and four open-ended questions. Qualitative answers were coded with an LLM-assisted codebook and independent human coding of 14 binary codes.
AI.result: Between 74.4% and 95.3% of participants rated each item 4 or 5, and all six one-sided exact sign tests stayed significant after Holm correction. Perceived correspondence between the revision analysis and the participant's thought process correlated with perceived usefulness, Spearman's rho 0.327, 95% bootstrap CI [0.009, 0.609], p=0.032, n=43. Participants often found the feedback and revision rationale accurate, while some reported misinterpreted surface corrections, time constraints, or misread rhetorical intent.
AI.conclusion: Learners distinguish between feedback that detects their revision activity and feedback that correctly interprets why the revision occurred.

title: ARTA: Graph Combinatorial Optimization for Robust Interbeat Interval Estimation from Wearable Electrocardiogram Signals
summary: Accurate heart rate (HR) and interbeat interval (IBI) estimation from wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) is essential for continuous physiological monitoring, but motion artifacts can create false QRS-like peaks and obscure true R-peaks. Conventional detectors and local interval-repair rules process detections independently and may become unreliable when several consecutive beats are corrupted. We present ARTA (Artifact-Robust Temporal Alignment), a graph-based combinatorial framework that estimates the heartbeat sequence through constrained temporal optimization. ARTA combines candidates from multiple ECG detectors, represents them as nodes in a directed acyclic graph and connects candidates through physiologically plausible RR intervals. Candidate confidence uses detector agreement and local ECG quality, while history-dependent transition costs capture recent IBI consistency and a soft heart-rate prior. Beam-search dynamic programming selects a coherent low-cost path across the recording, suppressing false detections and recovering missed beats when plausible auxiliary candidates are available. On the IEEE Signal Processing Cup exercise dataset with electrode-motion artifacts from -2 to 12 dB, ARTA achieved an HR mean absolute error of 1.79 beats per minute, 54% lower than the strongest single-detector baseline, with 92.38% of windows within +/-5 beats per minute, an R-peak F1 score of 0.95, and an IBI mean absolute error of 6.52 ms. Cross-dataset evaluation on the European ST-T Database further assessed transfer to long clinical ambulatory recordings and a label-free reliability analysis examined conditional performance without using reference annotations for segment selection. ARTA is single-channel, training-free, interpretable and computationally lightweight, operating approximately 27 times faster than real time with peak memory below 2.1 MB in a single-thread CPU simulation.

AI.tldr: ARTA estimates heartbeat sequences from wearable ECG by finding a coherent low-cost path through a graph of candidate beats, combining several detectors. On the IEEE Signal Processing Cup exercise dataset it reaches a heart-rate MAE of 1.79 bpm, 54% lower than the best single-detector baseline.
AI.motivation: Motion artefacts create false QRS-like peaks and hide true R-peaks, and conventional detectors and local interval-repair rules process beats independently, so they become unreliable when several consecutive beats are corrupted.
AI.method: ARTA combines candidates from multiple ECG detectors as nodes in a directed acyclic graph, linked by physiologically plausible RR intervals. Candidate confidence uses detector agreement and local signal quality, and transition costs reflect recent IBI consistency and a soft heart-rate prior. Beam-search dynamic programming selects the lowest-cost path.
AI.result: On the Cup exercise dataset with electrode-motion artefacts from -2 to 12 dB, ARTA achieves a heart-rate MAE of 1.79 bpm, 54% lower than the strongest single-detector baseline, with 92.38% of windows within ±5 bpm, an R-peak F1 of 0.95, and an IBI MAE of 6.52 ms. It also transfers to the European ST-T Database, and it runs about 27 times faster than real time with peak memory below 2.1 MB.
AI.conclusion: The method is single-channel, training-free, interpretable, and computationally light, and it suits continuous monitoring on constrained hardware.

title: Edge-Optimized YOLOv11n Architecture for Offline Recognition of Nigerian Sign Language Alphanumeric Gestures
summary: Deaf inclusion across sub-Saharan society faces regional hurdles, with Nigeria as the core empirical focus. Existing recognition models demand heavy computational infrastructure. However, standard mobile phones used locally rarely exceed 1 GB to 4 GB of RAM. This study addresses constraints through a lightweight YOLO11n object-detection framework. The system provides real-time Nigerian Sign Language recognition for low-resource hardware. A benchmark dataset containing 11,208 raw gesture images was established. The data spans 33 static classes collected from five signers. Partitioning isolates signers S1 through S3 for training. Signer S4 provides validation data. Signer S5 is reserved for testing. Spatial augmentations are restricted strictly to the training set. This yields 23,509 training images. The validation and test sets each maintain 1,681 images across varied environments. The framework integrates a quantization-aware compression objective. Loss functions merge with squared Frobenius-norm penalties to govern weight distortion. A Spatial-Density Occlusion Index quantifies background complexity and self-occlusion. A latency-profiling equation relates floating-point operations and memory bandwidth to chipset clock speed. Performance testing on physical Android hardware utilizes unquantized FP32 weights. Mean inference latencies span 405.5 ms to 1,759.4 ms. Measured against test data, the algorithm attains a Precision of 0.9975. Recall reaches 0.9991. Mean Average Precision is 0.9942. Outcomes support offline functionality on constrained mobile devices. Practical deployment operates through a mobile utility using CameraX. The application captures gestures in real time. Recognized signs display as text instantly.

AI.tldr: A lightweight YOLO11n detector recognises 33 static Nigerian Sign Language alphanumeric gestures offline on Android phones, with reported precision 0.9975, recall 0.9991, and mAP 0.9942 on the test signer. Mean inference latency ranges from 405.5 ms to 1,759.4 ms across devices.
AI.motivation: Existing sign recognition models need heavy computing infrastructure, while common mobile phones in Nigeria have limited RAM, so a low-resource offline system is needed.
AI.method: The benchmark has 11,208 raw gesture images from five signers, split by signer, with S1 to S3 for training, S4 for validation, and S5 for testing. Spatial augmentation is applied to the training set only, giving 23,509 training images. The framework adds a quantisation-aware compression objective with squared Frobenius-norm penalties, a Spatial-Density Occlusion Index, and a latency model. Inference runs on Android hardware with unquantised FP32 weights through a CameraX app.
AI.result: Precision 0.9975, recall 0.9991, and mAP 0.9942 on the test data. Mean inference latency spans 405.5 ms to 1,759.4 ms across the physical Android devices tested.
AI.conclusion: The results support offline recognition on constrained mobile devices, with a real-time app that displays recognised signs as text.

title: A Systematic Analysis of Live Intraoperative Surgical Expert Narrations
comment: Accepted as abstract at the SafeSurg Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Manual annotation remains the principal bottleneck in surgical video understanding. Live intraoperative narration by the operating surgeon is a scalable alternative that requires no manual annotation, but the information it contains has not been characterized. We analyzed 13 endoscopic lumbar spine decompression procedures (13.2 h) by two senior spine surgeons, using time-synchronized close-mic German audio. An annotation-free pipeline (word-level speech recognition, deterministic correction of surgical-term errors, utterance fusion, LLM-based translation to English, and relevance filtering) converted speech into time-stamped procedural cues labelled with the surgical entities they reference and their speech act. Of 3,171 utterances, 1,201 (37.9%) were retained as procedural cues, while 57.6% were non-procedural and removed. Retained cues referenced instruments (60.7%), anatomy (48.0%) and surgical actions (57.1%), and 98.5% carried at least one of these. 39% of cues (472 of 1,201) were directives, mainly instrument requests and commands. All 467 manually verified instrument requests preceded the instrument's appearance in the field, by a median of 8.2 s. Domain-term transcription corruption affected 18.0% of retained cues. Live narration is thus a dense, annotation-free supervisory signal describing instruments, anatomy, actions and team coordination, but it is noisy and temporally displaced from the events it names, and this displacement must be modelled before safe downstream use.

AI.tldr: The study analyses live narration by operating surgeons during 13 endoscopic lumbar decompression procedures and shows that 37.9% of utterances are procedural cues. Instrument requests precede the instrument's appearance by a median of 8.2 s, so the signal is useful but must be time-corrected before use.
AI.motivation: Manual annotation is the main bottleneck in surgical video understanding, and live surgeon narration could supply annotation-free supervision, but its content had not been characterised.
AI.method: Two senior spine surgeons' German audio, time-synchronised with close microphones, from 13 procedures totalling 13.2 h was processed by an annotation-free pipeline: word-level speech recognition, deterministic correction of surgical terms, utterance fusion, LLM translation into English, and relevance filtering. Retained cues were labelled with the surgical entities they reference and their speech act.
AI.result: Of 3,171 utterances, 1,201 (37.9%) were retained as procedural cues. Cues referenced instruments (60.7%), anatomy (48.0%), and surgical actions (57.1%), and 98.5% carried at least one of these. 39% were directives, mainly instrument requests and commands. All 467 manually verified instrument requests preceded the instrument's appearance, by a median of 8.2 s. Term transcription corruption affected 18.0% of retained cues.
AI.conclusion: Live narration is a dense, annotation-free signal about instruments, anatomy, actions, and team coordination, but it is noisy and offset in time from the events it names, and that offset must be modelled before safe downstream use.

title: When frequency domain classification is superior to spatial
summary: Modern image classification models largely rely on local characteristics and feature extraction for their predictions. This focused approach works well in the spatial domain, but reportedly falls short in the frequency domain, even though both representations contain the same information. This study demonstrates that the significant reduction in accuracy in the frequency domain stems from the lack of local features. Locally swapping data in the frequency domain significantly decreases its inverse spatial domain accuracy, even below that of the frequency domain; however, the frequency domain accuracy remains relatively constant. Moreover, the use of datasets containing global features in the spatial domain yields higher accuracy in the frequency domain. Using these results, a hybrid model is constructed, combining one model trained only in the frequency domain and another trained only in the spatial domain to achieve higher classification accuracy. The proposed visual geometry group (VGG) and vision transformer (ViT) architectures are trained on the ImageNet-100, WikiArt, DTD, FMD, PSVRT, and KTH-TIPS2-b datasets and evaluated.

AI.tldr: Image classifiers do worse in the frequency domain mainly because they lack local features, and a hybrid of a frequency-only and a spatial-only model improves accuracy. The study uses VGG and ViT on six datasets, including ImageNet-100 and WikiArt.
AI.motivation: Frequency-domain classification is reportedly much less accurate than spatial-domain classification, even though both representations hold the same information, and the cause was unclear.
AI.method: The authors locally swap data in the frequency domain to test how much local features matter, and train on datasets with global features in the spatial domain to test cross-domain accuracy. A hybrid model combines a frequency-only and a spatial-only model. VGG and ViT architectures are trained on ImageNet-100, WikiArt, DTD, FMD, PSVRT, and KTH-TIPS2-b.
AI.result: Local swapping in the frequency domain significantly reduces inverse spatial-domain accuracy, even below frequency-domain accuracy, which stays relatively constant. Datasets with global spatial features give higher frequency-domain accuracy. The hybrid model is reported to achieve higher accuracy. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-domain accuracy gap comes from missing local features, and combining the two domains can improve classification.

title: From Zero to OCR: A Data-Centric Framework for Unsupported Low-Resource Scripts
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Model: this https URL
summary: Optical character recognition (OCR) remains inaccessible to many low-resource scripts because annotated document images are unavailable and synthetic training data can fail to preserve script-specific visual structure. We present a data-centric framework that builds end-to-end OCR for such scripts from only an unannotated text corpus and digital fonts, without manually annotating a single training image. A synthetic data engine renders word, line and page images with correct complex-script shaping and automatically derived labels; a YOLOv8 word detector and a convolutional recurrent recognizer trained with connectionist temporal classification learn from these images; and a stage-gate evaluation protocol isolates recognition error before detection is introduced. We demonstrate the framework on Kashmiri, a Perso-Arabic Nastaliq script with approximately 6.8 million speakers that none of six widely used OCR engines supports. Three line-level recognizers, including one transferred from Arabic, stalled between 41% and 79% character error rate (CER), motivating a word-level formulation; subsequent improvements came primarily from rendering fidelity, diacritic-preserving crop margins and tuned non-maximum suppression. The resulting system achieves 0.39% CER on held-out words, 10.0% on synthetic pages and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages, and establishes reference results of 18.45% on typeset book pages and 49.8% on degraded historical documents. We publicly release the trained models, the inference code and a synthetic dataset of 285,864 Kashmiri text-line images, and we describe a step-by-step procedure for building OCR for other unsupported scripts.

AI.tldr: A data-centric framework builds end-to-end OCR for Kashmiri, a low-resource Perso-Arabic script, from an unannotated text corpus and digital fonts alone. The system reaches 0.39% CER on held-out words and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages.
AI.motivation: OCR is unavailable for many low-resource scripts because annotated document images are missing and synthetic data often fails to preserve script-specific visual structure. None of six widely used OCR engines supports Kashmiri, which has about 6.8 million speakers.
AI.method: A synthetic data engine renders word, line, and page images with correct complex-script shaping and automatically derived labels. A YOLOv8 word detector and a CRNN recogniser trained with CTC learn from these images. A stage-gate protocol isolates recognition error before detection is added. Line-level recognisers stalled at 41% to 79% CER, so a word-level formulation was adopted, and gains came mainly from rendering fidelity, diacritic-preserving crop margins, and tuned non-maximum suppression.
AI.result: The system achieves 0.39% CER on held-out words, 10.0% on synthetic pages, and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages, with reference results of 18.45% on typeset book pages and 49.8% on degraded historical documents. A synthetic dataset of 285,864 text-line images and the models are released.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a step-by-step procedure that the authors suggest can be used to build OCR for other unsupported scripts.

title: HistGramBench: Measuring Structural Recovery When Multimodal Models Redraw Historical Mathematical Diagrams as TikZ
comment: 34 pages, 8 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL ; data: this https URL
summary: Digital libraries preserve mathematical books printed from the sixteenth to the twentieth century, but the lettered diagrams in them, the figures on which Euclidean proofs depend, remain scanned images whose content cannot be searched. Redrawing such a diagram as a short drawing program would record which points lie on which lines and circles. But a printed plate offers no source code against which the redrawing could be checked. We introduce HistGramBench, a benchmark of 2,507 diagrams from 95 works printed between 1551 and 1933 in eight languages. For each diagram, two AI models from different providers agree on the facts a reader takes from the figure, such as which lines are parallel or where two lines meet, and every redrawing is checked against those facts on the model's own drawing. We evaluate six affordable AI models. The best recovers about three fifths of these facts, and most of what the models miss comes from programs that never produce a drawing. Parallels and tangencies are the hardest relations to reproduce. HistGramBench gives historians and librarians a way to measure when such tools can make old mathematical diagrams searchable.

AI.tldr: HistGramBench measures whether multimodal models can redraw historical mathematical diagrams as TikZ programs that preserve the geometric facts a reader takes from them. The best of six affordable models recovers about three fifths of these facts.
AI.motivation: Scanned diagrams in digitised mathematical books cannot be searched, and redrawing them as drawing programs would record their geometry, but printed plates provide no source code to check against.
AI.method: The benchmark has 2,507 diagrams from 95 works printed between 1551 and 1933 in eight languages. For each diagram, two AI models from different providers agree on the geometric facts a reader takes from it, such as parallel lines or intersections, and each redrawing is checked against those facts.
AI.result: The best of six affordable models recovers about three fifths of the facts. Most of what the models miss comes from programs that never produce a drawing. Parallels and tangencies are the hardest relations to reproduce.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark lets historians and librarians measure when such tools can make old mathematical diagrams searchable.

title: Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots
summary: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.

AI.tldr: The Teach-Abstract-Apply framework lets operators teach cobots workflows in natural language, abstract them into reusable skills, and apply them in new settings. In a structure-building case study, skill abstraction improves task success and reduces interaction cost for Qwen3-Coder and GPT5.2-Codex.
AI.motivation: Cobots share workspaces with humans and handle repetitive shop-floor tasks, but workflows change with production, so workers need intuitive ways to modify and generalise them.
AI.method: TAA has three stages: teaching new workflows to cobots in natural language, abstracting the taught workflows into skills, and applying those skills in different settings. It is applied to a collaborative structure-building task and tested with open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations, with a preliminary human-in-the-loop study.
AI.result: Skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. A preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests the pipeline also works with human instructions. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Natural-language teaching followed by skill abstraction is a feasible route to adaptable cobot workflows, though the human study is preliminary.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
comment: First two authors contributed equally. Project Page: this https URL
summary: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.

AI.tldr: ParallACT is a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks in shared repositories, and parallel agents perform far worse than a single-agent oracle, especially on contradictory tasks. Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8 falls from 62% to 16% on contradictory tasks.
AI.motivation: Coding agents working in shared repositories on independent requests can produce implementations that conflict when merged, and this multi-agent setting has not been studied in a controlled way.
AI.method: ParallACT contains complementary tasks, which need a shared interface to combine, and contradictory pairs, which edit the same code in incompatible ways. The authors compare a single-agent oracle given all tasks with multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel.
AI.result: The oracle solves most tasks, while parallel agents perform substantially worse, with a notable drop on complementary tasks and a sharp drop on contradictory tasks (62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8). The same gap appears in six further configurations pairing two harnesses with three open-weight models. Telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance at extra token cost.
AI.conclusion: Coordination is a core challenge that will grow as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and ParallACT provides a controlled test of which strategies help and at what cost.

title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
summary: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.

AI.tldr: SAC-Bench tests how audio-language models respond when a spoken claim contradicts the acoustic evidence in the same recording. Event identity accuracy is 24.8 to 46.5 percentage points lower under conflict than under compatible claims.
AI.motivation: Audio-language models are evaluated on speech and environmental sounds, but how they behave when speech contradicts the sound itself is underexplored.
AI.method: SAC-Bench has 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. Environmental recordings are paired with compatible or contradictory synthesised spoken claims, with audio-only controls where applicable. Five open-weight models are evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, and Spatial-Omni is studied as a spatial case.
AI.result: High audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims, and Event Identity accuracy is 24.8 to 46.5 percentage points lower in conflict conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the full event sequence. The spatial case study finds lower motion accuracy linked to spoken claims and to the speech source's trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects, showing that these are distinct properties of audio-language models.
